title: CYTOKINETIC BOTTLENECKS OF HEAT WAVES
title_norm: cytokinetic bottlenecks of heat waves
abstract_text: Plant cytokinesis requires phragmoplast expansion through coordinated microtubules and vesicles, and understanding its cellular response to high temperature stress across species is essential because elevated heat induces cytokinetic arrest and alters gene expression. This project will predict genetic bottlenecks under high temperature stress by reanalyzing single cell and whole organ omics data to construct and compare multi layered network models using orthology inference, differential gene expression, and multiplex network construction. Public transcriptomic, translatomic, and proteomic data from species including Zea mays and Arabidopsis thaliana will be integrated by creating single layer networks and linking these into a unified multiplex model. The identified cytokinetic bottlenecks will provide foundational knowledge for cellular heat adaptation theories and yield novel genetic markers to engineer heat resilient agricultural and landscaping plants.
full_text: This project investigates plant cytokinesis under high temperature stress to uncover molecular mechanisms and genetic factors governing cellular resilience. Heat arrests phragmoplast expansion in susceptible plants while resilient species maintain division despite undefined protein networks governing this process. The proposed study compares molecular changes between susceptible and tolerant species to predict genetic bottlenecks for engineering resilient plants. The study standardizes available single cell and whole organ omics data to construct and compare multilayered cytokinetic network models. Researchers will apply orthology inference and trajectory analysis alongside evaluations of differential gene expression to construct multiplex network models. Validation requires filtering transcripts present in fewer than half the datasets and benchmarking candidates against known mitotic target genes. Datasets include available transcriptomic and proteomic records from single cells and whole organs of species such as Arabidopsis thaliana. The team will integrate datasets by generating individual networks for each omics type before linking them into one model. The project mitigates variations from disparate growth conditions by applying a standardized reprocessing pipeline across a large data volume. The project spans two years with the submission of a primary manuscript scheduled for the end of this period. Cross disciplinary collaboration merges biological expertise in plant cytokinesis with the technical capabilities of a synthesis center for analysis. The team will disseminate findings through a primary research manuscript and a published review article for the scientific community. The research team includes domain experts in plant physiology and protein biochemistry alongside a bioinformatics scientist and an assistant.

abstract_original: The lack of motility makes plants highly vulnerable to environmental anomalies such as periods of extreme high temperature known as heat waves. Plants can search for better habitats by exploiting seed mobility, which relies on completing the life cycle and producing seeds. Formation of reproductive organs and seed development requires the production of cells through cell division. The last stage of cell division, cytokinesis, encompasses many key cellular processes, including vesicle trafficking, cell wall biosynthesis, cytoskeletal dynamics, and signaling. While cytokinesis is highly sensitive to heat stress in plants adapted to temperate climates, cytokinesis is more resilient in species adapted to tropical zones. However, how heat stress affects cytokinesis and the mechanisms of cytokinetic robustness across different plant species remains unknown. This project aims to compare changes in cytokinetic components under heat stress in susceptible and hardy species to characterize differential responses of genetic circuits responsible for specific cellular events during cytokinesis. The long term goal is to harness this data for identifying the bottlenecks of cytokinetic robustness. The experimental approach here will be systematic analysis of publicly available data from single-cell and whole-organ omics data collected under control and high-temperature conditions including transcriptomics, translatomics, and proteomics. Predicting cytokinetic bottlenecks will inform future experimental design for their functional characterization leading to better understanding of cellular adaptation mechanisms to heat stress. This knowledge may provide insight into evolutionary strategies of plant adaptation to different climates and improve predictions for heat resiliency at the level of individual plants and populations.

title: Transposable elements and the emergence of genomic innovation
title_norm: transposable elements and the emergence of genomic innovation
abstract_text: Within vertebrate evolutionary and regulatory genomics, transposable elements constitute nearly half of the human genome and critically generate functional regions like transcription factor binding sites to influence regulatory networks and phenotypic diversification. Precise functional characterization of these repetitive regions remains incomplete because standard analysis pipelines routinely discard short sequencing reads that map to multiple locations. To determine how transposable elements form novel transcripts, protein coding sequences, and cell specific enhancers, this project will reprocess data through repeat aware pipelines by aligning sequences to complete pangenome assemblies and utilizing probabilistic allocation tools. The research will integrate over 75,000 public functional genomic datasets from major consortia by intersecting signals with repeat annotations, modeling statistical associations, and applying tensor decomposition to link different data modalities. This approach will generate a systematic detection framework for functional elements within repetitive DNA, significantly advancing the understanding of how transposable elements drive evolutionary diversification across species.
full_text: This project in vertebrate regulatory genomics explores transposable elements because standard analysis pipelines discard reads from repetitive regions. Transposable elements originate half of the human genome and create regulatory elements while their functional characterization remains incomplete. This project determines how transposable elements form new regulatory sequences by utilizing probabilistic read allocation on previously discarded data. The two phase study design uses repeat aware pipelines and integrates data computationally to identify functional transposable elements. The team aligns reads to pangenome assemblies and applies hidden Markov models and tensor decomposition to analyze genomic dependencies. The project validates these results by assessing sequence conservation across species with the use of multi species alignments. The study analyzes numerous public genomic datasets like RNA-seq and ChIP-seq from the ENCODE and GTEx and FAANG consortia. The team integrates these datasets by intersecting functional genomic signals with RepeatMasker annotations and applying tensor decomposition techniques. The limitation of mapping short sequencing reads ambiguously is addressed by aligning data to pangenome assemblies with probabilistic allocation. The two year project dedicates the first year to data reprocessing and the second year to final integrated analyses. This massive scope requires collaboration because processing numerous genomic datasets exceeds single laboratory capabilities and necessitates cross disciplinary expertise. The team publicly releases a repository of reprocessed genomic datasets alongside reproducible analysis pipelines and empirical research publications. The cross disciplinary team includes computational staff scientists and researchers from multiple laboratories specializing in evolutionary and regulatory genomics.

abstract_original: Our working group aims to comprehensively investigate how transposable elements (TEs) contribute to genomic innovation and species diversification in vertebrates through the generation of novel functional elements. While TEs comprise nearly half of the human genome and are increasingly recognized as sources of regulatory innovation, their repetitive nature has complicated their analysis using short-read sequencing technologies. We propose a two-phase approach: First, we will reprocess tens of thousands of publicly available genomic datasets (including ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, RNA-seq, and Ribo-seq) using repeat-aware analysis pipelines and new telomere-to-telomere and pangenome assemblies. Second, we will synthesize this reprocessed data to understand how TEs generate new transcription factor binding sites, cell-specific and species-specific enhancers, novel transcripts, and protein-coding sequences. The project combines multidisciplinary expertise from multiple labs and will leverage advanced computational approaches to uncover complex relationships between TEs and regulatory networks. Our investigation represents a quintessential mesoscale emergence phenomenon, bridging molecular-level TE insertions with emergent regulatory networks and phenotypic innovations. The project will produce both a comprehensive public data resource of repeat-aware genomic analyses and new insights into how TEs drive biological innovation through regulatory network evolution.

title: Searching the crosslinking mass spectrometry universe for new protein-protein interactions
title_norm: searching the crosslinking mass spectrometry universe for new proteinprotein interactions
abstract_text: Structural proteomics utilizes crosslinking mass spectrometry and machine learning to map specific interacting residues within physical protein protein interactions, providing critical spatial information necessary to define large protein complexes. Existing proteome wide interaction maps lack physical evidence of specific interacting residues, while historical search algorithms and fragmented repository structures make current crosslinking data difficult to reuse. This project will standardize and reanalyze public crosslinking mass spectrometry data using the Scout algorithm and map the discovered interactions to AlphaFold structural models to create a catalog of validated protein protein interactions. The project will integrate legacy human and yeast PRIDE repository datasets with the huMAP3.0 network, populating a centralized repository and incorporating verified interaction mappings into the EBI Complex Portal. This comprehensive structural catalog will provide direct physical evidence for predicted protein complexes, improve public dataset usability, and generate functional hypotheses for uncharacterized proteins.
full_text: The structural proteomics domain studies physical interactions between proteins but lacks standardized data to map specific interacting residues. Current models identify broad networks but limited algorithms and structures of repositories keep data for specific residues highly fragmented. The study standardizes data from mass spectrometry to build a structural catalog and provide physical evidence for predicted complexes. The study design filters public experiments and applies standardized metadata to infer functions of unannotated proteins from networks. The project utilizes the Scout algorithm for data reprocessing and applies AlphaFold to generate models of protein structures. The analytical approach validates detected interactions against huMAP predictions and assesses spatial proximity using structural models from AlphaFold. The project analyzes legacy crosslinking datasets of human and yeast samples from the PRIDE repository alongside huMAP3.0 networks. The integration plan populates a centralized repository with reprocessed data and incorporates verified mappings into the EBI Complex Portal. The study mitigates historical limitations of inconsistent parameters by applying uniform metadata standards and modern algorithms to files. A fifteen month timeline dedicates six months to curation of datasets and six months to validation before result dissemination. The project scope requires integration of internal mass spectrometry expertise with external infrastructure for repositories and database engineering capabilities. The team deposits reanalyzed datasets into a PRIDE database and shares verified structures through the EBI Complex Portal. The team includes structural biology experts and database engineers alongside data scientists who execute curation and computational tasks.

abstract_original: Crosslinking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) is a powerful structural proteomics method that can provide high-resolution structural information about complex mixtures of proteins in their native physiological context.1,2,3 The method works by chemically crosslinking two reactive amino acid residues that are close to one another in 3-D space, thereby freezing this spatial information into a covalent bond, and then retrieving this information by sequencing crosslinked peptides following enzymatic digest of the constituent proteins (like Hi-C,4 but for proteins). Initially developed in the 2000s to interrogate purified proteins, by the late-2010s, methods became available to interrogate protein-protein interactions (PPIs) on the proteome-scale and in the cellular environment.5 This project seeks to standardize, combine, and integrate existing publicly available crosslinking datasets from PRIDE to make these data more re-usable and useful for integrative and hybrid modeling. We will also create a meta-dataset to catalogue PPIs in human and other model organisms. Because XL-MS encodes information about both protein identity and interacting residues, these findings can be cross-validated to structural predictions of protein complexes using AlphaFold3, thereby providing stronger evidence for their existence compared to huMAP3.0, which predicts protein complexes without structural evidence. We will integrate these findings into the EBI Complex Portal to make it accessible to the life science community.

title: Intelligent metadata compilation to enhance the reusability and discoverability of mass spectrometry-based proteomics data
title_norm: intelligent metadata compilation to enhance the reusability and discoverability of mass spectrometrybased proteomics data
abstract_text: Mass spectrometry based proteomics emphasizes the extraction and harmonization of experimental metadata for bottom up discovery workflows, utilizing frameworks like the SDRF Proteomics format to specify sample relationships. Despite these frameworks, widespread inconsistent annotation persists across existing datasets, yielding incomplete or unstructured metadata that currently limits the discoverability and reusability of proteomics data in public repositories. This project will develop automated workflows to extract metadata from raw mass spectrometry files and scientific publications, utilizing open modification searching, fine tuned large language models, and Nextflow automation to harmonize unstructured information. Extracted metadata will be harmonized via controlled vocabularies into the SDRF Proteomics standard and linked directly to datasets in the PRIDE repository and ProteomicsML tutorial databases for web interface querying. This automated metadata enhancement framework will allow researchers to systematically query repositories for large scale reanalyses and artificial intelligence training, establishing a scalable paradigm for other omics disciplines.
full_text: This project investigates integration of metadata within proteomics utilizing mass spectrometry to resolve limited discoverability of public datasets. Researchers utilize annotation frameworks like SDRF-Proteomics to specify relationships between samples and assays but widespread inconsistent annotation persists. This study develops automated workflows for extraction of metadata to enable systematic queries of repositories for large scale reanalyses. The overall design involves developing automated pipelines for extraction of raw data and crowdsourcing algorithms through a machine learning challenge. Key methods apply tools like Param-Medic for extraction of raw data and fine tuned language models for mining of text. The team evaluates precision of results against a gold standard of publicly curated datasets and a private test set. The project utilizes the PRIDE repository and ProteomicsML alongside curated sets of public datasets that contain SDRF-Proteomics metadata. The team harmonizes the metadata using controlled vocabularies and links this information directly to datasets in the PRIDE database. To mitigate limitations in accuracy of extraction the natural language processing models explicitly indicate when specific elements remain unavailable. The two year timeline dedicates the first year to compilation of metadata and the second year to generation of retrospective data. The project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to merge specialized expertise in bioinformatics and machine learning across multiple research entities. The team releases code on GitHub and shares tutorial datasets via ProteomicsML to ensure open access for researchers. The group includes specialists in bioinformatics and machine learning who provide training in team science for data scientists.

abstract_original: Mass spectrometry-based proteomics generates vast amounts of data, yet the effective reuse and discovery of these datasets remain challenging due to incomplete and inconsistent metadata. Metadata, which provides critical contextual information such as experimental conditions, sample characteristics, and data processing details, is essential for making data FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable). To address these challenges, our working group aims to develop intelligent, automated workflows for comprehensive metadata extraction, harmonization, and integration into PRIDE, the largest public proteomics data repository. We will develop powerful bioinformatics and natural language processing tools to extract metadata directly from raw mass spectrometry files and scientific publications. By leveraging structured data standards, metadata will be enriched with controlled vocabulary terms, enhancing dataset transparency and usability. Community engagement through a machine-learning challenge will further drive innovation in metadata extraction techniques. The outcomes of the working group's activities will include automated metadata compilation workflows integrated into user-friendly tools, advanced dataset querying capabilities in PRIDE, and the creation of educational resources for the scientific community. These efforts will enable researchers to efficiently locate and reuse proteomics datasets, facilitating secondary analyses such as AI model training and large-scale reanalysis.

title: Elucidating genome structure-function relationships in human brain cells
title_norm: elucidating genome structurefunction relationships in human brain cells
abstract_text: Single cell genomics and epigenetics characterize the relationship between three dimensional chromatin organization, chromatin accessibility, and gene expression, a phenomenon that drives distinct cellular identities in the human brain. Independent analysis of isolated modalities fails to capture causal relationships, leaving the functional role of three dimensional chromatin organization in gene regulation and Alzheimer disease pathology unresolved. This project will develop a multimodal generative AI model utilizing contrastive learning, cross attention layers, and tensor decomposition to determine how genomic architecture regulates cell type specific gene expression and influences Alzheimer disease progression. The study will integrate single cell RNA seq and single cell Hi C datasets from human brain tissues by mapping cells to consensus identities and aligning structural embeddings with scGPT gene expression data. This framework will directly link three dimensional structural changes to gene expression at the single cell level to identify specific epigenetic drivers of neurodegenerative disease.
full_text: The domain of single cell genomics studies chromatin organization but its role in the progression of Alzheimer's disease remains unresolved. This project develops a generative model to link chromatin structure with gene expression and identify drivers of Alzheimer's disease. The study uses contrastive learning to align datasets of single cells and predicts gene expression through fine tuning procedures. Key algorithms include vision transformers and tensor decomposition alongside language models to predict expression from structural embeddings of chromatin. Researchers validate predictive accuracy by benchmarking the multimodal framework against unimodal models that evaluate sequences of DNA in isolation. The project utilizes RNA-seq databases of single cells and bulk ATAC-seq data from human brain tissue and mouse cells. The team integrates distinct datasets by mapping individual cells to a consensus list of types using cross attention mechanisms. The team mitigates the lack of concurrent human measurements by imputing missing modalities through the decomposition of data tensors. Proposed milestones involve the development of two separate computational tools and the subsequent production of two distinct scientific manuscripts. This complex scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to merge bioinformatics methods with the accurate interpretation of results from neurobiology studies. The investigators will disseminate their scientific findings through the planned release of two computational tools and two academic manuscripts. The research team includes a requested staff scientist alongside experts in bioinformatics and deep learning from the NCEMS center.

abstract_original: Single-cell analysis has profoundly enhanced our understanding of brain tissue by facilitating the examination of gene expression and epigenetic features. However, investigating these modalities independently offers a fragmented view of gene regulation and its relationship to transcriptional activity. To overcome this limitation, we propose developing a multimodal generative AI model that integrates single-cell genomics datasets. This framework seeks to illuminate the interplay between three-dimensional genomic architecture and gene expression, uncovering the physical principles underlying the emergence of cell-type-specific gene expression programs, despite the inherent stochasticity of gene regulation at the single-cell level. Applied to datasets from Alzheimer's patients, this approach has the potential to identify epigenetic drivers of disease progression, thereby contributing to a deeper understanding of neurodegenerative processes.

title: MaiTool - LLM-powered bioinformatics tools for microbiome analysis
title_norm: maitool  llmpowered bioinformatics tools for microbiome analysis
abstract_text: The research domain of computational biology increasingly relies on large language models to extract information from scientific literature and locate dataset repositories for microbiome and ancient DNA sequencing data. However, current large language models lack the capacity to directly analyze bioinformatics datasets, execute computational workflows, or perform direct computational analysis on the underlying data. This project will develop MaiTool, a graphical interface linking fine tuned large language models like BioGPT and GeneGPT with taxonomic profiling pipelines to enable literature exploration, data extraction, and dynamic data analysis using REST APIs. The system will integrate databases including MGnify, the Human Microbiome Project, and the NCBI Sequence Read Archive by constructing a unified API that retrieves sample accessions, metadata, and raw data. This research will produce a novel framework connecting natural language processing with direct computational analysis, allowing automated execution of bioinformatics tasks and quality control from text based literature queries.
full_text: This computational biology project studies sequencing data from microbiomes and ancient DNA but large language models cannot directly analyze them. Current large language models locate data repositories and extract text from literature but lack capacity for direct computational analysis. This novel research asks how the MaiTool interface can automate bioinformatics tasks by connecting natural language processing with computational analysis. The study design involves evaluating language models and public databases to construct a unified application programming interface (API) and graphical interface. The analytical strategy applies BioGPT and BioMedLM and GeneGPT models alongside pipelines for taxonomic profiling and Java software development. The team will validate results through system testing and formal usability studies and sequential software releases to gather user feedback. The proposed study will utilize databases including MGnify and MG-RAST alongside the Human Microbiome Project and the NCBI Sequence Read Archive. The project integrates these datasets by constructing a unified API to retrieve sample accessions and raw data from repositories. The team will mitigate known issues regarding the reliability of datasets by embedding quality control measures within the bioinformatics pipeline. Milestones span two years from evaluating models and developing interfaces to conducting system testing and releasing the public software. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to integrate expertise regarding algorithms for metagenomics and processing of multimodal omics data. The team will publicly release the fully functional software system and publish the final system capabilities in scientific literature. The group includes experts in ancient DNA and molecular epidemiology alongside a language model scientist offering team science training.

These models have applications in microbiome research, where they can assist in identifying datasets in repositories like MGnify and MG-RAST. However, LLMs lack the ability to directly analyze datasets, necessitating integration with bioinformatics tools to enable robust computational analysis. This project aims to develop MaiTool, a graphical interface that combines LLM capabilities with bioinformatics workflows for microbiome and ancient DNA research. MaiTool will enable users to explore publications, access public datasets via APIs, and perform dynamic analyses, integrating quality control measures to enhance reliability. Existing GPT systems (e.g., BioGPT, BioMedLM, and GeneGPT) will be evaluated and fine-tuned for microbiome applications. We will assess repositories such as HMP, IMG/M, and SRA for their suitability and develop APIs for seamless data access and integration. By addressing queries such as studies involving specific taxa, MaiTool will allow LLMs to retrieve literature while bioinformatics pipelines analyze and visualize dataset profiles. This approach aims to advance interdisciplinary research workflows and establish a new standard for AI-driven bioinformatics.

title: Synthesizing gene expression data to create an atlas of bacterial cell states
title_norm: synthesizing gene expression data to create an atlas of bacterial cell states
abstract_text: Bacterial transcriptomics investigates global gene expression patterns that define distinct cell states, providing critical insights into how bacteria alter their physiology in response to environmental changes. This project will create a comprehensive reference map of bacterial cell states by applying the InGEST pipeline, unsupervised clustering, dimensionality reduction, and supervised machine learning to aggregated bulk microarray and sequencing datasets. Public repository data from OKgeneExpDB, E. coli Expression 2, Ecomics, PRECISE, COLUMBOS, and iModulonDB will be integrated through standardized filtering, mathematical batch effect adjustment, and ortholog mapping to align genomic features. The resulting reference map and predictive algorithm will systematically identify transcriptomic states, establishing a foundational resource for discovering uncharacterized biological phases and informing targeted bacterial reprogramming.
full_text: This project in bacterial transcriptomics investigates whether global gene expression patterns form discrete states or a continuous physiological spectrum. Bacteria alter gene expression to enter different physiological phases but technical variations force researchers to analyze transcriptomic datasets in isolation. The proposed study creates a comprehensive reference map of transcriptomic states to discover uncharacterized phases and inform targeted bacterial reprogramming. The study aggregates bulk microarray and sequencing datasets from multiple species to map distinct cellular states using unsupervised learning. The analytical approach utilizes a custom pipeline called InGEST alongside dimensionality reduction algorithms and ortholog mapping via Orthofinder. The team will validate classification models using synthetic data mixtures and benchmark them against empirical sequencing data from single cells. The proposed study utilizes public microarray and sequencing repositories such as OKgeneExpDB and PRECISE alongside COLUMBOS and iModulonDB. A custom pipeline merges datasets to apply standardized filtering while mathematical adjustments correct batch effects from varying sequencing protocols. The team addresses limited data from single cells and batch effects by applying bias correction algorithms to pure bulk samples. The two year timeline dedicates the first year to pipeline development and the second year to completing reference maps. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to provide specialized expertise in the synthesis of large scale data and computational analytics. The researchers will release the pipeline for data processing as open source software with containerized deployment options and user documentation. All compiled expression matrices and resulting reference maps will be hosted on public repositories as completely versioned digital resources.

abstract_original: Bacterial cells have evolved to adapt their molecular composition to maximize growth and survival. Our current knowledge of bacterial cell states is fragmented. Researchers often only analyze data they generate themselves—usually for just one strain under a limited number of conditions—because it is difficult to harmonize omics datasets collected with different technologies in different labs. Our NCEMS working group will synthesize bacterial gene expression data using machine learning to create a first-of-its-kind atlas of bacterial cell states. To manageably scale data collection and analysis, we will build from examining model Escherichia coli strains in lab conditions, to adding wild E. coli strains in natural environments such as the human gut, to including diverse bacterial species with additional cell states. We expect to identify distinct foci corresponding to bacterial growth states and lifestyles (e.g., replicating, starving, motile, biofilm, spore, viable but nonculturable) by mapping the organization and occupancy of cell state space with dimensional reduction approaches. We will examine to what extent the gene expression signatures of different cell states and the relationships among them are conserved during bacterial evolution. Finally, we will use this framework to create a classifier that predicts the cell state composition of a bacterial population from metatranscriptomic data. By following open-science practices, we will make our pipelines and datasets reusable and maintainable by the research community. Our project may reveal new bacterial cell states and ways that we can non-genetically reprogram bacteria to prevent them from adopting lifestyles that damage the environment and cause disease.

title: Energetic Origins of Connectivity within Protein Interaction Networks
title_norm: energetic origins of connectivity within protein interaction networks
abstract_text: Systems biology and biophysics investigate how protein stability and intrinsic disorder influence the architecture of protein protein interaction networks exhibiting scale free topologies that feature hubs with extensive interactions. The specific mechanisms linking biophysical constraints to network architecture remain incomplete, limiting comprehension of how cellular interaction networks maintain their topology as individual proteins evolve. To determine how stability, binding efficiency, and intrinsic disorder dictate connectivity and evolutionary trajectories, this project will map centrality metrics against biophysical descriptors using Python graph analysis, generative modeling, and genetic algorithms featuring mass action fitness functions. The study will synthesize multi species interactome databases, Gene Expression Omnibus single cell profiles, and WikiPathways data with empirical turnover records to correlate network topological metrics with computational stability estimates. This research will provide a biophysical framework connecting the physical properties of individual proteins to the emergent topology and robustness of cellular networks, significantly advancing structural systems biology.
full_text: This systems biology and biophysics project investigates how protein stability and intrinsic disorder constrain interaction networks during evolution. Protein networks exhibit scale free topologies featuring highly interactive hubs but mechanisms linking biophysical constraints to network architecture remain incomplete. The proposed study asks how protein biophysics dictate network connectivity and evolution to provide a framework for emergent cellular robustness. The study design maps centrality metrics against descriptors of protein stability before using genetic algorithms to simulate evolutionary constraints. Researchers will apply graph analysis using Python and Cytoscape alongside generative artificial intelligence and genetic algorithms with mass action functions. Results will be validated using empirical data from proteolysis experiments alongside measurements of cellular abundance and proteomic half life. The project will utilize interactome datasets across five species alongside information from Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and Gene Ontology databases. Researchers will integrate curated interactome data with single cell expression records and stability estimates to correlate network topology with biophysics. The team will mitigate experimental bias in network scaling by applying variable analytical thresholds to test the robustness of results. Project milestones include constructing multi species networks and computing centrality metrics before developing algorithms for simulations of network evolution. This comprehensive scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to integrate specialized expertise in computational biophysics and modeling of evolutionary biology. The proposed team includes principal investigators from four laboratories specializing in biophysics alongside systems biology and evolutionary modeling. This collaborative group will be supported by a dedicated staff scientist alongside an assistant and several cross disciplinary trainees.

abstract_original: At least 10% of cellular proteins are intrinsically unstable and fold with marginal efficiency. In the cell, these proteins are preferentially engaged by chaperones and quality control proteins that refold or degrade them. Similarly, intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) preferentially interact with specific partners that they require for folding and function. Such proteins must exhibit bias in the types of protein-protein interactions they form within the cell. We therefore hypothesize that the emergent scaling properties of protein interaction networks arise, in part, from the promiscuous interactions formed by unstable proteins and the obligate interactions formed by IDPs. To test this hypothesis, we will analyze existing large-scale interactome datasets to explore the context of unstable and disordered proteins within interaction networks. By extending this approach to evaluate how proteins with various conformational properties are distributed across several unicellular and multicellular networks, we aim to uncover generalizable insights into how protein biophysics shapes network architecture. Additionally, by mapping the centrality of proteins involved in various supramolecular organization regimes, we will identify topological niches associated with the occurrence of liquid-liquid phase separation and quinary structure. Finally, to determine the extent to which these biases constrain network evolution, we will utilize genetic algorithms to explore how changes in the stability of the proteome restrict the topologies that are accessible through evolution. Together, these investigations will provide insights into the role of protein stability and binding efficiency in the evolution of PPI networks and how this relates to the molecular mechanisms of evolution.

title: Elucidating emergent structures in cellular RNA-protein interaction networks
title_norm: elucidating emergent structures in cellular rnaprotein interaction networks
abstract_text: RNA biology investigates messenger RNA protein complexes assembling into higher order biomolecular condensates like stress granules and P bodies, making structural mapping of these architectures essential to predict complex behaviors. Researchers currently lack computational methods to synthesize diverse experimental data and merge fragmented, multi modal RNA protein interaction datasets into unified nanoscale and mesoscale network models. This research will build computational tools to generate comprehensive network maps by applying AlphaFold, FINCHES, community detection algorithms, Mpipi molecular dynamics, and neural networks to cluster aggregate datasets and predict condensate partitioning in K562 cells. The study will integrate public RNA protein and protein protein interaction datasets, K562 cell data, CD Code, and the RNA Granule Database by establishing measured or inferred shared metrics as normalization anchor points. These comprehensive network maps will provide a quantitative model to explain cell type specific effects of widely expressed RNAs and the functional cellular consequences of synonymous and non coding mutations.
full_text: The research domain of RNA biology requires computational tools to model messenger RNA protein complexes and their cellular condensates. Regulatory proteins bind messenger RNAs to form structures but researchers lack methods to synthesize data for mapping these complex architectures. The proposed study builds computational tools for mapping complexes to explain functional mechanisms of mutations and cell type specific effects. The analytical strategy aggregates public datasets to construct an interaction map of K562 cells and model partitioning into cellular condensates. Key tools include AlphaFold and FINCHES for predicting interactions and the Mpipi model to simulate dynamics at the residue level. The team benchmarks results against the beta actin complex and validates models using data from proximity labeling and mass spectrometry. The proposed study utilizes the CD-Code and RNA Granule databases alongside public RNA protein interaction sets for K562 cells. The researchers will integrate these diverse datasets by establishing shared mathematical metrics to serve as anchor points for data normalization. The researchers will address variations in data quality by assigning statistical confidence scores calibrated against the beta actin complex. This project spans a timeline of two years and features milestones for releasing data tools and models before publishing findings. The scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to integrate specialized knowledge across the fields of molecular biophysics and machine learning. The team will release open source code and public databases using the CyVerse platform for shared computing and data storage. The collaborative team spans three laboratories and includes undergraduate students receiving training through mentorship and virtual programs of team science.

abstract_original: Messenger RNA molecules are constantly bound by proteins that regulate all aspects of their function, including their processing, localization, translation, and degradation1. These mRNA-protein complexes (mRNPs) can also interact with each other and assemble into higher-order structures that play critical roles in cellular organization and response to environmental stimuli1-3. Despite their importance, we lack a comprehensive map of these cellular RNA-protein interaction networks at both the nano and micro scales. Years of efforts by researchers across the globe have yielded a large, but disjointed, collection of datasets that map different aspects of RNA-protein interactions. Currently, we lack tools to integrate these datasets, preventing their synthesis into a coherent and interpretable interaction map. Here, we propose to develop tools to combine disparate data types to build transcriptome-wide maps of mRNPs, and their higher-order interactions within cells. We will then apply these tools to gain insights into long-standing biological mysteries, including the impacts of synonymous mutations and cell-type specific effects of widely expressed RNAs.

title: Oceans of Disorder: Elucidating the Role of Disordered Proteins in Cellular Adaptation
title_norm: oceans of disorder elucidating the role of disordered proteins in cellular adaptation
abstract_text: Marine protein biophysics and metagenomics investigate the environmental adaptation and conformational dynamics of intrinsically disordered proteins, which play an important role by altering their conformations in response to physicochemical stimuli. However, the specific sequence level and biophysical mechanisms by which individual intrinsically disordered proteins adapt to function under extreme and fluctuating marine environmental conditions remain unmapped and uncharacterized. This project will characterize intrinsically disordered proteins as molecular sensors by simulating conformational dynamics using coarse grained LAMMPS models and applying diverse machine learning networks to correlate sequence features with marine environmental parameters. A unified dataset will be constructed by linking Ocean Gene Atlas and Tara Oceans sequences to spatial metadata, integrating OceanDNA genomic parameters, and combining these inputs with simulated biophysical properties. This research will establish large scale principles of protein plasticity, providing a novel foundational framework to engineer environmentally resilient synthetic biological systems for downstream applications.
full_text: This project on the biophysics of marine proteins investigates how intrinsically disordered proteins adapt to extreme and fluctuating environments. Existing data map the structures of microbial communities to environments but the adaptations of individual proteins remain unmapped. The primary objective characterizes intrinsically disordered proteins as molecular sensors to define principles of plasticity for synthetic systems. The analytical strategy extracts sequences from databases of metagenomics to simulate dynamics of structures and correlate features with environments. The pipeline integrates predictions of structures from AlphaFold3 with simulations of molecules in LAMMPS and graph neural networks (GNNs). The project validates predicted trajectories of evolution against experimental data and conducts empirical testing on the computationally designed sequences. This study utilizes information from the Tara Oceans dataset and the Ocean Gene Atlas alongside the OceanDNA database. Researchers integrate data on abundance and metadata from these databases with simulated biophysical properties into a unified dataset. Researchers address limitations of models under extreme conditions by adding labels from simulations and excluding effects of pressure. The timeline reserves the first year for cataloging proteins and executing simulations before generating models of prediction and publications. This scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in metagenomics and biophysics with infrastructure for computational modeling. Researchers will publicly release the database of marine proteins and tools for computational design alongside publications in academic journals. The research team features experts in metagenomics and machine learning alongside a dedicated staff scientist and an assistant.

abstract_original: Intrinsically disordered proteins and protein regions (collectively IDRs) are key regulators of environmental sensing, owing to their ability to undergo conformational changes in response to physicochemical fluctuations. Despite evidence from individual studies, a comprehensive understanding of IDR-driven adaptations across diverse environments remains elusive. The deep sea, characterized by extreme and variable conditions such as temperature, pressure, and salinity, offers a unique opportunity to address this knowledge gap. Over the past decade, large-scale ocean sampling expeditions using shotgun metagenomics have revolutionized our understanding of marine biodiversity, providing access to the genetic diversity of organisms, from microbes to fish, thriving in these extreme habitats. These datasets offer an unprecedented opportunity to explore how IDRs have evolved as molecular sensors to support survival across varied environmental conditions. Here, we will, for the same time, use these metagenomic datasets to systematically characterize IDRs as environmental sensors. Our multidisciplinary team, with expertise in metagenomics, protein biophysics, cell biology, and deep learning, will integrate bioinformatics, simulations, machine learning, and theoretical approaches to uncover sequence-level and functional adaptations of IDRs across marine environments. The outcomes of this research will produce a comprehensive map of IDR adaptations in marine systems, revealing their emergent properties as molecular sensors and actuators. In addition to advancing fundamental insights into stress adaptation and evolutionary biology, this work will inform biotechnological innovations, including engineering robust systems for extreme environments.

title: Multimodel single-cell frameworks for cell lines with extensive multi-omics data
title_norm: multimodel singlecell frameworks for cell lines with extensive multiomics data
abstract_text: Computational multiomics investigates relationships among DNA, RNA, proteins, and chromatin accessibility, an important domain that leverages bulk and single cell data from large scale consortia across thousands of cell lines. However, existing single cell datasets remain fragmented and lack a unified framework to model these molecules simultaneously without introducing confounding donor and cell type variability. The primary objective will be to develop unified multimodal frameworks across seven homogenous cell lines by applying machine learning, network biology methods, and custom computational pipelines to combine bulk sequencing, single cell sequencing, imaging, and perturbation data. The project will integrate Dependency Map and Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia databases with single cell perturbation datasets using computational pipelines to align RNA, protein, and chromatin accessibility within single cells. This research will produce a benchmark resource and unified multimodal framework that eliminates cell type heterogeneity, enabling precise cross modality alignment to study regulatory mechanisms and perturbation responses.
full_text: The computational multiomics domain lacks unified frameworks to model DNA and RNA and chromatin accessibility within single cells. Existing multimodal benchmarks frequently utilize diverse samples that introduce confounding variability from unique donors and distinct cell types. The proposed project constructs unified frameworks across seven homogenous cell lines to enable precise alignment of regulatory mechanisms. The overall study design isolates seven homogenous cell lines to establish a unified computational modeling framework for molecules. The core analytical strategy combines bulk sequencing and single cell sequencing datasets with comprehensive imaging and perturbation data. To execute this integration the team utilizes machine learning algorithms and network biology methods alongside custom computational pipelines. The proposed project utilizes the Dependency Map and the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia alongside single cell Perturb-seq datasets. Data wrangling techniques and computational pipelines will align measurements of RNA and proteins to model single cell interactions. The team mitigates the limitation of confounding variability in diverse datasets by restricting analysis to homogenous cell lines. The ambitious scientific scope of this proposed project requires cross disciplinary collaboration across machine learning and network biology. This essential collaboration combines broad genomics expertise with dedicated data wrangling support from the specialized personnel at NCEMS. The resulting computational tools and unified multimodal frameworks and benchmarking resources will be distributed for broad community use. The collaborative research team comprises specialists in machine learning and network biology and genomics alongside NCEMS support personnel.

abstract_original: Large-scale consortia like the Dependency Map and Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia have generated extensive multi-omics data for over 2000 primary cell lines, including bulk measurements of DNA, chromatin accessibility, RNA, and proteins. Recently, multi-omics single-cell sequencing and imaging data labeling RNA and proteins for these cell lines have become increasingly available. However, these datasets remain fragmented, lacking integration into a unified framework to model and quantify DNA, RNA, and protein within the same cell. While previous efforts have created multimodal benchmark datasets, these often include diverse samples from multiple donors and heterogeneous cell types. In contrast, our project focuses on single model systems, such as commonly used cell lines, which already feature extensive single-cell, bulk sequencing, and imaging data. By eliminating donor and cell type variability, our approach enables robust analyses and precise alignment across modalities, including RNA, protein, and chromatin accessibility. This focus on homogenous cell types within a consistent biological context facilitates mechanistic studies of regulatory interactions and perturbation responses, minimizing confounding variability. We aim to develop multimodal frameworks for 7 cell lines and computational pipelines to analyze relationships across DNA, RNA, and protein levels. By incorporating additional multi-omics data, including bulk and single-cell perturbation datasets (e.g., loss-of-function screens and Perturb-seq), we will create a comprehensive benchmarking resource. With expertise in machine learning, network biology, and genomics, and NCEMS support for data wrangling, our team will deliver tools to study regulatory mechanisms and cellular resource allocation. These efforts will foster fundamental discoveries, community-driven resource development, and innovation in multi-omics research.

title: From image data and biophysical simulations to principles of mesoscale organization through integrated transfer learning
title_norm: from image data and biophysical simulations to principles of mesoscale organization through integrated transfer learning
abstract_text: Understanding mesoscale cellular organization requires mapping essential physical interactions among the nucleus, centrosomes, microtubules, and mitochondria, which researchers analyze through morphological profiling, proteomics, and single cell data alignment. However, integrating these components across distinct multimodal data spaces remains incomplete, leaving researchers unable to quantitatively compare high dimensional data to understand how geometric constraints drive cellular architecture. This research will develop a transfer learning pipeline utilizing generative adversarial networks to synthesize in vitro and in silico data, extracting morphological features into alignment matrices to infer missing intrinsic physical properties driving cellular organization. The study will integrate high throughput images of fibroblasts, in vitro reconstitutions, and molecular simulations by extracting feature spaces and aligning them into pairwise similarity matrices anchored to the nucleus. This project will yield a novel cross space learning framework that shifts the field toward physical principles, enabling the quantitative comparison of high dimensional multimodal biological datasets.
full_text: This project investigates structural interactions among organelles to resolve the inability to integrate high dimensional data across experimental spaces. Researchers have mapped organizational patterns using morphological profiling and proteomics but integrating these components across biophysical models remains incomplete. The proposed study asks how physical principles drive architecture and provides a novel method to execute cross space learning. The study design features a two step pipeline to extract morphological features and utilize deep learning for predictive inference. Key methods include Gromov-Wasserstein distances and generative adversarial networks (GANs) alongside tools like TensorFlow and the POT Python library. Results will be validated by checking inferences against open source datasets and comparing predicted missing components to physical reconstitutions. Datasets include multi component cell images and physical simulations alongside high throughput images of healthy and diseased patient fibroblasts. Distinct datasets will be integrated by extracting feature spaces and aligning them into pairwise similarity matrices using Gromov-Wasserstein distances. Known limitations regarding dataset availability and computational demands will be mitigated by leveraging NCEMS and CYVERSE information technology (IT) infrastructure. The two year timeline allocates six months to develop core workflows before expanding pipelines to address three component systems. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in machine learning with pooled access to specialized cellular datasets. The team will release an open source data integration workflow alongside the resulting predictive models and integrated multimodal datasets. The team comprises experts in computational image analysis and mathematical modeling alongside a researcher developing interdisciplinary literature synthesis methods.

abstract_original: Mesoscale cellular organization emerges from complex interactions among chemical, structural, and physical components. Understanding how mesoscale structures influence local and collective cellular properties remains a significant challenge, often beyond the scope of individual experimental studies. While vast image datasets for cellular components exist, their full potential for deeper secondary analysis and synthesis remains untapped. We propose to synthesize morphological and physico-chemical measurements from cell image, in vitro, and in silico data to unravel the principles of mesoscale cellular organization. Our approach will develop a pipeline using transfer learning and mutual prediction, trained on complete datasets (all components of interest present) and applied to incomplete datasets (missing one or more components). This methodology will uncover relationships between cellular components and enable holistic systems-level predictions. These test cases will showcase how our method integrates and predicts complex systems relationships, advancing our understanding of mesoscale cellular organization.

title: Emergent Order Parameters of Allostery: An AI Framework for Predicting and Engineering Protein Regulation
title_norm: emergent order parameters of allostery an ai framework for predicting and engineering protein regulation
abstract_text: Protein allostery research investigates signal propagation networks within signaling proteins, transcription factors, and kinases to understand equilibrium structural shifts and identify allosteric locations across diverse protein families. Current models lack a general quantitative metric to calculate, compare, or predict the physical strength, directionality, and temporal propagation of allosteric regulation across different proteins. This project will develop a physics informed data science framework to achieve the primary research objective of calculating quantitative order parameters through molecular dynamics simulations, time dependent linear response modeling, and machine learning classifiers. The project will synthesize deep mutational scanning records from MaveDB and molecular dynamics trajectories from MDRepo by mapping simulation features and mutational effects onto residue networks embedded into a continuous parameter space. This research will yield a universal system independent scale for allostery to enable the prediction of mutational impacts and support the rational design of allosteric drugs and engineered proteins.
full_text: The field of protein allostery lacks quantitative metrics to predict signal propagation networks within kinases and transcription factors. Existing models identify structural shifts but cannot quantify the physical strength and temporal propagation of diverse allosteric signals. The proposed study develops a physics informed framework to establish a universal scale for designing new allosteric drugs. The overall design integrates molecular dynamics simulations and mutational data to compute metrics and test diverse structural variants. The analytical methods feature time dependent linear response modeling and structural prediction algorithms (AlphaFold) alongside machine learning classifiers. The project team validates the computational predictions through the execution of mutagenesis and biophysical assays on transcription factors. Data sources include mutational scanning records from MaveDB and molecular dynamics trajectories from MDVerse for specific target proteins. The team synthesizes these datasets by mapping simulation features and evolutionary conservation onto residue networks using machine learning. The project team mitigates the absence of molecular dynamics data by executing new simulations on the Folding@home network. The two year timeline allocates early months for data integration and later periods for experimental validation and data release. The scope demands cross disciplinary collaboration to merge specialized expertise in computational modeling and experimental biology across three laboratories. The team will release curated datasets and an open source analytical software tool named AllosteryMap into public repositories. The project team features principal investigators from three distinct laboratories alongside requested institutional staff scientists for successful project execution.

abstract_original: Allostery—the ability of a perturbation at one site in a protein to control function at a distant site— underlies enzyme catalysis, signaling, and gene regulation. Yet we still lack a general, quantitative way to define how “allosteric” a protein is, to compare that across systems, and to predict how substitutions will strengthen, weaken, or rewire that control. This project develops a physics-informed data science framework to obtain quantitative order parameters of allostery and use them to classify, predict, and ultimately engineer regulatory behavior. We will integrate molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, deep mutational scanning (DMS) datasets, and evolutionary information (Table 1) to extract dynamic coupling measures that report how a local perturbation propagates through the protein over time. From these data we will derive physically interpretable allosteric order parameters that quantify three key features: (i) strength of long-range communication, (ii) directionality/asymmetry of information flow, and (iii) timescale of propagation. These parameters will form the basis of an “allostery score” that allows us to categorize the degree and mode of allostery across proteins and across species. We will then train machine learning models to predict how specific amino acid substitutions alter these order parameters — i.e., how a mutation changes not just local stability, but global regulatory wiring. Finally, we will apply this framework to design mutations that reprogram allosteric regulation in transcription factors, and experimentally test these designs. The outcome is a generalizable, predictive map from sequence to allosteric control.

title: Integrating AI and Molecular Dynamics Simulations for Quantitative Prediction of Enzyme Functions
title_norm: integrating ai and molecular dynamics simulations for quantitative prediction of enzyme functions
abstract_text: Computational biomolecular modeling focuses on predicting enzyme function based on protein conformational dynamics, a phenomenon where molecular dynamics simulations capture temporal physicochemical mechanisms to augment static structural data. Current artificial intelligence models for predicting protein function rely on static sequence and structural data, leaving the integration of dynamic simulation data and environmental responses incomplete. This research will integrate multi scale molecular dynamics simulations and biophysical determinants into an artificial intelligence framework to improve enzyme function prediction, utilizing the MD4PLM model, spatio temporal graph neural networks, and causal self attention. Data from UniProt, the Protein Data Bank, and trajectory databases including ATLAS will yield independent structural embeddings across multiple resolutions that a gated fusion module will synthesize and aggregate with sequence embeddings. This framework will improve enzyme function prediction by introducing temporal resolution and conformational diversity into protein representations, modifying existing static sequence and structure paradigms.
full_text: Computational biomolecular modeling predicts enzyme function using artificial intelligence models that rely on static data instead of conformational dynamics. Artificial intelligence evaluates static structures accurately and molecular dynamics captures temporal mechanisms but their integration remains fundamentally incomplete. The proposed study integrates biophysical determinants and multi scale simulations of molecular dynamics into artificial intelligence to introduce conformational diversity. The study curates functional annotations and multi scale trajectories of molecular dynamics before synthesizing these inputs via artificial intelligence for prediction. Methods include frameworks for artificial intelligence (MD4PLM) and sequence embeddings (ESM-2) alongside simulations and extractors of biophysical features (MDtraj). The team will benchmark performance against models based on sequence and structure using precise metrics of evaluation and failure analyses. The project utilizes functional annotations from UniProt and experimental structures from the Protein Data Bank alongside databases of molecular dynamics trajectories. Structural embeddings from multiple resolutions of simulations will be synthesized via a gated fusion module and aggregated with sequence embeddings. The limitation of finite conformational sampling will be mitigated using coarse grained simulations and enhanced techniques for sampling like umbrella sampling. The two year timeline progresses from data curation and simulation execution to the analysis of biophysical determinants and model benchmarking. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to unite expertise in artificial intelligence and bioinformatics with large scale computational resources. Processed trajectories and code will be shared via open repositories while findings are disseminated through open access scholarly publications. The cross disciplinary team provides training opportunities for graduate students through short term exchanges within laboratories and targeted visits to facilities.

abstract_original: Recent AI advances have transformed biomolecular research, enabling accurate prediction of biomolecu- lar functions from sequence and structural data. However, the role of dynamic motions and environmental responses in shaping biomolecular function remains underexplored in AI-driven approaches. In this pro- posal, our working group aims to bridge this gap by integrating temporal and physicochemical insights from molecular dynamics (MD) with AI techniques to enhance predictive accuracy in protein function, focusing on enzymes. We will work closely with NCEMS in two phases: (I) Comprehensive data curation of enzyme function annotations, collection of multi-scale simulation trajectories, and biophysical deter- minants causally linked to enzyme activity. (II) Synthesizing simulations and biophysical determinants through a multi-modal AI model to enhance enzyme function predictions. The project integrates comple- mentary expertise across multiple labs and will leverage NCEMS computational resources to generate large-scale data. By synergizing AI and MD, we will advance biomolecular modeling beyond the static sequence-structure paradigm to include temporal resolution, guiding rational design of therapeutic and functional biomolecules.

title: Discovery and functional analysis of bacterial organelles through mining and refinement of omics data
title_norm: discovery and functional analysis of bacterial organelles through mining and refinement of omics data
abstract_text: The microbiology domain focuses on the distribution, regulation, and interactions of bacterial organelles within the human gut microbiome, representing a critical phenomenon for understanding cellular compartmentalization despite current knowledge relying on isolated model systems. The primary objective is to map organelle prevalence and environmental responsiveness; therefore, the project will apply Hidden Markov Models, Phaseek machine learning, and WGCNA networks to identify structural markers across MGnify processed omics data. This project will harmonize the GMrepo database and the Inflammatory Bowel Disease Multiomics Database, pairing metagenomic, metatranscriptomic, and metaproteomic datasets at the individual sample level to correlate microbial community structure with functional activity. This research will produce foundational metaomics data mapping bacterial organelle regulation, advancing the evolutionary study of cellular compartmentalization and supporting novel synthetic biology applications.
full_text: Structural classes are known from isolated models but the regulation of bacterial organelles in native environments remains uncharacterized. The proposed study maps the regulation of bacterial organelles using multi omics data to support synthetic biology applications. The study design identifies specific markers in metagenomic data and analyzes matched metatranscriptomic data to measure organelle expression. Key methods include Hidden Markov Models for structural proteins and the Phaseek machine learning tool for condensate proteins. The researchers will validate predictions of protein expression derived from the metatranscriptomic data against the corresponding metaproteomic data. The study uses the GMrepo database and the Inflammatory Bowel Disease Multi omics Database as primary data sources. The team will harmonize metagenomic datasets with metatranscriptomic and metaproteomic datasets to correlate community structure with functional activity. The researchers will mitigate high false positive rates for encapsulins by verifying sequence thresholds during the data analysis. The proposed timeline spans from February 2026 to January 2028 and includes milestones for model building and dataset processing. The project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine biological expertise in bacterial organelles with support for computational processing. The team will share data and findings through peer reviewed publications and a publicly accessible database of bacterial organelles. The team comprises established domain experts and data science staff while providing bioinformatics training for early career researchers.

abstract_original: Once considered exclusive to eukaryotes, subcellular organelles are now recognized as common features of prokaryotic cells. Bacterial organelles exhibit remarkable diversity and specialization, falling into three structural classes: protein-bounded compart- ments, lipid-bounded compartments, and biomolecular condensates. While recent model sys- tem studies have uncovered molecular mechanisms controlling the formation and function of several bacterial organelles, their activities in ecological contexts, environmental responsive- ness, and inter-organelle interactions remain poorly characterized. Here, we propose a com- munity synthesis approach to define the landscape of bacterial organelles in the human gut mi- crobiome using publicly available multi-omics data. We have assembled a team of experts on the genetics and biochemistry of bacterial microcompartments, encapsulins, ferrosomes, and biomolecular condensates. With input from NCEMS staff we will enumerate the occurrence of bacterial organelles from metagenomic datasets and examine meta-transcriptomic and meta- proteomic data to characterize their regulation and expression. This framework will allow us to test key hypotheses, such as whether organelles with overlapping functions can co-exist within the same organisms as well as various members of a microbial community and how organelle expression patterns change in response to environmental conditions. We will also examine co- ordinated expression between organelles, which will provide insights into potential inter-orga- nelle interactions. These studies will form the basis for publications on the distribution, co-oc- currence, and functional roles of bacterial organelles. The generated data will guide future hy- potheses, shed light on the evolutionary trajectory of cellular compartmentalization, and enable the rational design of biotechnological applications based on the unique features of bacterial organelles.

title: From Protein Knots to Pierced Lassos: Unraveling the Evolutionary Origin of Complex Topologies
title_norm: from protein knots to pierced lassos unraveling the evolutionary origin of complex topologies
abstract_text: Evolutionary structural biology investigates the origins of complex three dimensional protein topologies, specifically knots, slipknots, and lassos, which possess established sequence homologies and common ancestry critical for understanding protein function. Despite known homologies, the exact evolutionary branch points dictating when entangled protein topologies first emerged and how these complex structures correlate with pathogenicity and adaptive function remain uncharacterized. This project will identify precise evolutionary branch points for topological changes by applying structural bioinformatics, sequence based machine learning, and GPU accelerated computational modeling of ancestral structures across 9 knotted superfamilies and 26 lasso families. The investigation will integrate extensive datasets, including UniProt, PDB, AlphaFold DB, and LassoProt, by aligning topological predictions and functional annotations onto reconstructed phylogenetic trees to track sequence to topology relationships. Mapping the evolutionary origins of these entangled protein structures will yield essential baseline data for predicting topology emergence, designing structural proteins, and identifying novel therapeutic targets in pathogenic organisms.
full_text: This project studies the evolutionary origins of complex three dimensional protein topologies and identifies unmapped evolutionary branch points. Existing research identifies sequence homologies and manual annotations for knotted families but the timing of emergence remains uncharacterized. The proposed study locates exact branch points of topological changes to provide baseline data for identifying therapeutic targets. The core analytical strategy maps topological features of knotted protein superfamilies onto reconstructed phylogenetic trees to model structures. Key methods include structural bioinformatics and machine learning to support computational modeling of three dimensional ancestral protein structures. Topological predictions undergo validation against manually verified annotations of knotted families to address false positives in structural modeling. The project incorporates data from repositories like UniProt and AlphaFold DB alongside topological collections including KnotProt 2.0 and TimeTree. The team integrates distinct datasets by aligning sequence features via UniProt references to overlay data onto phylogenetic trees. The project offsets the absence of structural data at evolutionary branch points by generating models of ancestral structures. The 24 month timeline schedules initial data integration and structural model generation before the publication of final findings. The massive volume of structural modeling demands cross disciplinary expertise spanning evolutionary analysis and large scale data integration. The proposed project yields an open data platform containing publicly accessible phylogenetic trees and peer reviewed journal articles. The team unites a principal investigator and a student researcher with staff scientists trained in protein structure prediction.

abstract_original: Proteins can adopt intricate three-dimensional structures, including complex topologies such as knots, slipknots, pierced lassos, and even more complex structures. These entangled architectures challenge traditional views of protein folding and stability, suggesting that nature may use topological complexity as a mechanism to fine-tune function, regulation, or mechanical resilience. Despite growing structural data, the evolutionary origins and functional consequences of these nontrivial topologies remain largely unexplored. This project aims to leverage existing databases to identify the evolutionary turning points at which topological changes first arose within protein families. By integrating sequence, structural, and phylogenetic data from resources such as UniProt, PDB, AlphaFold, AlphaKnot, and AlphaLasso, we will reconstruct annotated phylogenetic trees that map the emergence and diversification of entangled proteins across evolutionary time. We will analyze whether specific sequence motifs, disulfide patterns, or intrinsically disordered regions are associated with the onset of entanglement, and whether such proteins are enriched in pathogenic or stress-adapted organisms. Furthermore, we will assess how topological complexity correlates with functional hotspots, including catalytic or allosteric regions, to reveal possible adaptive advantages. This work will establish a framework to trace, predict, and design protein topologies with distinct structural and functional characteristics. The outcomes will not only deepen our understanding of how topology shapes evolution and biomolecular behavior but also provide an open, data-driven platform for studying entanglement as a functional and evolutionary principle in protein science.

title: Deciphering systemic biological networks through AI-driven multi-omic integration
title_norm: deciphering systemic biological networks through aidriven multiomic integration
abstract_text: The research domain of organismal physiology examines multi organ communication networks that coordinate systemic adaptation, yet previous studies predominantly examine the single organ level or rely on heterogeneous datasets that reduce biological accuracy. The molecular structure, directionality, and temporal regulation of inter organ signaling remain uncharacterized at the whole organism level, preventing the construction of interpretable multi organ network models. Addressing the primary objective to map inter organ molecular networks, this project will build a computational model simulating biological responses by integrating longitudinal data through principal component analysis, a reaction diffusion graph network, and physics informed neural networks. The project will integrate multi omic data from eighteen solid tissues of exercising rats in the public MoTrPAC dataset vertically across omic layers and horizontally across organs using graph Laplacian operators and neural networks. The resulting computational model will identify predictors of phenotypic adaptation and simulate multi organ communication to predict system level physiological regulation, direct future experiments, and reduce animal testing.
full_text: This project studies organismal physiology because the molecular structure and temporal regulation of multi organ communication networks remain uncharacterized. Previous studies of communication focus on single organ systems while existing multi organ models lack accuracy and interpretability. The proposed study maps molecular networks to simulate biological responses for predicting physiological regulation and reducing animal testing. The research strategy integrates longitudinal multi organ data using a mathematical framework to model temporal and spatial dynamics. Key analytical tools include principal component analysis alongside graph Laplacian operators and neural networks with physics informed loss. The team will validate computational predictions of genomic states through an iterative testing process using in vivo experiments. This project utilizes the publicly available MoTrPAC dataset containing comprehensive omic measurements from eighteen solid tissues of rats. Data integration occurs vertically across omic layers and horizontally across organs using graph Laplacian operators and neural networks. The team manages dataset heterogeneity by using matched subjects while mitigating sparse data volume via a hybrid model. First year milestones include initial data integration and grant submission while second year goals involve mapping complete networks. Constructing models from large scale datasets necessitates cross disciplinary collaboration between the lead biologist and machine learning specialists. The proposed research team features a lead biology investigator alongside required specialists in bioinformatics and computational data science. This collaborative group incorporates artificial intelligence professionals and may receive supplementary assistance from the dedicated institutional support staff.
