abstract_original: Organ cross-talk refers to the bidirectional communication between different organs that enables the body to maintain physiological homeostasis, respond and adapt during dynamic states. Disturbances to these inter-organ communication networks may result in inappropriate physiological responses, thereby compromising systemic function. This proposal will leverage a unique publicly available large-scale, multi-organ, multi-omic dataset comprising 18 solid tissues from rats subjected to an endurance exercise training program. Our hypothesis is that organ-specific signaling hierarchies will determines the coordinated multiorgan responses that drive systemic adaptation. Following organ-specific multi-omic vertical integration, we will determine 1) the predictors of phenotypic adaptations, and 2) the cross talk between organs via horizontal integration. The computed networks will provide the foundation to generate a digital twin rat which will serve as a valuable tool to model organismal responses to physiological, environmental and pharmacological challenges. This comprehensive, temporally resolved analysis will offer unprecedented insights into how molecular interactions are coordinated across organs and levels of organization to determine whole-organism physiological function.

title: Conserved Disorder: Learning Sequence Conservation from Functional Constraints in Intrinsically Disordered Regions
title_norm: conserved disorder learning sequence conservation from functional constraints in intrinsically disordered regions
abstract_text: The fields of protein biophysics and bioinformatics investigate evolutionary conservation patterns in intrinsically disordered regions, which contain sequence features like short linear motifs and charge patterning that encode vital molecular functions. This project will define conserved intrinsically disordered regions by integrating human and viral proteomic data through AIUpred disorder prediction, explicit solvent all atom molecular dynamics simulations, sequence descriptors over moving windows, and machine learning. The study will integrate UniProt, Eukaryotic Linear Motif, IDRome, MaveDB, and GISAID databases by filtering sequences for disorder thresholds and cross referencing them with deep mutational scanning and post translational modification data. This research will provide a unified map of conserved disordered regions, establishing essential baselines for functional annotation and creating reference points for future sequence alignments and comparative analyses.
full_text: This protein biophysics and bioinformatics project investigates how evolutionary sequence variations of intrinsically disordered regions encode functional specificity. Subsets of intrinsically disordered regions contain functional motifs but current annotations favor folded protein domains over these flexible segments. The team asks how sequence features generate conserved functions to establish reference points for analyzing the disordered proteome. The core strategy integrates evolutionary and structural data across human and viral proteomes to identify patterns of functional conservation. Key methods include structural predictions using the AIUpred algorithm and explicit solvent molecular dynamics simulations alongside machine learning models. The team validates all analytical results by measuring sequence conservation across diverse species using independent databases of orthologous proteins. Researchers utilize primary databases like UniProt and MaveDB alongside supplementary resources including OrthoDB and the Eukaryotic Linear Motif repository. The team synthesizes datasets by cross referencing filtered sequences with scanning data and predicted motifs to construct unified maps. Because current functional annotations favor structured domains the researchers mitigate missing information by utilizing alternative data repositories like MobiDB. The two year project timeline progresses from infrastructure setup and structural investigations to concluding database releases and manuscript submissions. This broad scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to unite expertise in bioinformatics and biophysical modeling across three independent laboratories. The project guarantees open access by hosting a public database of conserved regions on the CyVerse computational infrastructure. The team incorporates members from three distinct laboratories and provides robust training opportunities in computational and experimental analysis techniques.

While folded domains exhibit clear conservation of structure and function, IDRs evolve rapidly and appear sequence diverse, obscuring how they encode functional specificity. Bridging the sequence function relationship in IDRs and even their reliable functional annotation remains a major challenge. Emerging evidence, however, suggests that subsets of IDRs harbor conserved sequence features such as short linear motifs (SLiMs), charge patterning and aromatic clustering that give rise to transient structural elements and encode critical molecular functions. This project aims to systematically identify and characterize the most conserved IDRs across proteomes by integrating large-scale sequence alignments, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and experimental functional annotations from publicly available databases. By combining resources such as UniProt, Eukaryotic Linear Motif (ELM), IDRome, and MaveDB, we will quantify the interplay between evolutionary, structural, and functional signatures of conservation in disordered regions. Our multidisciplinary Working Group unites computational and experimental biophysics to build a curated, open-access database of conserved IDRs. This synthesis effort will reveal how dynamic, flexible protein regions maintain specific and evolvable functions, an emergent property at the mesoscale interface between sequence evolution, molecular structure, and cellular regulation.

title: Integrative Multi-Omics Synthesis to Identify Shared Molecular Mechanisms of Mammalian Hibernation
title_norm: integrative multiomics synthesis to identify shared molecular mechanisms of mammalian hibernation
abstract_text: Mammalian hibernation is a distinct physiological state involving decreased metabolism, lowered body temperature, and fasting, making the investigation of its underlying gene expression mechanisms crucial for understanding metabolic adaptation across taxa. To identify conserved molecular processes controlling metabolic suppression, this project will map gene orthology and model longitudinal gene expression changes between active and hibernating states using custom bivariate Ornstein Uhlenbeck trait evolution models. The study will integrate Sequence Read Archive RNA sequencing datasets and reference genomes across multiple tissues by processing raw reads through a uniform mapping pipeline and cross referencing species data via orthology maps. Identifying these conserved differentially regulated genes will clarify mammalian metabolic evolution and establish a biological foundation for downstream research concerning human metabolic regulation, ischemia tolerance, and organ preservation.
full_text: This project investigates mammalian hibernation to determine if metabolic suppression relies on shared or lineage specific transcriptional mechanisms. Although transcript data exists for individual hibernating mammals the field lacks comparative analyses of expression across multiple species. The proposed study identifies conserved genes for metabolic suppression to clarify mammalian evolution and inform human organ preservation. The team integrates RNA sequencing data from multiple tissues to model changes of gene expression using phylogenetic frameworks. The analytical pipeline incorporates transcript quantification with featureCounts alongside phylogenetic analyses using custom bivariate models of trait evolution. The proposed study will validate the custom bivariate models of trait evolution through the use of simulation tests. The project uses public RNA sequencing data from the Sequence Read Archive alongside published genomes and sequence alignments. The team integrates distinct datasets through uniform processing pipelines and maps of gene orthology derived from genome alignments. The team will mitigate sparse sampling of tissues across species by developing phylogenetic tools to handle missing data. The two year timeline begins with transcript processing and concludes with data synthesis and preparation of academic manuscripts. Managing these diverse variables requires a cross disciplinary team with distinct expertise in molecular biology and computational phylogenetics. The team will distribute project findings through primary literature alongside open source software and datasets of hibernation studies. This diverse research group spans multiple career stages and provides technical mentoring for support personnel in the laboratory.

Despite decades of study, the shared molecular and cellular regulatory mechanisms that drive and sustain hibernation remain largely unresolved. This project aims to unify existing omics-scale datasets, mostly transcriptomic, from numerous hibernating mammals to identify conserved pathways and molecular signatures underlying this extreme phenotype. Our project will leverage publicly available datasets and apply cutting-edge computational tools that are developed in the context of this project to analyze transcriptional variation underlying hibernation in a phylogenetic context.

title: Revealing the Ontology of Allostery through Community-Scale Synthesis
title_norm: revealing the ontology of allostery through communityscale synthesis
abstract_text: Protein biophysics and molecular evolution research investigates allosteric regulation in transporter proteins including the P type ATPase superfamily, utilizing existing databases and algorithms to catalog regulated proteins and predict binding sites. This project will identify amino acid sites controlling allosteric mechanisms and determine their evolutionary origins by statistically comparing transporter families using tools including AlphaFold, Direct Coupling Analysis, and Adaptive Steered Molecular Dynamics. The study will integrate data from UniProt, InterPro, the Protein Data Bank, and the Allosteric Database to build an augmented allosterome database combining sequence alignments, protein structures, and molecular dynamics trajectories. Identifying these allosteric control sites will enable the annotation of uncharacterized allosteric systems, the interpretation of disease associated mutations, and the experimental design of synthetic allosteric proteins.
full_text: Existing databases catalog regulated proteins and algorithms predict binding sites but lack curated negative examples of non regulated proteins. The proposed study compares transporter homologs to uncover allosteric mechanisms and enable the experimental design of synthetic allosteric proteins. The team will assemble a comparative database of transporter families and map evolutionary landscapes through statistical comparisons of properties. The methodology utilizes AlphaFold and PyTorch alongside established methods for direct coupling analysis and adaptive steered molecular dynamics. The team will benchmark results by testing the ability of models to categorize proteins and propose functional point mutations. The study draws data from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and the Allosteric Database (ASD) alongside the UniProt repository. The team will build an augmented database by combining structural data and sequence alignments for fifty distinct protein families. The team will mitigate the known lack of negative examples by utilizing domain insertions as proxy markers for allosteric regulation. The two year timeline progresses from data curation and analysis to the final evaluation of models and manuscript preparation. This project requires multi lab collaboration to combine diverse expertise in machine learning and the computational modeling of molecular evolution. The team will publish their evolutionary findings and host the augmented database publicly on the CyVerse platform for community access. The research group features principal investigators and staff scientists specializing in machine learning and the biophysics of chemical materials.

abstract_original: Allostery is a fundamental property of proteins wherein perturbations at one site can influence another distant site. Understanding the sequence, structural, and dynamic determinants of allostery is critical to engineering new biosensors, designing allosteric modulators, and predicting the functional impact of mutations. For many proteins, allostery allows control of protein activity in response to external stimuli, such as ligand binding, protein or nucleic acid interactions, post-translational modifications, light, and redox state. There are proteins, though, that do not clearly exhibit such regulatory mechanisms, and are thus rarely included in publicly available allosteric databases. Consequently, it remains unclear what features distinguish regulated systems and regulatory sites from their non-regulated counterparts. To this end, we will focus our work on a specific class of proteins—namely transporter proteins—and assemble a database that is, on the one hand, very specific—restricted to all such proteins, and broad because it includes proteins for which there is a lack of evidence for allosteric regulation. This augmented allosteric database will provide a basis for identifying the degree of allostery in proteins. Through these databases, and associated computational interrogations, we will reveal the determinants of allostery in transporter proteins, a large and diverse family of membrane proteins comprised of allosteric and non-allosteric members.

title: SynEvo: Discovering Evolutionary Principles of Molecular Organization through Cross-Species Data Synthesis
title_norm: synevo discovering evolutionary principles of molecular organization through crossspecies data synthesis
abstract_text: Evolutionary systems biology studies the intermediate scale organization of gene regulation and metabolism in humans and mosquitoes, demanding the integration of population genetic variation with cross species multi omics data through biochemical models. Currently, no analytical framework connects population level genetic variation with isolated cross species multi omics data to explain how evolution structures regulatory and metabolic networks. This project will develop a machine learning framework using graph neural networks, variational autoencoders, and genome scale metabolic models to merge population genetics with multi omics data, determining the rules that govern cross species network adaptation. A standardized pipeline will integrate datasets from GTEx, TOPMed, Ag1000G, and VectorBase with databases like Reactome and BiGG through metadata harmonization and cross species feature alignment based on orthology frameworks and pathway scaffolds. This research will yield a novel framework that maps physiologically plausible network modules, providing fundamental knowledge directly applicable to evolutionary theory, human health, and vector biology.
full_text: Evolutionary systems biology lacks frameworks connecting population level genetic variation with intermediate scale organization for humans and mosquitoes. Systems biology models network dynamics using isolated datasets while integration with population genetics through biochemical models remains incomplete. The proposed study develops machine learning frameworks to determine network adaptation rules benefiting human health and vector biology. The study design utilizes hybrid machine learning models and cross species manifold alignment to identify conserved network modules. Key methods incorporate variational autoencoders and graph neural networks alongside genome scale metabolic models and orthology mapping tools. The team validates results through cross validation and benchmarks findings against flux balance analysis and curated pathway databases. The study utilizes population datasets from GTEx and All of Us alongside pathway databases including Reactome and BiGG. A standardized pipeline integrates these distinct datasets through metadata harmonization and cross species feature alignment using orthology frameworks. The team mitigates data sparsity for mosquito variants by prioritizing human datasets and developing adaptable transfer learning models. The two year timeline progresses from data harmonization and model training toward the final release of comprehensive toolkits. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to merge specialized expertise spanning machine learning and genome scale metabolic modeling. The project distributes version controlled workflows and interactive atlas data through open access repositories alongside comprehensive training materials. The team features principal investigators and staff scientists who provide mentorship for students and host specialized instructional workshops.

abstract_original: Living systems exhibit emergent organization that bridges molecular and evolutionary scales. Genetic variation, regulatory control, and metabolic dynamics interact across levels of complexity to produce coordinated cellular behavior, yet most datasets capture only one layer at a time. Despite vast genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic resources across species and environments, no synthesis framework connects these data to reveal how evolutionary forces shape the mesoscale—the intermediate level where genes, proteins, and metabolites assemble into adaptive networks. The SynEvo Working Group will develop a machine-learning–driven synthesis framework that unites population-genetic and multi-omics data to uncover conserved and divergent axes of molecular organization. Using well-characterized human and mosquito datasets, we will identify how genetic variation, regulatory control, and metabolic flux interact to produce conserved mesoscale modules reflecting evolutionary constraint and innovation. These contrasting systems serve as testbeds for uncovering evolutionary design principles of molecular coordination—how selection and constraint shape regulatory–metabolic organization across life. SynEvo integrates interpretable machine learning with genome-scale metabolic (GEM) and MiReN (Minimal Regulatory Network; MILP-based regulatory inference) approaches, producing an open SynEvo Atlas hosted within NCEMS infrastructure—a reusable resource for evolutionary systems biology. By revealing both species- specific adaptations and conserved mesoscale design principles, SynEvo will advance conceptual and computational frontiers, providing fundamental insight into how life organizes itself across molecular, physiological, and evolutionary dimensions, with applications to human health, malaria transmission, and environmental resilience.

title: A Unified Framework for Analyses of Proteome Turnover Dynamics
title_norm: a unified framework for analyses of proteome turnover dynamics
abstract_text: The proteostasis domain focuses on protein turnover rates across species and kingdoms of life, recognizing that degradation signals and protein stability mechanisms exhibit broad conservation throughout evolutionary history. This project will construct the Protein Stability Database to analyze protein turnover conservation by standardizing public data, refitting measurements using uniform kinetic models, and applying deep neural networks and protein language models to correlate biophysical traits with degradation rates. Dynamic labeling mass spectrometry data from the PRIDE repository will be integrated with structural and thermodynamic databases by reanalyzing raw intensity data using uniform kinetic models and controlled vocabularies for experimental metadata. This research will produce a standardized metadata resource connecting protein half lives to molecular features, enabling comprehensive cross kingdom comparisons of biophysical properties that govern protein turnover across species.
full_text: This proteostasis research investigates rates of protein turnover to understand how molecular mechanisms determine protein stability across different evolutionary contexts. Eukaryotic degradation signals exhibit broad conservation but unstructured existing datasets obscure how sequence properties and proteostasis networks determine protein lifetimes. This project builds a standardized database to analyze evolutionary conservation and identify biophysical properties governing cross kingdom protein turnover. The study design standardizes public data regarding turnover by refitting measurements with uniform models and applying machine learning to orthologs. Methods involve exponential decay modeling and Bayesian sampling combined with deep neural networks and protein language models including ESM2. Validation of model performance requires calculating reconstruction loss for proteins with fast turnover and measuring prediction accuracy against established databases. Primary sources feature mass spectrometry data from PRIDE alongside structural predictions from AlphaFold and repositories of genomic sequences including OrthoDB. Data integration involves reanalyzing raw intensities with uniform kinetic models and combining resulting rates with corresponding structural and omics variables. The team mitigates incompatible formats of data and physiological variations by correcting enrichment kinetics and applying unified models with metadata. The two year timeline spans initial development of the database during the first year and subsequent validation of models. The project requires cross disciplinary collaboration because harmonizing quantitative mass spectrometry data with computational modeling exceeds individual laboratory capacity. The project provides open access to the resulting database and analytical code through established repositories including CyVerse and GitHub. The research team includes principal investigators from proteomics and computational biology working alongside staff scientists to provide training opportunities.

abstract_original: Proteins vary widely in how long they persist within cells, from minutes to years, and this variation plays a central role in regulating biological function and maintaining cellular homeostasis. Decades of research have revealed several mechanisms that influence protein half-lives across the kingdoms of life. However, the differential impact of these mechanisms on protein half-lives within and between species remains incompletely understood. This knowledge gap can be addressed by comprehensive analyses of global proteome stability datasets enabled by recent advances in mass spectrometry-based proteomics. However, these datasets are currently fragmented across heterogeneous studies that are not easily amenable to meta-analysis. This Working Group will bring together complementary expertise in proteomics, computational biology, systems biochemistry, and evolution to systematically harmonize and integrate publicly available datasets on protein turnover across four representative species across two kingdoms of life - E. coli, S. cerevisiae, M. musculus, and H. sapiens. By reanalyzing existing data using consistent approaches and unifying metadata standards, we will generate a comprehensive, comparable, and publicly accessible resource, the Protein Stability Database (PSD). This database will enable us to identify the molecular and evolutionary principles that govern protein stability and assess how turnover patterns vary across different cell types and organisms. Beyond addressing these core questions, our Working Group aims to establish best practices and a shared vocabulary for measuring and reporting protein turnover, enabling seamless incorporation of future datasets and integration with other NCEMS data resources.

title: Predictive Synthesis Framework for Elucidating Biophysical Cell State from Spatial Transcriptomics and Proteomics
title_norm: predictive synthesis framework for elucidating biophysical cell state from spatial transcriptomics and proteomics
abstract_text: The spatial omics field evaluates how subcellular molecular location influences cellular function, making the integration of spatial transcriptomics and spatial proteomics essential because bulk RNA and protein levels correlate poorly. Current analytical methods evaluate molecular abundances separately because the technical difficulty of aligning adjacent tissue sections restricts the ability to measure how subcellular organization determines cell behavior. This project will build a computational framework utilizing STalign diffeomorphic mapping, SEraster grid harmonization, and SubCell deep learning models with contrastive multimodal embedding algorithms to extract spatial relationships and predict cell fate decisions. The study will integrate human cancer datasets from the Spatch database by registering adjacent spatial transcriptomics and spatial proteomics sections into a common coordinate framework rasterized onto a shared pixel grid. This framework will shift spatial omics from abundance only observations to predictive models that link spatial molecular patterns directly to biophysical mechanisms and cellular phenotypes.
full_text: The field of spatial omics analyzes subcellular organization and lacks tools to integrate RNA and protein spatial locations. Subcellular location influences cellular function while difficult alignment of adjacent tissue sections limits comparisons of RNA and proteins. This computational framework tests whether integrated spatial relationships predict cell states better than abundance to uncover biophysical mechanisms. The strategy maps adjacent tissue sections onto a shared grid to train models for classification of cell states. Key tools include mapping algorithms like STalign and SEraster alongside deep learning models like SubCell for contrastive embedding. The team will benchmark results against models of abundance and validate the alignments using root mean square errors. The project utilizes the public Spatch database of human cancers and additional cohorts containing transcriptomic and proteomic data. The team will integrate distinct datasets by registering tissue sections into a common coordinate framework to generate patches. Adjacent tissue sections undergo non rigid distortions during imaging and the team will apply non linear alignment algorithms. The project spans two years and includes intermediate milestones for data harmonization before final release of a toolchain. The scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in machine learning and biophysics with scalable computing infrastructure. The team will release code and harmonized datasets under permissive licenses alongside a peer reviewed publication of findings. The collaborative team includes principal investigators specializing in artificial intelligence and staff scientists with expertise in cloud computing.

abstract_original: Cell states reflect not only molecular abundance but also where molecules reside. Public spatial omics (Spatch) now provide high-plex RNA (Xenium/CosMx) and protein (CODEX) maps, yet cross-modal synthesis at subcellular scales remain fragmented. We will develop an open, end-to-end synthesis framework that (i) registers adjacent-section spatial RNA-Protein images at subcellular resolution using diffeomorphic alignment (STalign), (ii) harmonizes RNA features into protein-scale rasters (SEraster) to create a one-to-one correspondence of patches to be compared (iii) quantify membrane/nuclear proximity, polarity, local density, and other features (iv) trains RNA-to-protein predictors and learn a unified biophysical fingerprint of cell state. Using the paired Xenium/CosMx-CODEX cancer atlas as a validation set and curated public cohorts as application sets, we will benchmark against abundance-only baselines. Framework performance will be assessed by overall registration quality, verified patch correspondence, and cross-modal predictive accuracy, with appropriate positive and negative controls to rule out leakage and spurious structure. We will test the hypotheses that RNA-protein spatial relationships yield predictive signals for cell state beyond abundance and that low- dimensional biophysical fingerprints precede and predict cell fate decisions. All code, trained models, and harmonized datasets generated from this work will be released under permissive licenses with containerized, reproducible workflows and scheduled public snapshots. This community-scale synthesis will convert dispersed spatial imaging datasets into predictive, interpretable models of cell state, while leveraging NCEMS (CyVerse compute, data harmonization, and project management) for scalable analysis and dissemination.

title: Emergent Phase Separation Grammar: Decoding How Intrinsically Disordered Region Sequence Patterns Drive Mesoscale Condensate Properties
title_norm: emergent phase separation grammar decoding how intrinsically disordered region sequence patterns drive mesoscale condensate properties
abstract_text: The research domain investigates mesoscale biomolecular condensates, specifically how intrinsically disordered proteins utilize specific amino acids and electrostatic interactions to drive liquid liquid phase separation and form functional membraneless organelles. The field lacks comprehensive models explaining how sequence features synergistically dictate phase behavior, leaving a critical gap in connecting protein sequences to condensate material properties and disease states. This project will identify rules linking intrinsically disordered protein sequences to condensate properties and cell type specific organization by applying transformer based natural language processing and graph neural networks to aggregated structural and genetic data. The study will integrate databases including DisProt, ClinVar, and the Human Cell Atlas into a unified schema using a Neo4j graph database mapped via UniProt accession numbers and genomic coordinates. The resulting computational framework will translate sequence data directly into cellular phenotypes, significantly advancing the fundamental connection between linear molecular sequences, three dimensional mesoscale structures, and complex disease states.
full_text: This study investigates biomolecular condensates to explain how protein sequences govern liquid phase separation and influence phenotypes of disease. Researchers recognize specific amino acids that drive phase separation but lack knowledge regarding synergistic combinations for functions of condensates. The primary question asks how sequences dictate properties of condensates to directly link linear molecules with states of disease. The study design aggregates genetic and structural data to train computational models for predicting behavior of phase separation. Key methods include transformer based processing of natural language and graph neural networks alongside algorithms for clustering of data. The team will validate results using five fold cross validation and benchmarking against predictions from AlphaFold-Multimer and control proteins. Researchers will utilize datasets from UniProt and ClinVar along with structural information from the Protein Data Bank and AlphaFold Database. The project integrates data within a Neo4j graph database using accession numbers from UniProt and coordinates from genome reference GRCh38. The team addresses variable quality of data by enforcing cutoffs for structural resolution and applying normalization to the datasets. The three year timeline dedicates the first year to pipelines for data before developing networks and releasing tools in year three. This cross disciplinary collaboration is necessary because integrating molecular and genetic data requires expertise exceeding a single laboratory. The researchers will share code and models under open source licenses via Zenodo alongside publications with open access. The cross disciplinary team unites principal investigators and graduate students who will receive training through workshops for the community.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates represent a paradigmatic example of mesoscale emergence, where intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) self-organize into membraneless organelles with properties not predictable from individual molecular components. This synthesis project will decode the 'grammar' connecting IDP sequence features to emergent condensate behaviors by integrating multiple public datasets. We will synthesize structural data from the Protein Data Bank (PDB), disorder predictions from MobiDB and DisProt, phase separation propensity scores from PhaSePro and LLPSDB, proteomics data from the Human Protein Atlas, and single-cell RNA-seq data from the Human Cell Atlas to understand how sequence-encoded information translates to mesoscale organization. The central hypothesis is that specific combinations of sequence motifs—rather than individual features—create emergent interaction networks that dictate condensate material properties, composition, and cellular function. We will employ natural language processing approaches adapted for protein sequences, treating amino acid patterns as a 'language' with grammatical rules governing phase behavior. Machine learning models will identify synergistic motif combinations that predict condensate viscosity, surface tension, and client recruitment capacity. title: Temporal Dynamics of Ribosome Clustering: Synthesizing Cryo-ET and Ribosome Profiling Data to Understand Emergent Translation Factories
title_norm: temporal dynamics of ribosome clustering synthesizing cryoet and ribosome profiling data to understand emergent translation factories
abstract_text: Translation biology investigates polysomes, which are 50 to 500 nanometer mesoscale ribosome clusters that dictate crucial translational behaviors including processivity, coordinated protein folding, and localized mRNA regulation. A quantitative framework connecting structural polysome geometry to dynamic translation output remains lacking, leaving an inability to predict emergent translational properties from individual ribosome behaviors or mRNA sequences. This project will determine how mesoscale spatial arrangements of ribosomes generate unique translational properties by integrating structural and sequencing data using convolutional neural networks, stochastic kinetic modeling, and gradient boosting machine learning models. The analysis will synthesize electron tomography, ribosome sequencing, and proteomics datasets from EMPIAR, GEO, and PRIDE by matching mRNA sequence characteristics with corresponding polysome geometries and protein abundance measurements across multiple organisms. This work will establish polysome architecture as a regulatory layer in gene expression, providing predictive models of protein abundance for synthetic biology applications and translation dysregulation disease treatments.
full_text: This project investigates translation biology to establish a quantitative framework connecting polysome geometry to the dynamic output of translation. Ribosomes translate messenger RNA (mRNA) within polysomes of varying configurations and rates but predicting emergent properties remains currently impossible. The study asks how spatial arrangements of ribosomes generate emergent properties to establish architecture as a regulatory layer. The study integrates structural data with metrics of sequencing and proteomics to construct predictive models of dynamic translation. The analytical approach utilizes neural networks for segmentation of images alongside stochastic kinetic modeling and machine learning algorithms. Researchers will validate results using cross dataset evaluation and held out test sets for machine learning alongside positive controls. The project utilizes cryogenic electron tomography (cryo-ET) data from EMPIAR and Ribo-seq data from GEO alongside structural information. The team will synthesize datasets by matching characteristics of sequences with polysome geometries before executing cross species integration. Researchers will mitigate technical variation across heterogeneous experimental conditions by standardizing coordinate systems and applying tools of batch correction. The scope demands cross disciplinary collaboration to unite distributed expertise in analysis of images and mathematical modeling across separate laboratories. The team will deposit databases in Zenodo and publish computational tools on GitHub under permissive open source licenses. The team features postdoctoral researchers and graduate students alongside a software engineer to facilitate training in integration of data.

abstract_original: Translation occurs not through isolated ribosomes but within dynamic mesoscale clusters called 'translation factories' or polysomes, where emergent properties arise from ribosome cooperation. This synthesis project investigates how ribosome clustering creates emergent translational behaviors—including enhanced processivity, coordinated protein folding, and localized mRNA regulation—that cannot be predicted from single ribosome properties. We will integrate cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) data from EMPIAR and EMDB revealing in-situ ribosome spatial organization, ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) data from GEO and GWIPS-viz capturing translation dynamics, structural data from PDB on ribosome-associated factors, and proteomics from PRIDE quantifying translation machinery stoichiometry. The central question is: how do spatial arrangements of ribosomes at the mesoscale (50-500 nm polysome structures) create emergent translational properties distinct from summed individual ribosome activities? Our computational approach combines spatial statistics analysis of cryo-ET reconstructions to characterize ribosome clustering patterns, kinetic modeling of translation dynamics informed by Ribo-seq pausing patterns, and agent-based simulations of polysome behavior. We will develop novel algorithms to segment and classify polysome architectures from tomographic data, then correlate these structures with mRNA-specific translation efficiencies from Ribo-seq. Machine learning will identify features of polysome organization predictive of translation output, protein folding efficiency, and co-translational assembly. Integration with protein-protein interaction networks from STRING and BioGRID will reveal how nascent chain interactions within polysomes enable emergent co-translational complex assembly. This project demands expertise spanning cryo-ET image analysis, translation biology, mathematical modeling, and machine learning—capabilities distributed across specialized laboratories. The data synthesis challenge involves reconciling structural snapshots with dynamic sequencing readouts across different experimental systems. Expected insights include principles governing polysome architecture, quantitative relationships between mesoscale ribosome organization and translation output, and mechanisms of emergent co-translational protein folding. Deliverables include open-source tools for polysome analysis, curated cross-referenced datasets, and predictive models of translation factory behavior. Understanding these emergent translation properties has implications for synthetic biology and diseases involving translation dysregulation.

title: Emergent Mechanics of the Nuclear Pore Complex: Integrating Structural, Biophysical, and Transport Data to Model Collective Gating Behavior
title_norm: emergent mechanics of the nuclear pore complex integrating structural biophysical and transport data to model collective gating behavior
abstract_text: Research examines the nuclear pore complex and its constituent phenylalanine glycine nucleoporins, which function as a selective barrier regulating cellular transport where scaffold features and bulk transport speeds are documented. However, the spatial arrangement of the unstructured nucleoporin meshwork inside the pore remains undetermined, highlighting the lack of a mechanistic model linking structural organization to selective permeability. The objective is to determine how combined nucleoporin movements allow specific molecules to pass while blocking others; the project will integrate structural and kinetic data into computational simulations using coarse grained molecular dynamics and machine learning. Data from UniProt, Protein Data Bank, and AlphaFold Protein Structure Database will be consolidated into a relational database using sequence identifiers to align structural data and standardize transport conditions using a defined ontology. The research will explain how unstructured proteins combine into functional cellular barriers, providing information relevant to viral infection processes, neurodegenerative disease mechanisms, and the construction of synthetic biological filters.
full_text: The research examines transport through the nuclear pore complex to link the physical movements of nucleoporins with selective permeability. The structures of scaffolds and transport speeds are established but the internal spatial arrangement of unstructured nucleoporins remains undetermined. The proposed study investigates how collective movements of nucleoporins filter molecules to clarify the formation of functional cellular barriers. The overall study design integrates published structural and molecular data to construct computational simulations of pore gating behavior. The analytical approach applies coarse grained molecular dynamics simulations using OpenMM alongside Markov state modeling and machine learning algorithms. Computational predictions will be evaluated against independent experimental transport measurements and results from chemical perturbations and mutation studies. The project analyzes datasets from the Electron Microscopy Data Bank and UniProt alongside the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database. Researchers will integrate this information into a relational database using sequence identifiers to align structural and modification data. The researchers will mitigate variations across historical transport studies by establishing an ontology to adjust for differing temperatures. The three year project advances from database construction to model parameterization and concludes with the public release of results. This scope requires a cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in structural biology and polymer physics with bioinformatics. The researchers will share materials by depositing databases in institutional repositories and maintaining project code on public platforms. The research group includes faculty and graduate students from four academic institutions to provide cross disciplinary training opportunities.

abstract_original: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) exemplifies mesoscale emergence: ~500 intrinsically disordered FG-nucleoporins create a selective barrier with transport properties unpredictable from individual protein behaviors. This synthesis project will develop comprehensive models of emergent NPC gating by integrating diverse public datasets. We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB capturing NPC architecture, molecular dynamics trajectories from GPCRmd and similar repositories, single-molecule transport kinetics from published studies compiled in curated databases, FG-nup sequence data from UniProt, and nuclear proteomics from the Human Protein Atlas defining cargo flux. The fundamental question is: how do collective FG-nup dynamics create the emergent selective barrier that simultaneously enables rapid transport of specific cargoes while excluding others? We hypothesize that emergent selectivity arises from mesoscale FG-nup network properties—including collective conformational states, transient crosslinks, and cargo-induced reorganization—rather than simple additive binding interactions. Our analytical approach employs coarse-grained molecular dynamics informed by structural data to simulate FG-nup meshwork behavior, network theory to model connectivity patterns, and machine learning to identify collective states from simulation ensembles. We will develop Markov state models capturing transitions between emergent barrier configurations, correlating these with experimental transport rates. Integration of phosphoproteomics data from PhosphoSitePlus will reveal how post-translational modifications tune emergent barrier properties. Cross-species comparative analysis using orthologous NPC data will identify conserved principles of emergent selectivity. This project requires collaboration between structural biologists interpreting NPC architecture, polymer physicists modeling FG-nup behavior, computational chemists running simulations, and cell biologists understanding transport regulation. The synthesis challenge—connecting angstrom-scale structural data to nanometer-scale meshwork organization to micron-scale transport phenotypes—exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include mechanistic models of emergent NPC selectivity, identification of collective FG-nup states governing transport, and principles applicable to designing synthetic selective barriers. All simulation protocols, analysis code, and model parameters will be openly shared, enabling community refinement of NPC models.

title: Chromatin Compartmentalization Dynamics: Synthesizing Hi-C, Imaging, and Epigenomic Data to Model Emergent Nuclear Organization
title_norm: chromatin compartmentalization dynamics synthesizing hic imaging and epigenomic data to model emergent nuclear organization
abstract_text: Within chromosome biology, multivalent protein interactions drive the phase separation of chromatin into mesoscale compartments and domains to form the hierarchical genome structures essential for cellular function. The biophysical parameters of histone modifications remain unquantified, leaving a critical lack of quantitative rules to link molecular level changes to mesoscale compartmentalization and structural variability. This project will perform a cross cell type meta analysis to integrate multimodal data, applying block copolymer physics simulations, approximate Bayesian computation, and deep neural networks to determine the molecular drivers of nuclear compartmentalization. The study will align public datasets from ENCODE, Roadmap Epigenomics, and the 4D Nucleome Data Portal to common reference genomes, merging the information into a unified coordinate system using transfer learning. This research will yield predictive models for nuclear architecture, establishing the mechanistic frameworks necessary to understand downstream biological functions such as transcription, replication, and DNA repair.
full_text: The domain of chromosome biophysics explores chromatin organization but lacks quantitative rules connecting molecular modifications to mesoscale nuclear compartments. Genomes assemble into hierarchical structures via phase separation but the exact biophysical parameters of histone modifications remain entirely unquantified. The proposed study integrates multimodal data to uncover the molecular drivers of nuclear architecture and predict downstream biological functions. The analytical strategy relies on a secondary synthesis of public multimodal data to train computational models without new experiments. Key methods involve physics simulations of block copolymers via OpenMM and deep neural networks paired with transfer learning algorithms. The team validates predictions computationally using held out cell types and direct correlations with expression data from matched RNA-seq. The project analyzes fifty terabytes of data from the 4D Nucleome Data Portal and the Human Cell Atlas. Researchers align datasets to common reference genomes and utilize transfer learning to map unmatched information between related cell types. Investigators mitigate technical batch effects across laboratories by applying ComBat to sequencing information and intensity normalization to imaging sets. The three year timeline progresses from the initial harmonization of data to the final release of public software tools. This ambitious scope exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory and requires extensive cross disciplinary collaboration across multiple domains. The team distributes integrated datasets through public portals and shares analysis pipelines using permanent repositories such as GitHub. The cross disciplinary group provides comprehensive training for doctoral students and postdoctoral researchers working alongside five principal investigators.

abstract_original: Chromatin organization into A/B compartments, topologically associating domains (TADs), and nuclear bodies represents emergent mesoscale structure arising from DNA-protein interactions. This synthesis project will integrate multi-modal data to understand how molecular-level chromatin modifications create emergent nuclear compartmentalization with functional consequences. We will synthesize Hi-C contact maps from 4DN Data Portal and ENCODE, super-resolution imaging data from the Image Data Resource and Cell Image Library, ChIP-seq for histone modifications and chromatin proteins from ENCODE and Roadmap Epigenomics, ATAC-seq accessibility data, and single-cell multi-omics from the Human Cell Atlas. The central hypothesis is that emergent compartmentalization arises from phase separation driven by multivalent interactions among modified histones and reader proteins, creating mesoscale domains (100 nm - 1 μm) with distinct biochemical environments. We will develop integrative computational frameworks combining polymer physics models of chromatin, machine learning for predicting 3D organization from sequence and epigenetic features, and spatial statistics for analyzing imaging data. Novel algorithms will integrate contact frequencies with spatial positions, resolving the relationship between measured interactions and physical distances. Network analysis will identify emergent chromatin communities and their hierarchical organization. We will correlate compartmentalization patterns with transcriptional output using RNA-seq from matched samples, testing whether emergent nuclear organization causally influences gene expression or vice versa. Cross-cell-type analysis will reveal conserved versus cell-specific emergent organizational principles. This project demands expertise in chromosome biology, polymer physics, image analysis, machine learning, and genomics—requiring collaboration across traditionally separate fields. The data integration challenge spans contact maps, images, and sequencing data at different resolutions and from different experimental systems. Expected insights include quantitative models of compartmentalization emergence, identification of key molecular drivers of mesoscale organization, and understanding of how nuclear structure influences function. All analysis pipelines, trained models, and integrated datasets will be publicly released, establishing resources for the chromosome biology community.

title: Emergent Allostery in Protein Complexes: Mining Structural Databases to Discover Long-Range Communication Networks
title_norm: emergent allostery in protein complexes mining structural databases to discover longrange communication networks
abstract_text: Within the domain of structural biology and computational biophysics, long range allosteric regulation emerges as a fundamentally important communication network within assembled multi subunit protein complexes at the nanometer scale. Despite abundant large scale structural databases, the specific mechanisms governing mesoscale allosteric communication remain undetermined, presenting a critical gap in predicting allosteric sites within uncharacterized multi subunit protein assemblies. This project will identify features enabling long range allosteric communication and construct predictive computational models by synthesizing data across thousands of protein complexes using graph theoretical network analysis, elastic network models, and machine learning ensemble classifiers. The research will integrate major structural and mutational repositories such as the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold, and ClinVar by mapping information to standardized structures using UniProt accessions, TM align, and SIFTS. This approach will produce computational models for predicting allosteric sites, providing a novel framework for designing selective allosteric modulators in drug development and functionally explaining disease associated mutations.
full_text: Identifying structural features that drive allosteric regulation across multi subunit complexes remains unsolved within structural biology and computational biophysics. Extensive databases reveal allosteric behavior emerging in assembled complexes but specific mechanisms governing networks for mesoscale communication remain undetermined. Identifying features of allosteric communication will yield computational models for designing modulators and explaining mutations associated with disease. This computational project integrates diverse biological records to statistically compare assemblies with allosteric behavior against non allosteric assemblies. The methodology applies graph theoretical analysis and direct coupling analysis alongside methods of machine learning for prediction of allosteric sites. The team will validate results through comparisons of independent datasets and benchmarking against positive controls and mutations causing disease. The study utilizes datasets including the Protein Data Bank and AlphaFold alongside databases of mutations like ClinVar and COSMIC. The team will integrate distinct datasets by mapping information to structures and standardizing numbering of residues using mappings from SIFTS. The project manages limitations like missing residues and mismatches in sequences through pipelines for automated detection and manual curation by experts. The three year timeline progresses from harmonization of data to predictive modeling before culminating in deployment of public tools. Integrating diverse streams of biological information demands cross disciplinary collaboration across specialized domains of structural biochemistry and machine learning. The team will release public databases and open source tools while archiving data and sharing early findings through preprints. The group combines principal investigators and early career researchers to provide training in cross disciplinary synthesis and development of software.

This synthesis project will systematically discover and characterize emergent allosteric networks by mining structural databases. We will integrate the Protein Data Bank (>200,000 structures), molecular dynamics trajectories from MDAnalysis and related repositories, hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) data from HDXsite, and mutational fitness landscapes from deep mutational scanning datasets in MaveDB. The central question is: what structural and dynamic features enable emergent long-range communication in protein complexes that individual subunits lack? We hypothesize that emergent allostery requires specific mesoscale organizational features—interface geometries, dynamic coupling patterns, and evolutionary constraints—that create communication pathways spanning 10-100 nm distances. Our computational approach combines graph-theoretical analysis of structure networks, normal mode analysis for collective motions, machine learning to predict allosteric sites from structural features, and evolutionary analysis to identify co-evolving residue networks. We will develop algorithms to automatically identify allosteric pathways by analyzing conformational ensembles across ligand-bound and apo states. Integration with disease mutation databases (ClinVar, COSMIC) will connect disrupted allosteric networks to pathological phenotypes. Comparative analysis across protein families will reveal conserved principles of emergent allostery versus family-specific mechanisms. This project requires expertise spanning structural biology, protein dynamics, evolutionary biology, and machine learning—necessitating collaboration between computationally-focused and experimentally-informed laboratories. The synthesis of structural, dynamic, evolutionary, and phenotypic data across thousands of protein complexes exceeds any single lab's capacity. Expected outcomes include a comprehensive atlas of emergent allosteric networks, predictive models for allosteric site identification, and mechanistic principles governing long-range communication. All databases, analysis tools, and predictive models will be openly released, enabling rational design of allosteric modulators and understanding of how complex-level properties emerge from subunit assembly.

title: Cytoskeletal Crosstalk at the Mesoscale: Integrating Structural and Live-Cell Data to Model Emergent Mechanical Properties
title_norm: cytoskeletal crosstalk at the mesoscale integrating structural and livecell data to model emergent mechanical properties
abstract_text: The field of cytoskeletal biology investigates how mesoscale interactions among actin filaments, microtubules, and intermediate filaments govern cellular mechanical properties by bridging nanometer scale behaviors and micrometer scale mechanics. However, the principles of intervening mesoscale organization remain unmapped, leaving a scientific gap in understanding how network topology, crosslinker dynamics, and filament arrangement determine cellular mechanical outcomes. This project will determine how dynamic structural organization and specific crosslinker proteins generate mechanical properties by applying deep learning image segmentation, graph based filament tracing, machine learning, and finite element modeling. The study will integrate imaging, proteomic, and transcriptomic datasets from repositories including EMPIAR, BioPlex, and GEO by extracting uniform mathematical descriptors of mesoscale organization to enable multiscale computational modeling. This framework will produce novel knowledge explaining how cellular mechanical properties regulate basic biological processes, tissue dynamics, and disease pathology to advance downstream research across scales.
full_text: Cytoskeletal biology lacks understanding of how mesoscale network topology and filament interactions determine the mechanical properties of cells. Nanometer scale filament properties and micrometer scale cellular mechanics are established but the intervening mesoscale organization remains unmapped. The project determines how mesoscale network topology generates mechanical properties to explain the regulation of basic biological processes. The overall strategy integrates public datasets across multiple modalities by combining custom pipelines for image analysis and computational modeling. The analytical approach utilizes U-Net architectures for segmentation of images alongside agent based simulations in Cytosim and XGBoost. Results will be validated using cross validation on held out data and benchmarking against phenotypes of crosslinker knockouts. Sources include structural data from the BioImage Archive and transcriptomics from the Gene Expression Omnibus and the Human Cell Atlas. The project integrates these datasets by extracting uniform mathematical descriptors of mesoscale organization to enable registration across modalities. The heterogeneity of repositories and formats will be addressed by developing standardized structural descriptors and utilizing multiscale modeling. The three year timeline involves building a database of mechanics before validating predictive models and finalizing functional principles. This scope requires multi lab collaboration to integrate domain expertise across cytoskeletal biology and computational modeling and data science. The team will deposit datasets in Zenodo and share code on GitHub while publishing in open access journals. The group includes principal investigators and graduate students to provide cross disciplinary training in data management and systems biology.

title: Emergent Specificity in Kinase-Substrate Networks: Synthesizing Phosphoproteomics and Structural Data to Decode Signaling Fidelity
title_norm: emergent specificity in kinasesubstrate networks synthesizing phosphoproteomics and structural data to decode signaling fidelity
abstract_text: Cellular signaling networks rely on mesoscale organizational features such as scaffolds and subcellular localization to determine kinase substrate specificity, but models relying only on sequence motifs remain limited in predictive accuracy. There is no systematic proteome wide framework explaining how mesoscale spatial and temporal organization establishes signaling specificity despite overlapping sequence preferences or how mutations disrupt this organization. This study will determine how mesoscale organization controls kinase substrate specificity, temporal dynamics, and aberrant signaling by integrating multi omics data into knowledge graphs and applying graph neural networks, gradient boosted trees, and ordinary differential equations. Datasets from PhosphoSitePlus, Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold, and BioGRID will be synthesized into a unified knowledge graph where nodes represent proteins and compartments while edges define structural interactions and spatial relationships. This work will deliver an organization centric framework of cellular signaling that provides quantitative mechanisms for context dependent pathway variations and off target effects of kinase inhibitors.
full_text: This project investigates cellular signaling networks to understand how mesoscale organization controls the specificity of kinase substrates despite overlapping preferences. Current models acknowledge sequence motifs and spatial compartmentalization but lack a systematic framework integrating temporal dynamics with disease mutations. The study asks how mesoscale features establish specificity to provide quantitative mechanisms for context dependent variations of cellular signaling. This computational synthesis of public datasets builds a knowledge graph to train machine learning models for predicting phosphorylation. The team will apply gradient boosted trees and graph neural networks alongside modeling of ordinary differential equations and AlphaFold-Multimer. The researchers will validate results using temporally split datasets and computational benchmarking against well characterized pathways like MAPK. The project utilizes databases including PhosphoSitePlus and UniProt alongside the Protein Data Bank and the Human Protein Atlas. These distinct datasets will form a unified knowledge graph where nodes represent proteins and edges capture distinct spatial relationships. The study mitigates data heterogeneity by filtering phosphosites using evidence levels and weighting interactions with scores of established confidence. The three year timeline encompasses harmonization of data followed by modeling of temporal dynamics and analysis of disease mutations. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to integrate massive datasets using distributed expertise in structural biology and data science. The team will release open source software packages and deposit the knowledge graph into public repositories like Zenodo. This interdisciplinary team includes postdoctoral researchers and a software engineer who will host annual training workshops for students.

abstract_original: Cellular signaling networks achieve remarkable specificity despite kinases sharing similar catalytic mechanisms—an emergent property arising from mesoscale organization including scaffolds, localization, and temporal dynamics. This synthesis project will decode how emergent specificity arises by integrating phosphoproteomics, structural biology, and cell biology datasets. We will synthesize phosphoproteomic data from PhosphoSitePlus and PRIDE (>300,000 phosphosites), kinase-substrate relationships from PhosphoSitePlus and KinaseNET, structural data from PDB on kinase-substrate complexes, protein localization from the Human Protein Atlas, and protein-protein interactions from BioGRID and STRING. The central hypothesis is that signaling specificity emerges from mesoscale organizational features—scaffold-mediated co-localization, compartmentalization, and kinetic proofreading networks—rather than intrinsic kinase-substrate affinity alone. We will develop computational frameworks integrating sequence-based kinase specificity predictions with spatial and temporal context. Machine learning models will predict phosphorylation events by combining kinase motif recognition with localization overlap, scaffold interactions, and network topology. We will construct dynamic models of signaling cascades incorporating mesoscale organization, testing whether emergent specificity requires spatial constraints. Analysis of phosphoproteomic time-series data will reveal how temporal ordering creates emergent pathway specificity. Integration with disease mutation data from COSMIC and ClinVar will identify how disrupted mesoscale organization causes aberrant signaling. Cross-species comparative analysis will distinguish conserved emergent specificity mechanisms from species-specific adaptations. This project requires collaboration between signaling biologists, structural biologists, computational modelers, and data scientists—expertise distributed across institutions. The synthesis of structural, proteomic, localization, and interaction data at proteome scale exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent signaling specificity, identification of key organizational features enabling fidelity, and principles for predicting signaling outcomes. All predictive models, analysis pipelines, and integrated datasets will be openly released, enabling rational intervention in signaling pathways.

title: Metabolon Assembly and Emergent Metabolic Channeling: Integrating Structural, Metabolomic, and Interactome Data
title_norm: metabolon assembly and emergent metabolic channeling integrating structural metabolomic and interactome data
abstract_text: Cellular metabolism relies on transient mesoscale enzyme assemblies called metabolons to facilitate substrate channeling, which represents a crucial biological phenomenon supported by physical and chemical evidence from structural and metabolomic studies. Systematic knowledge regarding the full landscape of metabolon forming pathways, their structural principles, and cross species architectural conservation remains incomplete because existing data is highly fragmented. To systematically characterize metabolon organization and substrate channeling, this project will apply network clustering algorithms, computational docking tools, machine learning classifiers, and constraint based metabolic models to determine how mesoscale enzyme clustering alters metabolic properties. The research will integrate datasets from structural and metabolic databases including the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, and BRENDA by mapping all entries to common UniProt accessions within a unified schema. This effort will generate foundational resources detailing mesoscale cellular organization to facilitate the identification of therapeutic targets in metabolic diseases and the engineering of microbial cell factories.
full_text: This project studies cellular metabolism and metabolons to resolve fragmented knowledge regarding pathway formation and structural assembly principles. Structural evidence demonstrates transient complex formation for substrate channeling while understanding of regulatory mechanisms and cross species conservation remains incomplete. The proposed study systematically characterizes metabolon organization to uncover basic organizational principles and identify therapeutic targets for metabolic diseases. The overall study design acquires public data to identify metabolons before developing kinetic models and performing cross species comparisons. The core strategy utilizes network clustering algorithms and machine learning classifiers (XGBoost) alongside computational docking tools and constraint based models. The team validates results by comparing computational predictions against measured intermediate concentrations and evaluating models through cross validation metrics. This project extracts information from public databases like the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and the Human Metabolome Database (HMDB). The synthesis plan integrates datasets by mapping entries to common accessions (UniProt) and organizing pathway annotations within a unified schema. The team mitigates missing experimental structures through computational docking and estimates missing kinetic parameters using trained machine learning models. The three year timeline encompasses initial database releases and subsequent algorithm publications before concluding with final synthesis publications and workshops. This project requires multi lab collaboration because the vast data volume and diverse analytical methods exceed single laboratory capacities. The team shares findings in open access journals and deposits reproducible analysis pipelines alongside computational models into public repositories. The cross disciplinary team combines principal investigators and early career researchers to facilitate comprehensive training opportunities across multiple scientific fields.

abstract_original: Metabolons—transient enzyme assemblies enabling substrate channeling—represent emergent mesoscale organization where metabolic efficiency exceeds predictions from isolated enzyme kinetics. This synthesis project will systematically characterize metabolon organization and emergent channeling by integrating diverse public datasets. We will synthesize protein-protein interaction data from BioGRID and IntAct, structural data from PDB on enzyme complexes, metabolomics from MetaboLights and the Human Metabolome Database, enzyme kinetics from BRENDA, and proteomics from the Human Protein Atlas. The fundamental question is: how does mesoscale enzyme clustering create emergent metabolic properties—enhanced flux, reduced intermediate accumulation, pathway insulation—that isolated enzymes cannot achieve? We hypothesize that metabolon assembly creates microenvironments with emergent kinetic properties determined by enzyme stoichiometry, spatial arrangement, and dynamic association/dissociation. Our computational approach combines constraint-based metabolic modeling incorporating channeling, molecular docking to predict enzyme complex geometries, and kinetic simulations of substrate transfer within assemblies. We will develop algorithms to identify putative metabolons from interaction networks, validating predictions against metabolomic signatures of channeling (reduced free intermediate pools). Machine learning will predict metabolon formation propensity from enzyme properties and cellular conditions. Integration with transcriptomic data will reveal how metabolon assembly responds to metabolic demands. Analysis across organisms will identify conserved metabolon architectures versus species-specific adaptations. This project demands expertise in metabolism, structural biology, systems biology, and computational chemistry—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of interaction, structural, kinetic, and metabolomic data across metabolic pathways exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include a comprehensive metabolon atlas, predictive models of emergent channeling efficiency, and principles governing metabolon assembly. Understanding emergent metabolic organization has implications for metabolic engineering and diseases involving metabolic dysfunction. All databases, models, and analysis tools will be openly released following FAIR principles.

title: Emergent Selectivity of Autophagy Receptors: Synthesizing Structural and Proteomic Data to Decode Cargo Recognition Networks
title_norm: emergent selectivity of autophagy receptors synthesizing structural and proteomic data to decode cargo recognition networks
abstract_text: The selective autophagy domain investigates crucial interactions between autophagy receptors and cellular cargo at the 10 to 1000 nanometer mesoscale, where distinct receptor domains govern oligomerization, phase separation, and cargo binding. This project will determine how autophagy receptors generate cargo selectivity through structural oligomerization, multiple feature detection, and liquid liquid phase separation by synthesizing proteomic data via graph neural networks and GROMACS coarse grained simulations. Datasets from the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, BioGRID, and PhosphoSitePlus will be integrated by converting identifiers to UniProt standards and merging network interactions utilizing normalized, confidence weighted scores. Quantifying how receptors achieve cargo selectivity will yield a novel framework for manipulating autophagy and modeling other mesoscale biological systems, addressing defects that drive Parkinson disease and inflammatory disorders.
full_text: The field of selective autophagy lacks understanding of how weak interactions of receptors achieve recognition of cargo through mesoscale properties. This study determines how structural oligomerization generates selectivity of cargo to provide frameworks for treating diseases like Parkinson disease. The overall design synthesizes existing structural data to build models and compare mechanisms across pathways of selective autophagy. The team applies predictive algorithms like XGBoost for machine learning and GROMACS for complex simulations of molecular dynamics. Researchers validate analytical results by comparing predicted effects of mutations against documented clinical phenotypes and independent experimental datasets. The proposed study utilizes several large databases including the Protein Data Bank and the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database. The team integrates distinct datasets by converting identifiers of proteins to UniProt standards and merging interactions using normalized scores. The research team mitigates missing structural data for specific proteins by substituting predicted models from the AlphaFold database. This project follows a thirty six month timeline moving from initial acquisition of data to final release of software. This scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration because building predictive models demands specialized computational expertise beyond a single laboratory. The researchers will publish open access papers and distribute computational code via GitHub to ensure broad public availability. The research group encompasses diverse career stages and disciplines to provide students with rigorous training in curation of data.
