abstract_original: Selective autophagy achieves remarkable cargo specificity through receptor proteins that bridge substrates to autophagosomes—an emergent property arising from multivalent interactions at the mesoscale. This synthesis project will decode how autophagy receptors create emergent selectivity by integrating structural biology, proteomics, and cell biology datasets. We will synthesize structural data from PDB on receptor-cargo and receptor-LC3 complexes, autophagy interactomes from BioGRID and published studies, ubiquitin-modified proteomics from PhosphoSitePlus, organelle proteomics from the Human Protein Atlas, and autophagy flux measurements from published screens. The central question is: how do autophagy receptors create emergent selectivity at the mesoscale (10-1000 nm cargo structures) through avidity effects, coincidence detection, and cooperative binding that individual receptor-cargo interactions cannot achieve? We hypothesize that emergent selectivity arises from receptor oligomerization, multivalent cargo recognition, and phase separation creating receptor condensates that amplify weak individual interactions. Our computational approach combines structural modeling of receptor-cargo assemblies, network analysis of autophagy interactomes, and machine learning to predict cargo selectivity from receptor and cargo features. We will develop coarse-grained simulations of receptor clustering on cargo surfaces, testing how avidity emerges from receptor density and cargo geometry. Integration with disease mutation data will connect disrupted receptor-cargo recognition to pathological cargo accumulation. Comparative analysis across selective autophagy pathways (mitophagy, aggrephagy, xenophagy) will reveal shared versus pathway-specific emergent selectivity mechanisms. This project requires expertise in autophagy biology, structural biology, computational modeling, and proteomics—necessitating collaboration across specialized laboratories. The synthesis of structural, proteomic, and phenotypic data across autophagy pathways exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include mechanistic models of emergent selectivity, identification of key features determining cargo recognition, and principles for engineering selective autophagy. All analysis tools, models, and curated datasets will be openly released, advancing understanding of this therapeutically important pathway.

title: Emergent Timing in Circadian Protein Networks: Integrating Structural Dynamics with Systems-Level Oscillations
title_norm: emergent timing in circadian protein networks integrating structural dynamics with systemslevel oscillations
abstract_text: Circadian biology examines how 24 hour periodic rhythms emerge from mesoscale protein interaction networks, essential for understanding how individual molecular components integrate to produce system level oscillatory delays and rhythmic robustness. To determine how mesoscale protein assembly dynamics and modification cascades generate emergent 24 hour timing, this project will computationally synthesize multiscale datasets using ordinary differential equation modeling, molecular dynamics simulations, and machine learning models. Structural, proteomic, and transcriptomic data from repositories including Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold, PRIDE, and CircaDB will be integrated by mapping entities to UniProt identifiers and converting time series data into standardized circadian phases. This research will define the physical mechanisms of biological timing, yielding predictive multiscale models that will facilitate advanced clinical applications in chronotherapy and metabolic disease management.
full_text: This project within circadian biology investigates how identical components within networks of proteins generate distinct oscillatory periods across species. Current knowledge details structures of circadian proteins but understanding of their integration to produce robust oscillatory delays remains incomplete. The primary question asks how dynamics concerning the assembly of proteins generate circadian timing to yield models for chronotherapy. The overall design uses a computational synthesis of existing datasets to perform kinetic modeling without new experimental collection. Key methods include simulations of molecular dynamics and models of machine learning alongside modeling with ordinary differential equations. The team will evaluate predictions through validation across datasets and comparisons against positive controls from independent experimental literature. The study uses sources like the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database alongside UniProt. The team will integrate distinct datasets by mapping entities to UniProt identifiers and applying algorithms for batch correction. The researchers will substitute missing structures of proteins with predictions and manage inconsistencies across laboratories using automated pipelines. The project spans three years and progresses from integration of databases to the public release of analytical resources. Integrating diverse types of data across biological scales requires collaboration across disciplines among laboratories specializing in computational biology. The team will publish findings in open access journals and release all databases for public use and maintenance. The diverse team includes principal investigators and graduate students who will receive training through workshops and computational tutorials.

This synthesis project will decode how circadian timing emerges by integrating structural biology, proteomics, and systems biology datasets. We will synthesize structural data from PDB on clock protein complexes, phosphoproteomics time-series from published circadian studies, protein-protein interactions from BioGRID, transcriptomics from CircaDB and CGDB, and protein stability measurements from published datasets. The fundamental question is: how do post-translational modifications and protein-protein interactions at the mesoscale create emergent oscillatory behavior with ~24-hour periodicity? We hypothesize that emergent timing arises from coupled feedback loops operating through mesoscale protein complexes whose assembly/disassembly dynamics create delays essential for oscillation. Our computational approach combines mathematical modeling of circadian networks, molecular dynamics simulations of clock protein complexes, and machine learning to identify structural features governing interaction kinetics. We will develop models incorporating explicit protein complex formation, testing how mesoscale assembly creates emergent delays. Analysis of phosphoproteomic time-series will reveal how modification cascades propagate through clock protein networks. Integration with tissue-specific expression data will explain how the same molecular components generate different emergent periods across tissues. Comparative analysis across species will identify conserved emergent timing mechanisms versus species-specific adaptations. The synthesis of structural, dynamic, and systems-level data across circadian networks exceeds single-lab scope. title: Emergent Proton Gradients in Mitochondrial Cristae: Synthesizing Cryo-ET and Bioenergetic Data to Model Mesoscale Energy Transduction
title_norm: emergent proton gradients in mitochondrial cristae synthesizing cryoet and bioenergetic data to model mesoscale energy transduction
abstract_text: Mitochondrial bioenergetics investigates how the mesoscale three dimensional architecture of inner membrane cristae relates to emergent proton gradients and ATP synthesis, which is essential to ground theoretical models in empirical reality. The field currently lacks quantitative correlations that link cristae morphological geometry and the spatial organization of respiratory chain supercomplexes to actual tomographic geometries and empirical bioenergetic measurements. This project will determine how cristae morphology and supercomplex arrangement generate high ATP synthesis rates by applying a multi scale computational synthesis featuring deep learning based image segmentation, finite element modeling, and coarse grained molecular dynamics. The synthesis will integrate inputs from databases including EMPIAR, the Protein Data Bank, and MitoCarta by mapping experimental variables to a custom metadata ontology stored within a standardized relational database. This framework will establish a quantitative structure to function link for mitochondrial architecture, providing a mechanistic basis to evaluate how physical defects contribute to metabolic and aging related diseases.
full_text: This project investigates mitochondrial bioenergetics to resolve the missing quantitative correlation between three dimensional cristae architecture and ATP synthesis. Current models of proton diffusion remain incomplete without rigorous testing against tomographic geometries and empirical measurements of bioenergetic activity. The research determines how cristae morphology drives ATP synthesis to provide a quantitative foundation for evaluating metabolic diseases. The study design features a retrospective computational synthesis integrating progressive phases of data harmonization and comprehensive biophysical modeling. Researchers will apply deep learning image segmentation alongside coarse grained molecular dynamics and finite element modeling of transport. The team will validate computational predictions of ATP synthesis and local gradients against published experimental data and clinical records. This project relies on diverse databases including the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and ClinVar to gather structural information. Investigators will integrate datasets by mapping inputs to a custom metadata ontology within a standardized relational database system. The team will mitigate the known limitation of experimental variability by applying hierarchical Bayesian models during data harmonization. The three year timeline prioritizes initial data collection before advancing to computational modeling and final predictive model generation. The project requires cross disciplinary collaboration because successful data integration demands concurrent expertise in structural biology and biophysical modeling. The team will release the integrated database on Zenodo and publish open access findings alongside shared simulation code. The collaborative team includes postdoctoral researchers and a software engineer alongside graduate students receiving cross disciplinary biophysics training.

This synthesis project will decode how cristae geometry creates emergent bioenergetic properties by integrating structural and functional datasets. We will synthesize cryo-ET data from EMPIAR showing cristae ultrastructure, respiratory chain complex structures from PDB, proteomics of mitochondrial composition from MitoCarta and IMPI, metabolomics from MetaboLights, and bioenergetic measurements from published studies. We hypothesize that cristae geometry creates microcompartments where local proton concentrations exceed bulk predictions, and that respiratory chain supercomplex organization within cristae optimizes proton delivery to ATP synthase. Our computational approach combines finite element modeling of proton diffusion within cristae geometries extracted from tomograms, molecular simulations of supercomplex organization, and systems biology modeling of oxidative phosphorylation incorporating spatial structure. We will develop image analysis pipelines to quantify cristae morphology across cell types and conditions, correlating architecture with bioenergetic output. Integration with disease mutation data will connect cristae morphology defects to mitochondrial dysfunction. Comparative analysis across species and tissues will reveal how emergent bioenergetic optimization adapts to metabolic demands. This project requires expertise in mitochondrial biology, cryo-ET, biophysical modeling, and systems biology—necessitating collaboration across specialized fields. The synthesis of structural, proteomic, and bioenergetic data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent proton gradients, identification of key architectural features optimizing ATP synthesis, and principles governing cristae-bioenergetics relationships. Understanding emergent mitochondrial function has implications for aging and metabolic diseases. All simulation code, analysis pipelines, and integrated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Antigen Processing in the Immunoproteasome: Integrating Structural and Immunopeptidomic Data to Model Epitope Generation
title_norm: emergent antigen processing in the immunoproteasome integrating structural and immunopeptidomic data to model epitope generation
abstract_text: Within structural biology and immunology, the immunoproteasome complex alters peptide cleavage patterns for major histocompatibility complex presentation, utilizing distinct catalytic subunits to produce different peptide repertoires compared to constitutive proteasomes. How the assembled physical architecture and spatial arrangement of specific immunosubunits mechanically cause these distinct cleavage specificities is currently not understood. This project will determine how immunoproteasome architecture dictates epitope generation by applying structural feature extraction, deep learning sequence encoding, and bipartite network analysis to correlate physical variations with peptidome composition across physiological conditions. The approach will integrate the Protein Data Bank, Immune Epitope Database, Gene Expression Omnibus, and The Cancer Genome Atlas using a relational model that aligns structural data to link subunit expression with peptide repertoires. This resulting predictive framework will establish general principles for protein complexes and provide fundamental knowledge to advance vaccine design, cancer immunotherapy, and autoimmune disease treatment.
full_text: This structural biology and immunology project investigates how the spatial arrangement of immunoproteasome subunits alters peptide cleavage patterns. The proposed study asks how immunoproteasome architecture dictates epitope generation to inform vaccine design and cancer immunotherapy development. The research team will conduct a computational synthesis of public data to correlate structural features with cleavage preferences. The analytical approach relies on the extraction of structural features and deep learning models to predict cleavage sites. The team will validate results through replication across datasets and testing against known immunoproteasome epitopes as positive controls. The project utilizes resources including the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and the Immune Epitope Database alongside various transcriptomic archives. A relational model will integrate these databases by mapping peptide sequences to reference proteins and aligning structural data. The team will mitigate batch effects across independent datasets by reanalyzing raw data through standardized pipelines and correction tools. The three year timeline includes initial model development followed by dataset integration and a final release of analytical tools. This cross disciplinary collaboration is necessary because the integration of diverse datasets requires concurrent expertise in machine learning and immunology. The team will publish results in open access journals and archive all code on repositories with permanent digital identifiers. The research group includes principal investigators and early career researchers who will receive methodological training during the project.

This project will determine how immunoproteasome architecture dictates epitope generation by applying structural feature extraction, deep learning sequence encoding, and bipartite network analysis to correlate physical variations with peptidome composition across physiological conditions. The approach will integrate the Protein Data Bank, Immune Epitope Database, Gene Expression Omnibus, and The Cancer Genome Atlas using a relational model that aligns structural data to link subunit expression with peptide repertoires. This resulting predictive framework will establish general principles for protein complexes and provide fundamental knowledge to advance vaccine design, cancer immunotherapy, and autoimmune disease treatment.
abstract_original: The immunoproteasome generates MHC-presented peptides through emergent cleavage patterns that differ from constitutive proteasomes—a mesoscale phenomenon where subunit composition alters processing outcomes. This synthesis project will decode how immunoproteasome assembly creates emergent epitope generation by integrating structural biology and immunopeptidomics. We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB of proteasome variants, immunopeptidomic data from IEDB and SysteMHC Atlas, protein sequence data from UniProt, and transcriptomics correlating proteasome subunit expression with peptide repertoires. The central question is: how does immunoproteasome subunit incorporation create emergent cleavage specificities at the mesoscale (the ~15 nm proteasome barrel) that individual catalytic subunits cannot produce? We hypothesize that emergent cleavage patterns arise from allosteric communication between subunits, altered substrate threading, and cooperative effects among catalytic sites that depend on mesoscale proteasome architecture. Our computational approach combines structural modeling of substrate processing through proteasome channels, machine learning to predict cleavage sites from sequence and proteasome composition, and network analysis of epitope generation pathways. We will develop algorithms correlating proteasome subunit expression patterns with immunopeptidome composition across cell types. Integration with T cell epitope databases will connect emergent cleavage to immune recognition. Analysis across disease states (cancer, infection, autoimmunity) will reveal how altered proteasome composition shifts emergent epitope generation. This project demands expertise in proteasome biology, immunology, structural biology, and machine learning—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of structural, immunopeptidomic, and expression data exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include predictive models of emergent epitope generation, identification of key subunit interactions governing cleavage specificity, and principles for modulating antigen processing. Understanding emergent immunoproteasome function has implications for vaccine design and cancer immunotherapy. All predictive models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Selectivity in Nuclear Export: Synthesizing Structural and Transport Data to Model CRM1-Mediated Cargo Recognition
title_norm: emergent selectivity in nuclear export synthesizing structural and transport data to model crm1mediated cargo recognition
abstract_text: Cellular nuclear transport depends on the CRM1 receptor binding to nuclear export signal sequences and forming a ternary complex with RanGTP to selectively move cargo proteins into the cytoplasm. The primary objective is to determine how structural and kinetic ternary complex assembly dynamics control export selectivity; this secondary data analysis will construct computational models using molecular dynamics, kinetic networks, and machine learning. Datasets from the Protein Data Bank, NESdb, ValidNES, the Human Protein Atlas, UniProt, and ClinVar will be linked into a unified relational database and integrated via a Bayesian statistical framework. Modeling these transport mechanics will produce a novel framework to predict the functional effects of disease associated mutations and could clarify the variable efficacy of clinical CRM1 inhibitors.
full_text: This project studies cellular nuclear transport to determine how the CRM1 receptor selectively exports diverse cargo with RanGTP. The CRM1 receptor requires RanGTP to bind export sequences but existing models contradict actual transport kinetics and localization. The study asks how complex assembly dynamics control export selectivity to predict mutation effects and clinical inhibitor efficacy. This secondary data analysis synthesizes existing biological measurements to construct and validate computational models of the export cycle. The team will apply structural clustering and molecular dynamics alongside machine learning algorithms like random forests and neural networks. The team will evaluate computational predictions against independent datasets and published transport kinetics alongside known functional export sequences. The project utilizes information from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and UniProt alongside cancer genome databases and the Cell Atlas. The team will link these sources using common identifiers before a Bayesian statistical framework integrates the heterogeneous variables. The Bayesian framework will mitigate the lack of experimental kinetic measurements by computing missing data to generate uncertainty estimates. The three year project involves database creation in the first year before developing computational models and releasing public resources. The broad scope necessitates a cross disciplinary collaboration because no single research group possesses all the required technical expertise. The team will release datasets and source code through a public web database and established repositories with digital object identifiers (DOIs). The group includes postdoctoral researchers and a scientific programmer alongside graduate students who will receive supervised training in modeling.

This synthesis project will decode emergent export selectivity by integrating structural biology, proteomics, and transport kinetics. We will synthesize structural data from PDB on CRM1-cargo complexes, nuclear export signal (NES) sequences from NESdb and ValidNES, proteomics of nuclear/cytoplasmic distribution from the Human Protein Atlas, and transport kinetics from published single-molecule studies. The central question is: how does CRM1 achieve emergent selectivity for diverse cargoes through mesoscale ternary complex formation with RanGTP that binary CRM1-cargo interactions cannot explain? We hypothesize that emergent selectivity arises from conformational selection, where RanGTP binding creates allosteric changes in CRM1 that differentially stabilize cargo complexes based on NES properties beyond simple affinity. Our computational approach combines molecular dynamics simulations of CRM1-RanGTP-cargo assemblies, machine learning to predict export efficiency from NES sequence and structure, and kinetic modeling of transport incorporating complex assembly dynamics. We will develop algorithms correlating NES features with export kinetics, identifying sequence and structural determinants of emergent selectivity. Integration with disease mutation data will connect disrupted export to pathological phenotypes. Comparative analysis across CRM1 cargoes will reveal shared versus cargo-specific emergent recognition mechanisms. This project requires expertise in nuclear transport, structural biology, computational chemistry, and proteomics—necessitating collaboration across specialized laboratories. The synthesis of structural, sequence, localization, and kinetic data exceeds single-lab capabilities. title: Emergent Cooperativity in Transcription Factor Clusters: Synthesizing ChIP-seq, Structural, and Imaging Data to Model Enhancer Activation
title_norm: emergent cooperativity in transcription factor clusters synthesizing chipseq structural and imaging data to model enhancer activation
abstract_text: Transcriptional regulation relies on the mesoscale clustering of transcription factor molecules at enhancer elements, an essential phenomenon where cooperative assemblies at multiple binding sites drive critical changes in gene expression. The structural rules governing cooperative binding in multiple factor assemblies, the quantitative effects of phase separation, and the ways genetic variants disrupt emergent transcriptional activation currently lack comprehensive definition. This project will determine how transcription factor clustering produces unique emergent activation by applying a computational synthesis strategy that uses thermodynamic modeling, agent based spatial simulations, and machine learning techniques within a graph based cross modal data structure. The research will integrate genomic, structural, and transcriptomic databases including ENCODE, AlphaFold, and the Human Cell Atlas by mapping all coordinates to the GRCh38 genome and connecting enhancer binding patterns to target genes. This predictive framework will link molecular interactions to cellular phenotypes, providing mechanistic explanations for noise buffering and facilitating the identification of critical genetic variants and novel therapeutic targets.
full_text: This project studies transcriptional regulation to explain how clusters of transcription factor molecules at enhancer elements create emergent activation. The field understands structures of isolated interactions but lacks knowledge regarding structural rules for cooperative binding and phase separation. The proposed study investigates how clustering produces unique activation to connect molecular interactions directly to observable cellular phenotypes. The overall design is a computational synthesis project integrating structural and transcriptomic data for analysis of cross modal relationships. Key methods include thermodynamic modeling and convolutional neural networks alongside spatial simulations and models for prediction of variant effects. The team validates models computationally through comparisons against known cooperative pairs and orthogonal datasets of existing genetic perturbations. The project utilizes genomic resources from ENCODE and structural databases including the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and AlphaFold. The team integrates these resources by mapping genomic coordinates to a reference genome to build a graph based framework. The team mitigates missing experimental structures with AlphaFold predictions and resolves heterogeneous data through application of a uniform pipeline. The three year timeline begins with harmonization of data and advances through spatial simulations before concluding with comprehensive integration. This broad scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to provide essential expertise across domains of computational genomics and single cell biology. The project deposits all integrated datasets into Zenodo and releases software pipelines publicly on GitHub as open source packages. The diverse team includes postdoctoral researchers and graduate students who receive training through direct project involvement and annual workshops.

abstract_original: Transcription factor (TF) clustering at enhancers creates emergent transcriptional outputs through cooperative DNA binding and co-activator recruitment—mesoscale phenomena where clustered TFs achieve regulatory outcomes impossible for isolated factors. This synthesis project will decode emergent TF cooperativity by integrating genomics, structural biology, and imaging datasets. We will synthesize ChIP-seq data from ENCODE and ReMap, structural data from PDB on TF-DNA complexes, super-resolution imaging of TF clusters from published studies, and transcriptomics correlating TF binding with gene expression. The central question is: how does TF clustering at enhancers (mesoscale assemblies of 10-100 TF molecules) create emergent transcriptional activation that isolated TF binding cannot achieve? We hypothesize that emergent cooperativity arises from multivalent interactions among TF activation domains, DNA-mediated TF-TF communication, and phase separation creating transcriptional condensates. Our computational approach combines thermodynamic modeling of cooperative DNA binding, machine learning to predict enhancer activity from TF binding patterns, and spatial simulations of TF clustering dynamics. We will develop algorithms integrating ChIP-seq occupancy with structural constraints on TF spacing, predicting cooperative binding configurations. Analysis of single-cell transcriptomics will connect TF cluster heterogeneity to transcriptional noise. Integration with GWAS data will link variants affecting emergent cooperativity to disease phenotypes. This project demands expertise in transcriptional regulation, structural biology, imaging analysis, and computational modeling—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of genomic, structural, and imaging data across regulatory elements exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent TF cooperativity, identification of key features enabling enhancer activation, and principles for predicting transcriptional output from TF binding. Understanding emergent transcriptional regulation has implications for gene therapy and developmental biology. All models, analysis pipelines, and integrated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Viral Assembly: Synthesizing Cryo-EM and Sequence Data to Model How Capsid Geometry Arises from Protein Interactions
title_norm: emergent viral assembly synthesizing cryoem and sequence data to model how capsid geometry arises from protein interactions
abstract_text: Within structural virology and biophysics, the emergent mesoscale organization of viral capsid assembly into icosahedral structures relies upon identical proteins using quasi equivalence to occupy non equivalent shell positions. However, the molecular rules defining how local protein protein interactions dictate geometry, drive conformational switching across viral families, and constrain kinetic assembly pathways remain incompletely understood. This project will determine how local interactions generate global mesoscale capsid geometry by combining structural and sequence data using graph theoretical analysis, coarse grained molecular dynamics in HOOMD blue, and ESM 2 machine learning language models. Data from resources including the Protein Data Bank, EMDB, VIPERdb, and UniProt will be integrated into a PostgreSQL relational database using UniProt accession numbers to connect structural and sequence cross references. This systematic synthesis across viral families will produce predictive models of capsid assembly, establishing a novel framework applicable to antiviral drug design and other mesoscale protein structures.
full_text: Within structural virology and biophysics this project explores how local protein interactions dictate global geometry of mesoscale viral capsids. Extensive databases show identical proteins use quasi equivalence but knowledge regarding the molecular rules for assembly and evolution remains incomplete. By asking how local interactions generate global geometry this project provides the first systematic data synthesis for predicting mesoscale assembly. The study design centers on computational data synthesis to integrate structural analysis with simulations of coarse grained molecular dynamics. Key methods apply tools like BioPython and NetworkX alongside algorithms such as XGBoost and HOOMD-blue for molecular dynamics. The team will validate results using nested cross validation and benchmark predicted interaction rules against withheld structures of high resolution. The project utilizes datasets from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and VIPERdb alongside robust resources from UniProt and NCBI Virus. The team will integrate distinct datasets into a PostgreSQL database by using accession numbers from UniProt to connect structural tables. The team will mitigate inconsistencies in resolution of data by excluding poor structures and validating correspondence between sequences and structures. The three year timeline includes building a curated database initially and releasing tools for prediction during the final year. This scope demands cross disciplinary collaboration because the required synthesis of diverse data exceeds the capacity of one single laboratory. The team will publish findings in open access journals and release pipelines for analysis via GitHub with identifiers from Zenodo. This team spans multiple stages of careers and provides training opportunities for graduate students through funded positions and planned workshops.

This synthesis project will decode emergent capsid assembly by integrating structural biology, biophysics, and evolutionary data. We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB across viral families, capsid protein sequences from UniProt and NCBI, assembly kinetics from published studies, and evolutionary data on capsid diversification. The central question is: how do local protein-protein interactions create emergent global capsid geometry at the mesoscale (20-200 nm particles) with precise curvature, symmetry, and stability? We hypothesize that emergent geometry arises from conformational switching at quasi-equivalent positions, where identical proteins adopt different local environments to achieve global curvature—a mesoscale organizational principle. Our computational approach combines coarse-grained molecular dynamics of capsid assembly, graph-theoretical analysis of protein interaction networks in capsids, and machine learning to predict assembly outcomes from protein sequences. We will develop algorithms to extract interaction rules from structural data, testing whether minimal rule sets can recapitulate emergent capsid geometries. Evolutionary analysis will reveal how emergent assembly properties constrain capsid protein evolution. Integration with fitness data from deep mutational scanning will connect assembly defects to viral phenotypes. This project requires expertise in virology, structural biology, polymer physics, and evolutionary biology—necessitating collaboration across specialized fields. The synthesis of structural, sequence, kinetic, and evolutionary data across viral families exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include general principles of emergent capsid assembly, predictive models of assembly from sequence, and understanding of how evolution shapes emergent viral architecture. Understanding emergent viral assembly has implications for antiviral design and nanotechnology. All simulation code, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Membrane Curvature Sensing: Integrating Structural and Lipidomic Data to Model BAR Domain Collective Behavior
title_norm: emergent membrane curvature sensing integrating structural and lipidomic data to model bar domain collective behavior
abstract_text: Within membrane biology and biophysics, documented individual BAR domain protein structures and binding affinities are essential to understand mesoscale collective behavior in sensing and generating membrane curvature. Currently fragmented data fail to explain how individual proteins interact collectively with lipid heterogeneity to produce emergent membrane curvature sensing and remodeling properties. To determine how BAR domain proteins collectively assemble to generate emergent curvature sensitivity, this project will correlate structural features with cellular localization using coarse grained molecular dynamics, machine learning, and continuum mechanical modeling. The study will integrate datasets from the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, and LIPID MAPS by applying a unified ontology schema, standardizing units, and aligning structures to a common reference frame. By synthesizing these inputs into predictive models of mesoscale membrane remodeling, this computational framework will advance fundamental biological research spanning endocytosis, cell division, viral infection, and neurological disorders.
full_text: Membrane biophysics lacks knowledge of how individual BAR domain proteins assemble to drive mesoscale curvature sensing and remodeling. Current data on individual protein structures and binding affinities cannot explain how mesoscale sensing emerges during collective assembly. This project builds predictive models of collective protein assembly to illuminate cellular processes including endocytosis and viral infection. The study uses a computational approach to correlate structural features of proteins with cellular localization and curvature preferences. Methods include coarse grained molecular dynamics and continuum modeling alongside machine learning and mapping of electrostatic surface potentials. Results will be benchmarked against characterized domains and validated through cross validation across subfamilies and held out sets. The project integrates data from the Protein Data Bank and UniProt alongside the Human Protein Atlas and LipidBank. The team will integrate these datasets by aligning protein structures to a common frame and applying unified schemas. Missing structural data will be mitigated by imputing protein structures with AlphaFold predictions paired to specific confidence scores. The three year project progresses from initial data harmonization toward systematic simulations and final release of integrated tools. Integrating these diverse datasets requires cross disciplinary collaboration to provide essential expertise in membrane biophysics and computational biology. The team will release code on GitHub and share findings through open access publications and public community workshops. The team integrates principal investigators and postdoctoral researchers to provide training opportunities in data science and computational biology.

title: Emergent Prion Strain Properties: Synthesizing Cryo-EM Structures with Clinical Data to Model How Fibril Architecture Determines Pathology
title_norm: emergent prion strain properties synthesizing cryoem structures with clinical data to model how fibril architecture determines pathology
abstract_text: In prion biology and protein misfolding diseases, high resolution structures of the mesoscale fibril architecture of prions, tau, α synuclein, and amyloid β provide critical insights into disease phenotypes. However, quantitative models linking this fibril architecture to specific clinical outcomes remain absent because existing structural and clinical datasets are not systematically integrated to determine how structure influences pathology. To determine how physical dimensions and structural architecture of protein fibrils dictate strain specific pathological behaviors, this project will computationally extract features and correlate them with clinical phenotypes using random forests, graph neural networks, and stochastic mathematical simulations. The study will integrate data from the Protein Data Bank, Electron Microscopy Data Bank, and clinical surveillance archives into a single schema, mapping metrics to the Human Phenotype Ontology and Allen Human Brain Atlas. This framework will establish that biological information is encoded in three dimensional protein assembly architecture, providing a foundational predictive resource to forecast neurodegenerative disease outcomes directly from structural data.
full_text: Research in prion biology lacks quantitative models that connect the mesoscale architecture of fibrils to specific clinical outcomes. Investigators have identified high resolution structures and clinical datasets but have not systematically integrated them for pathological analysis. The proposed study asks how the architecture of fibrils dictates pathology to prove that three dimensional assemblies encode biological information. This project of data synthesis integrates independent databases using machine learning to correlate features of structures with clinical phenotypes. The team will apply graph neural networks and stochastic mathematical simulations alongside tools for structural analysis including UCSF ChimeraX. The researchers will validate results using independent datasets for testing and calculate statistical significance through bootstrapping and permutation testing. Primary data sources include the Protein Data Bank and archives of clinical surveillance such as the European CJD Surveillance Network. A single schema will link features of structures to pathological outcomes using common identifiers and standard clinical ontologies. The study mitigates the limited quantity of available structures by applying regularized regression and ensemble methods of machine learning. The three year timeline progresses from initial acquisition of data to development of models and concludes with public dissemination. The required synthesis of data demands cross disciplinary collaboration to unite expertise in structural biology and clinical neurology. The team will release the resulting database on Zenodo and publish the software for structural analysis on GitHub. The research team unites principal investigators and postdoctoral scholars alongside a graduate student receiving training in data synthesis.

We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB of prion and prion-like fibrils, clinical data from published prion disease cohorts, neuropathological descriptions from brain bank studies, and sequence data from UniProt. The synthesis of structural, clinical, and pathological data exceeds single-lab capabilities. title: Emergent Cell Polarity from Protein Localization Networks: Synthesizing Imaging and Interactome Data to Model Symmetry Breaking
title_norm: emergent cell polarity from protein localization networks synthesizing imaging and interactome data to model symmetry breaking
abstract_text: The domain of cell polarity investigates how mesoscale spatial organization and biological symmetry breaking emerge from initially homogeneous networks of PAR proteins, Rho GTPases, and Crumbs and Scribble complexes. A quantitative systems level understanding of collective emergent dynamics in full polarity networks remains incomplete because current theoretical models only address simplified systems disconnected from comprehensive molecular data. title: Emergent Specificity in Ubiquitin Chain Recognition: Synthesizing Structural and Proteomic Data to Decode the Ubiquitin Code

abstract_text: Ubiquitin biology investigates how mesoscale polyubiquitin chain conformations produce distinct cellular signaling outcomes, which is important because specific linkages correspond to particular cellular functions despite low ubiquitin binding domain affinities. The mechanism by which multivalent cellular receptors selectively recognize specific polyubiquitin chain types remains an open question, particularly regarding how chain length and receptor mutations influence target specificity. The primary objective is to determine how mesoscale polyubiquitin chain conformations generate signaling specificity unachievable by monoubiquitin; this project will synthesize structural and proteomic datasets utilizing molecular dynamics simulations and graph neural networks. Resources including the Protein Data Bank, BioGRID, and AlphaFold Protein Structure Database will be integrated into a relational database utilizing ontology based annotation, UniProt mapping, and uniform conformational descriptor computations. The defined polyubiquitin chain recognition mechanisms will inform the design of targeted protein degradation therapeutics and identify the molecular basis of diseases linked to ubiquitin signaling dysregulation.
full_text: The proposed project within ubiquitin biology investigates how multivalent cellular receptors selectively recognize specific mesoscale polyubiquitin chain conformations. The researchers will publish open access papers and release all simulation code on GitHub alongside public data deposits in Zenodo. title: Emergent RNA Localization: Synthesizing Spatial Transcriptomics and RNA Structure Data to Model mRNA Targeting Networks
title_norm: emergent rna localization synthesizing spatial transcriptomics and rna structure data to model mrna targeting networks
abstract_text: Mesoscale cellular biology investigates the spatial localization of mRNA via RNA binding protein networks and RNA granules, a critical phenomenon currently mapped across large scale spatial, structural, and protein interaction datasets. This project will determine how RNA binding protein networks achieve precise mRNA targeting despite weak affinities by synthesizing diverse datasets using multi modal deep learning architectures, weighted correlation network analysis, community detection algorithms, and spatial statistics. The study will integrate databases including ENCODE, the Human Cell Atlas, and POSTAR3 by mapping transcript annotations to GENCODE v38, establishing unified coordinate systems, and applying platform specific normalization alongside batch correction. Uncovering these targeting mechanisms will elucidate membraneless organelle formation, outline the mechanisms underlying neurodegenerative diseases linked to RNA binding protein mutations, and provide foundational parameters for mRNA therapeutics.
full_text: This project explores mesoscale cellular biology to understand how weak RNA binding networks and secondary structures direct mRNA localization. The team will validate computational models using test data and cross validation alongside evolutionary conservation and positive controls. The project utilizes data from ENCODE and the Human Cell Atlas alongside repositories including Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). The synthesis plan aggregates data on isoforms to the level of genes and establishes a unified coordinate system. Algorithmic normalization mitigates biases in transcriptomics while automated filtering removes poor data and computational predictions supplement missing structures. The three year timeline encompasses the development of frameworks before modeling granules and releasing software tools and databases. Integrating these diverse datasets requires cross disciplinary expertise in biology and machine learning that exceeds a single laboratory. The project will publish open access findings and distribute packages of Python code alongside datasets hosted on Zenodo. The team combines postdoctoral researchers and graduate students receiving cross disciplinary training alongside a dedicated research software engineer.

title: Emergent Mechanics of Bacterial Microcompartments: Synthesizing Structural and Metabolic Data to Model Encapsulated Pathway Efficiency
title_norm: emergent mechanics of bacterial microcompartments synthesizing structural and metabolic data to model encapsulated pathway efficiency
abstract_text: Structural and systems biology investigates bacterial microcompartments, wherein protein shells encapsulate enzyme pathways to organize mesoscale metabolism, yielding extensive high resolution structural data on complete shells and building block proteins. This project will determine the physical principles governing microcompartment function through a computational synthesis utilizing finite element modeling in FEniCS, ordinary differential equation kinetic modeling via COPASI, and machine learning algorithms built with PyTorch Geometric. The research will integrate repositories including Protein Data Bank, BRENDA, and GenBank into a unified relational database by mapping structural data and kinetic parameters to specific proteins using UniProt accession numbers. Ultimately, this work will provide a mechanistic understanding of mesoscale cellular organization and yield the quantitative design rules required to engineer synthetic bacterial microcompartments for metabolic engineering applications.

title: Emergent Receptor Clustering in Immune Synapses: Synthesizing Super-Resolution and Signaling Data to Model T Cell Activation Thresholds

abstract_text: Immunology and cellular biology research highlights how the mesoscale spatial organization of T cell receptor microclusters and the physical exclusion of CD45 phosphatase at the immune synapse control critical cellular signaling events. However, the quantitative relationships linking cluster geometry and phosphatase exclusion efficiency to signaling network dynamics remain unresolved due to a lack of systematic data integration. This project will determine how microcluster geometry sets bistable activation thresholds by synthesizing public imaging and molecular data into computational models using Smoldyn spatial stochastic simulations, graph neural networks, and cellpose image analysis. The study will integrate datasets from the Image Data Resource, BioImage Archive, PRIDE, and Human Cell Atlas by standardizing formats and aligning cross modality features through a hierarchical Bayesian framework. This research will provide a quantitative framework explaining how spatial organization dictates cellular decision making, which will advance immune response modeling and immunotherapy design for autoimmune diseases.

title: Emergent DNA Repair Pathway Choice: Synthesizing Damage Proteomics and Chromatin Data to Model Repair Mechanism Selection
title_norm: emergent dna repair pathway choice synthesizing damage proteomics and chromatin data to model repair mechanism selection
abstract_text: The biological mechanisms dictating DNA repair pathway selection involve 100 to 1000 nanometer protein assemblies at damage sites, uniting known biochemical functions and chromatin configurations to influence crucial repair tendencies. However, an integrated model connecting recruitment dynamics to genomic outcomes is missing, leaving a gap in understanding how mesoscale protein clusters dictate final pathway selection. This research will integrate proteomic, chromatin, and cellular data to determine pathway selection by employing mathematical modeling with ordinary differential equations, gradient boosting machine learning algorithms, and network analysis of protein recruitment kinetics. The analytical strategy will synthesize resources including PRIDE, ENCODE, BioGRID, and COSMIC by standardizing identifiers through the Cell Ontology and utilizing a custom Bayesian framework to combine chromatin priors with proteomic likelihoods. This project will yield a predictive framework for DNA repair outcomes that establishes rules for mesoscale biological decision making to ultimately guide clinical cancer therapies and precision genome editing.

This synthesis project will decode emergent pathway choice by integrating damage proteomics, chromatin biology, and cell biology datasets. We will synthesize DNA damage proteomics from PRIDE and published studies, ChIP-seq of repair factors from ENCODE, chromatin accessibility from ATAC-seq datasets, and cell cycle proteomics from published studies. The central question is: how do repair protein assemblies at damage sites (mesoscale foci of 100-1000 nm) create emergent pathway selection that individual protein-DNA interactions cannot explain? We hypothesize that emergent pathway choice arises from competitive recruitment kinetics, chromatin-mediated accessibility, and feedback loops that amplify initial pathway commitment. Our computational approach combines kinetic modeling of repair protein recruitment, machine learning to predict pathway choice from chromatin and damage features, and network analysis of repair factor interactions. We will develop algorithms integrating damage site proteomics with chromatin context to model pathway selection. Integration with mutation signature data from COSMIC will connect pathway choice to genomic outcomes. Comparative analysis across cell types will reveal how emergent repair decisions adapt to different genomic contexts. This project requires expertise in DNA repair, chromatin biology, proteomics, and computational modeling—necessitating collaboration across specialized fields. The synthesis of damage, chromatin, and proteomic data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include predictive models of emergent pathway choice, identification of key features determining repair selection, and principles for modulating repair outcomes. Understanding emergent repair decisions has implications for cancer therapy and genome editing. All models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates organize cellular biochemistry through intrinsically disordered regions and multivalent interaction motifs, making their mesoscale material properties such as viscoelasticity and multiphase organization crucial for understanding cellular function. A critical scientific gap is the lack of quantitative predictive models explaining how specific sequence features dictate physical condensate states and systematically alter transcriptional bursting. This project will test the hypothesis that condensate material states control cell to cell gene expression noise by applying deep learning image segmentation, multimodal representation learning, and hierarchical Bayesian models to synthesize sequence, imaging, and single cell transcriptomic data. The approach will integrate databases including UniProt, the Human Protein Atlas, and the Human Cell Atlas, applying multiview representation learning to fuse sequence and imaging features into a unified latent space. This framework will connect physical condensate properties directly to emergent cellular phenotypes, providing a quantitative mechanism to explain context dependent gene regulation and disease related phase transitions.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates (10–500 nm substructures within micron-scale droplets) exhibit emergent material properties—viscosity, elasticity, percolation, and multiphase organization—that cannot be predicted from individual protein/RNA components. This project will test the hypothesis that condensate “material state” is a mesoscale emergent variable that systematically tunes transcriptional bursting and cell-to-cell gene expression noise across cell types and perturbations.

We will synthesize publicly available datasets that jointly report (i) condensate composition and disorder features (UniProt, Pfam, MobiDB, DisProt; LLPS/LLPT databases such as PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS), (ii) condensate morphology and dynamics from imaging repositories (Image Data Resource/IDR, BioImage Archive, Cell Image Library; published FRAP time-series where available), (iii) subcellular localization and puncta statistics from the Human Protein Atlas (immunofluorescence), (iv) single-cell RNA-seq and multiome measurements capturing transcriptional variability (Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens, GEO; scATAC where available), and (v) perturbation signatures affecting phase behavior (LINCS L1000; CRISPR screens in DepMap where linked to condensate regulators).

Analytically, we will build a unified latent-variable model that maps composition/disorder/sequence grammars and imaging-derived mesoscale features (puncta size distributions, coarsening kinetics proxies, FRAP recovery parameters) onto a low-dimensional “material state manifold.” We will then connect that manifold to emergent transcriptional outcomes using hierarchical Bayesian models of bursting (inferring burst size/frequency from scRNA distributions), and causal discovery on perturbation datasets to identify regulators that shift condensates between states. Deep learning segmentation will standardize puncta calling across imaging sources; meta-analysis will harmonize batch effects and imaging modalities.

Expected insights include: (1) whether distinct condensate classes (nucleoli subcompartments, speckles, stress granules, P-bodies) occupy conserved regions of the material-state manifold across cell types; (2) which sequence grammars and interaction motifs predict transitions between liquid-like and gel-like substructures at 10–1000 nm; and (3) how these mesoscale states correlate with gene expression noise, enabling mechanistic hypotheses for robustness vs. plasticity.

This requires team science because it integrates polymer physics, image analysis, statistical genomics, and protein biophysics; no single lab typically spans high-throughput bioimage mining, scRNA noise modeling, and LLPS sequence/interaction theory. NCEMS support is essential for convening domain experts, creating open pipelines for condensate feature extraction, and producing a community resource: an open, reproducible atlas linking condensate mesoscale material states to emergent gene regulatory phenotypes.

title: Emergent Membrane Curvature Codes: Synthesizing Cryo-ET, Proteomics, and Lipidomics to Predict Organelle Contact Site Morphologies
title_norm: emergent membrane curvature codes synthesizing cryoet proteomics and lipidomics to predict organelle contact site morphologies
abstract_text: The research domain investigates membrane contact sites between organelles, focusing on how specific lipid compositions and diverse tethering proteins govern the mesoscale emergent properties of gap width, membrane curvature, and tether spacing. A unified geometric taxonomy of contact site morphotypes remains absent, and current biophysical models lack the parameterization necessary to predictively integrate molecular composition with structural geometry across different studies. This project will determine how combinations of lipids and tethering proteins generate mesoscale morphologies by applying discrete differential geometry, hierarchical Bayesian models, and multimodal graph neural networks to translate extracted imaging data into biophysical parameters. The analysis will integrate public databases including EMPIAR, EMDB, PRIDE, and AlphaFold using a metadata schema that standardizes condition variables and orthology mappings to produce derived physical feature tables and structural interaction graphs. Elucidating the precise relationship between molecular composition and morphology will explain how contact site geometry regulates lipid transfer, calcium microdomain formation, membrane remodeling, and organelle identity.
full_text: This project studies emergent properties of membrane contact sites to build predictive models linking molecular composition and geometry. Tethering proteins produce specific structures but varied measurement conventions prevent synthesis and models of bending lack cellular parameterization. The primary question asks how molecular composition generates morphologies to explain regulation of lipid transfer and organelle identity. The study uses computational data synthesis to extract geometric measurements and train predictive machine learning models on public datasets. Key methods include discrete differential geometry for surface analysis alongside hierarchical Bayesian models and multimodal graph neural networks. Computational validation involves testing across multiple studies and species alongside controls using feature randomization and databases of genetic perturbations. The project utilizes extensive public databases including EMPIAR and UniProtKB alongside the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database and OrthoDB. The team integrates distinct datasets through a metadata schema to combine data streams into graphs of structural interactions. The study mitigates measurement biases by using established public segmentations alongside hierarchical models and aggregation by organelle identity. The project spans 36 months with milestones including schema finalization alongside training of networks and publication of resources. Cross disciplinary collaboration is necessary because integration of fields like proteomics and machine learning exceeds expertise of one laboratory. The research team will release versioned datasets on Zenodo and OSF alongside public code repositories hosted on GitHub. The team includes principal investigators and postdoctoral researchers alongside a graduate student with training provided to early career members.

abstract_original:
Membrane contact sites (MCS) between organelles are mesoscale structures (10–50 nm gaps; 50–500 nm lateral extents) whose emergent curvature, tether spacing, and protein crowding enable lipid exchange and signaling. The core emergent phenomenon is that collective organization of tethers, scaffolds, and lipids generates stable, functionally specific contact morphologies that are not inferable from single tether proteins.

We will synthesize existing public datasets spanning structure, composition, and function: (i) cryo-electron tomography subtomogram averages and annotations of ER–mitochondria, ER–PM, ER–endosome contacts (EMPIAR, EMDB; published tomograms with segmentation), (ii) proximity labeling and contact-site proteomes (BioID/APEX datasets in PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iii) organelle-resolved lipidomics and membrane composition (LIPID MAPS, Metabolomics Workbench; published organelle fraction lipidomics), (iv) protein structures and predicted complexes for tethers and curvature generators (PDB, AlphaFold DB, EBI Complex Portal), and (v) genetic perturbation phenotypes affecting contacts (DepMap CRISPR screens; SGD for yeast; MGI for mouse cell lines where applicable).

We will develop a multiscale inference framework that predicts mesoscale contact morphology from molecular components. First, we will extract quantitative geometry from cryo-ET (gap width distributions, curvature tensors, tether density estimates) using standardized segmentation and geometric morphometrics. Second, we will map proteome/lipidome composition to physical parameters (spontaneous curvature, bending rigidity proxies, crowding pressure) using coarse-grained biophysical models. Third, we will train graph neural networks that integrate tether interaction graphs (from structures/predicted interfaces) with lipid composition features to predict observed morphotypes. Finally, we will test whether specific “curvature codes” (combinations of lipid species and tether architectures) generalize across organisms and contact types.

Expected outcomes: (1) a taxonomy of MCS morphotypes grounded in quantitative geometry; (2) predictive rules linking lipid unsaturation, sterol content, and tether oligomerization to emergent curvature and spacing; (3) identification of minimal sets of components sufficient to produce particular morphologies; and (4) hypotheses for why some contacts are robust to perturbations while others switch states.

The work is inherently transdisciplinary: cryo-ET experts, lipidomics/proteomics analysts, structural biologists, and membrane physicists must align data standards and models. NCEMS support enables coordinated curation of heterogeneous datasets, shared open pipelines for geometry extraction and model fitting, and training for trainees in both quantitative imaging and biophysical machine learning. All code, derived features, and models will be released openly to seed community-scale predictive cell biology of mesoscale contact sites.

title: Mesoscale Cytoskeletal Percolation: A Synthesis of Actin/Microtubule Network Architecture and Emergent Intracellular Transport Efficiency
title_norm: mesoscale cytoskeletal percolation a synthesis of actinmicrotubule network architecture and emergent intracellular transport efficiency
abstract_text: The research domain of intracellular transport requires understanding the mesoscale organization of actin and microtubule networks, specifically connectivity and anisotropy at the 10 to 1000 nanometer scale, which fundamentally influences cellular transport behaviors. However, existing data remains fragmented across modalities, creating a scientific gap where no standardized framework connects molecular composition and mesoscale cytoskeletal architecture to transport phenotypes across different conditions. This project will synthesize public data into a unified phase diagram linking cytoskeletal states to transport efficiency by converting imaging data into network graphs using deep learning segmentation, graph theoretic feature extraction, and physics informed machine learning. The study will integrate databases including BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, and Cell Tracking Challenge by standardizing files and applying a tiered linkage system that maps datasets across shared transcriptomic and proteomic profiles. This approach will produce a mechanistic model that relates molecular perturbations directly to cellular transport phenotypes, providing critical insights into how network thresholds fundamentally alter cellular dynamics.
full_text: This project investigates intracellular transport and mesoscale organization of actin and microtubule networks lacking a standardized framework for cellular architecture. Current knowledge reveals that mesoscale organization of cytoskeletal networks influences transport behaviors despite fragmented data across modalities lacking quantitative descriptors. The study synthesizes public data into a unified phase diagram linking states of cytoskeletal networks to transport phenotypes using statistical physics. The computational study design converts public imaging data into network graphs and extracts transport metrics for correlation using machine learning. Key methods feature deep learning models and graph theoretic extraction alongside hierarchical Bayesian modeling and physics informed machine learning. The team will validate results using cross dataset hold out testing and variance quantification on repeated image acquisitions. Data sources encompass BioImage Archive and Image Data Resource alongside repositories such as Zenodo and the Human Cell Atlas. The study integrates datasets by standardizing files to OME-NGFF formats and applying tiered linkage systems across paired conditions. The team will address batch effects across imaging modalities by applying domain adaptation techniques to the descriptor space. The proposed timeline spans 30 months to encompass initial pipeline development and final omics integration with an atlas release. Cross disciplinary collaboration is necessary to integrate expertise spanning machine learning and cell biology for community scale dataset harmonization. The team will distribute an open source predictive toolkit and a public dataset registry deposited in the BioImage Archive. The research group features multidisciplinary principal investigators alongside postdoctoral researchers and a graduate student to provide valuable training opportunities.

abstract_original:
Intracellular transport emerges from the collective mesoscale organization of actin and microtubule networks (10–1000 nm filament spacing, crosslinking, and branching) rather than from individual motors or filaments. The emergent phenomenon of interest is percolation-like connectivity and anisotropy in composite cytoskeletal networks that governs cargo routing, traffic jams, and robustness to perturbations.

We will synthesize public datasets across imaging, proteomics, and trafficking phenotypes: (i) super-resolution and expansion microscopy images of actin/microtubules and associated proteins (BioImage Archive, IDR; published STORM/SIM/ExM datasets), (ii) live-cell single-particle tracking of vesicles/organelles (Cell Tracking Challenge datasets; published tracking data in Zenodo/GEO supplements), (iii) proteomics of cytoskeletal fractions and crosslinkers (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iv) single-cell transcriptomics for cytoskeletal regulators across cell types (Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens), and (v) perturbation screens affecting trafficking (DepMap CRISPR, genome-wide RNAi datasets; LINCS signatures for cytoskeletal drugs).

Computationally, we will build a standardized pipeline to reconstruct mesoscale network graphs from images: filament segmentation, orientation fields, junction detection, and estimation of mesh size and crosslink density. We will compute graph-theoretic and statistical physics descriptors (giant component size, betweenness centrality, anisotropy order parameters, percolation thresholds) and relate them to transport metrics derived from tracking (mean squared displacement regimes, directional persistence, stop-and-go statistics). A key methodological innovation is a multiscale “network-to-transport” emulator that predicts transport efficiency from network descriptors using physics-informed machine learning, enabling cross-dataset generalization.

The central hypothesis is that cells occupy constrained regions of a universal phase diagram for composite network organization, and that transitions between phases (e.g., isotropic mesh to aligned bundles; microtubule-dominant highways to actin-dominant cages) correspond to sharp changes in emergent transport behavior. We will test whether these phase boundaries are conserved across cell types and whether specific regulators (crosslinkers, severing enzymes, nucleators) move cells along predictable trajectories in this diagram.

Expected insights include mechanistic explanations for why certain cell types exhibit robust long-range transport despite noisy molecular composition, and how mesoscale architecture buffers or amplifies perturbations. The project requires team science: computer vision for filament reconstruction, statistical physics for percolation modeling, cell biology for interpretation, and data integration for harmonizing diverse imaging modalities. NCEMS support is needed to convene these communities, curate benchmark datasets, and deliver open, reproducible tools and an atlas linking cytoskeletal mesoscale states to emergent transport phenotypes.

title: Emergent Chromatin Nanodomain Topology: Integrating Hi-C, Super-Resolution Imaging, and Epigenomics to Explain Cell-Type-Specific Gene Regulation
title_norm: emergent chromatin nanodomain topology integrating hic superresolution imaging and epigenomics to explain celltypespecific gene regulation
abstract_text: Mesoscale chromatin organization involves nanoscale domains and topological motifs that dictate essential gene regulatory behaviors like enhancer promoter communication and transcriptional bursting, representing a critical extension beyond traditional genome wide contact maps. To determine whether nanodomains organize into recurrent topological motifs driving cell type specific regulation, this project will synthesize multimodal datasets using multi resolution community detection, coarse grained polymer simulations, and unsupervised representation learning. Researchers will integrate ENCODE, Roadmap Epigenomics, and 4D Nucleome Data Portal repositories by matching cell type ontologies, harmonizing genomic resolutions, and performing cross study calibration to construct joint multimodal feature vectors. This framework will produce a mesoscale model of chromatin regulation, converting descriptive structural catalogs into predictive knowledge by revealing the physical shapes underlying contact derived genomic patterns.
full_text: The domain of mesoscale chromatin organization lacks quantitative maps connecting physical nanodomains to shared topological motifs across diverse cell types. Existing contact maps provide geometric constraints but remain degenerate and fail to analyze combinations of structures for inferring regulatory behaviors. The study integrates imaging geometry with contact maps to determine if nanodomains form recurrent motifs driving regulatory behaviors of cells. This project for data synthesis builds pipelines to extract multimodal features and infer a dictionary of motifs predicting regulatory phenotypes. Methods include polymer simulations and community detection alongside representation learning and Bayesian regression to connect discovered motifs with regulatory phenotypes. The team validates results through replication across datasets and sensitivity analyses alongside benchmarking against known locus archetypes and published simulations. Data sources include the Human Cell Atlas and the BioImage Archive alongside public repositories like ENCODE and the GWAS Catalog. The team integrates diverse datasets by standardizing genome builds and applying calibration across studies to construct multimodal vectors of features. Researchers mitigate the degeneracy of contact maps by utilizing distance distributions from imaging data to calibrate and select polymer models. This project of thirty months advances from ingestion of data to motif discovery and concludes with releases of final software. The broad scope necessitates collaboration across multiple laboratories to synthesize diverse modalities and combine technical expertise spanning physics and modeling. The project distributes open source code via GitHub and releases versioned datasets through Zenodo to ensure complete public data reproducibility. The cross disciplinary team includes principal investigators and postdoctoral researchers providing opportunities for training through virtual tutorials and collaborative sprints.

Chromatin forms mesoscale nanodomains (50–300 nm) whose collective folding and compartmentalization produce emergent regulatory behaviors—enhancer–promoter communication, insulation, and transcriptional bursting—that cannot be inferred from individual nucleosome modifications. This project will synthesize 3D genome conformation and imaging data to test whether a small set of mesoscale topological motifs explains cell-type-specific gene regulation across mammals.

We will integrate publicly available datasets: (i) population and single-cell Hi-C / Micro-C maps (4D Nucleome, GEO, ENCODE), (ii) super-resolution and multiplexed DNA FISH imaging of chromatin domains (4DN data portal, BioImage Archive; Oligopaint datasets), (iii) epigenomic marks and accessibility (ENCODE ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq; Roadmap Epigenomics), (iv) transcriptional outputs (single-cell RNA-seq from Human Cell Atlas; nascent transcription where available), and (v) structural constraints from nucleosome and chromatin fiber models (PDB where relevant; polymer simulation benchmarks).

Methodologically, we will create a joint inference framework that maps between contact matrices and physical 3D domain geometries. We will (1) infer nanodomain boundaries and interaction strengths from Hi-C/Micro-C using multi-resolution community detection; (2) calibrate polymer models with imaging-derived distance distributions to resolve degeneracies in contact-based reconstructions; (3) learn a “motif dictionary” of recurrent mesoscale folding patterns (e.g., loop clusters, rosettes, compartment microdomains) using unsupervised representation learning that ingests both contact and imaging features; and (4) link motif occupancy to emergent regulatory phenotypes—bursting parameters, enhancer responsiveness, and lineage stability—using hierarchical models across cell types.

The hypothesis is that despite molecular diversity, chromatin nanodomain topology falls into a limited set of mesoscale motifs whose combinations predict regulatory capacity and noise. We will test whether developmental transitions correspond to motif switching, and whether disease-associated noncoding variants preferentially disrupt specific motifs rather than individual loops.

Expected outputs include: a cross-cell-type atlas of chromatin nanodomain motifs, quantitative relationships between motif composition and transcriptional variability, and open tools for jointly analyzing Hi-C and imaging. This synthesis requires collaboration among genome informaticians, polymer physicists, microscopy experts, and statistical modelers; no single lab typically has access to and expertise across these modalities. NCEMS working group support is essential for harmonizing standards, building reproducible pipelines, and training trainees to bridge 3D genomics and quantitative imaging under open-science practices.

title: Protein Crowding as an Emergent Mesoscale Regulator: A Pan-Proteome Synthesis of Cytoplasmic Viscosity, Diffusion, and Reaction Rates
title_norm: protein crowding as an emergent mesoscale regulator a panproteome synthesis of cytoplasmic viscosity diffusion and reaction rates
abstract_text: Investigations into the physical properties of cellular interiors at the 10 to 1000 nanometer scale reveal that macromolecular density and viscosity drive complex diffusion behaviors critical across distinct cellular compartments and environmental states. To determine whether intracellular transport metrics can be mathematically derived from existing proteomic data, this project will synthesize multi omics and structural information into spatial crowding maps using obstruction scaling models, hierarchical Bayesian calibration, and gradient boosted trees. The study will integrate resources including ProteomeXchange, AlphaFold, and the Human Protein Atlas by linking UniProt identifiers and normalizing spatial compartments with Gene Ontology terms to calculate combined spatial probability arrays. This research will establish computational methods to infer spatial viscosity shifts directly from omics data, allowing intracellular transport speeds to be analyzed as physical outcomes of protein organization.
full_text: This project explores physical properties of cellular interiors at nanometer scales to determine if protein composition predicts transport metrics. Current evidence reveals that intracellular diffusion varies by compartment but mathematical links to molecular composition lack generalizable precision. The proposed study investigates if transport metrics derive mathematically from proteomic data to establish computational methods for inferring viscosity. The overall design aggregates existing data from multiple omics fields to construct spatial maps that link molecular composition to transport metrics. The team will apply fractional Brownian motion and hierarchical Bayesian calibration alongside gradient boosted trees and elastic net algorithms. The analytical approach validates these results through comparisons across datasets against published parameter estimates and posterior predictive checks. This project utilizes databases including the Human Protein Atlas and ProteomeXchange alongside structural archives like the Protein Data Bank. The synthesis plan integrates data by linking proteins via UniProt identifiers and normalizing compartments with Gene Ontology (GO) terms. The team mitigates inconsistent metadata formats by applying strict inclusion criteria and establishing rubrics for scoring quality of physical measurements. The timeline of thirty months progresses from initial data integration to physical modeling before concluding with software finalization and manuscripts. The broad scope requires collaboration across disciplines to combine domain knowledge spanning quantitative proteomics and soft matter theory. The team will distribute data archives and analysis pipelines with open source code via platforms including Zenodo and GitHub. The research group includes principal investigators and postdoctoral researchers alongside a software engineer and a graduate student receiving biophysics training.
