The emergent phenomenon is that collective recruitment and chromatin reorganization creates threshold responses, pathway choice (HR vs NHEJ), and repair timing not predictable from individual repair factors.

We will synthesize: (i) live-cell imaging datasets of repair foci dynamics (53BP1, RAD51, γH2AX) from IDR/BioImage Archive, including time-lapse series, (ii) proteomics and phosphoproteomics of DNA damage response (DDR) time courses (PRIDE), (iii) 3D genome and chromatin context maps (Hi-C/Micro-C from 4DN; ENCODE epigenomics), (iv) CRISPR screens for DDR genes and pathway choice modifiers (DepMap; published DDR screens), and (v) variant datasets for DDR genes in cancer (TCGA; COSMIC).

We will develop a unified model linking chromatin context and protein network state to mesoscale foci morphodynamics. Imaging analysis will quantify foci nucleation rates, growth/coalescence, and dissolution, extracting mesoscale kinetic parameters. We will integrate these with phosphoproteomic signaling states and with chromatin compartment features at damage-prone loci. Causal inference will identify regulators that shift foci dynamics and pathway choice.

Hypotheses: (1) repair foci exhibit discrete mesoscale dynamical regimes (diffuse recruitment vs coalescing droplets vs stable scaffolds) corresponding to repair pathway choice; (2) chromatin nanodomain topology constrains foci growth and coalescence; and (3) cancer-associated DDR alterations manifest as shifts in mesoscale regimes rather than complete pathway loss.

Expected insights include a cross-study atlas of foci dynamical regimes, mechanistic links between 3D genome context and emergent assembly kinetics, and open pipelines for foci tracking and integrative DDR modeling.

This requires collaboration among DDR biologists, quantitative imaging experts, proteomics analysts, and 3D genomics researchers. NCEMS support is needed to curate heterogeneous time-lapse datasets and omics, build reproducible multi-modal workflows, and train trainees in integrative analysis of mesoscale nuclear assemblies.

title: Emergent Mesoscale Patterning in Bacterial Division Machinery: A Synthesis of FtsZ Ring Architecture, Dynamics, and Cell Shape Outcomes
title_norm: emergent mesoscale patterning in bacterial division machinery a synthesis of ftsz ring architecture dynamics and cell shape outcomes
abstract_text: Bacterial cytokinesis relies on the mesoscale architecture of the FtsZ based divisome, an essential biological process whose biochemical properties and single molecule dynamics drive functional ring structures and filament treadmilling. Unintegrated genomic, proteomic, and imaging datasets currently obscure how dynamic FtsZ filaments and accessory proteins coordinate to produce symmetric cell constriction across different bacterial species. This project will synthesize multi modal public datasets to identify accessory proteins and structural variables controlling bacterial cytokinesis by applying image segmentation, unsupervised clustering, hierarchical statistical modeling, active polymer physics models, and machine learning. Diverse datasets from BioImage Archive, PRIDE, EMPIAR, and NCBI RefSeq will integrate into a unified relational database by standardizing measurement units, assigning orthogroup identifiers, and enforcing a uniform metadata schema. The resulting framework will establish parameters for polymer self organization, link single molecule properties to cellular morphology, and map morphological responses to critical genetic and antimicrobial perturbations.
full_text: This project explores bacterial cytokinesis to understand how FtsZ filaments and accessory proteins coordinate to produce symmetric cell constriction. Biochemical properties are known but unintegrated omics and imaging datasets prevent the correlation of molecular composition with division phenotypes. The proposed study synthesizes datasets to identify variables controlling cytokinesis and links properties of single molecules to cellular morphology. The analytical strategy integrates multimodal public datasets for evaluation through statistical analysis and machine learning alongside mechanistic modeling. The team applies U-Net image segmentation and particle tracking alongside agent based simulations and Approximate Bayesian Computation models. Validation involves cross dataset comparisons out of sample predictions and baseline comparisons against well characterized bacteria and unrelated gene sets. Data sources include the BioImage Archive and Image Data Resource alongside omics databases like PRIDE and NCBI RefSeq. The team integrates datasets into a relational database by converting measurements to standard units and applying a uniform metadata schema. Limitations like batch effects and protocol differences will be mitigated through automated quality control checks and species level covariates. The thirty month timeline progresses from establishing metadata schemas to training predictive models and finalizing a public database release. This cross disciplinary collaboration is necessary because the integration of datasets demands concurrent expertise in biophysics and software engineering. The team will share data and code via a public relational database alongside open source toolkits and preprints. The team includes faculty and graduate students receiving training through embedded project tasks and annual workshops in data science.

abstract_original:
Bacterial cytokinesis is driven by the FtsZ-based divisome, which forms a mesoscale ring/band (typically ~500–1000 nm circumference; ~10–50 nm filament bundles) with dynamic treadmilling. The emergent phenomenon is that collective filament organization and accessory protein patterning produce robust constriction and shape maintenance, not predictable from FtsZ polymerization alone.

We will synthesize: (i) super-resolution and cryo-ET datasets of divisome architecture across species (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR), (ii) single-molecule and time-lapse measurements of FtsZ dynamics (published tracking datasets), (iii) proteomics and interaction networks of divisome components (PRIDE; BioGRID), (iv) comparative genomics of division genes across bacteria (NCBI RefSeq), and (v) morphological phenotypes under gene perturbations and antibiotics (BacDive; published high-content imaging screens).

We will quantify ring architecture (bundle thickness, continuity, patchiness) and dynamics (treadmilling speeds, turnover) and relate these to emergent cell shape outcomes (septum symmetry, division timing, size control). Using statistical physics models of active polymers and agent-based simulations, calibrated to observed architectures, we will infer which mesoscale parameters control robustness. Comparative analysis will test how different bacteria achieve similar division outcomes with different accessory proteins.

Hypotheses: (1) divisomes operate in a constrained mesoscale regime where filament dynamics and crosslinking yield self-correcting constriction; (2) accessory proteins tune emergent ring continuity and force distribution; and (3) antibiotic susceptibilities reflect shifts in mesoscale architecture rather than direct inhibition levels.

Expected insights include a cross-species atlas of divisome mesoscale architectures, quantitative links between architecture and division robustness, and open tools for analyzing divisome imaging. This synthesis will unify structural and dynamical observations into general principles of emergent cytokinetic machinery.

Team science is required across bacterial cell biology, quantitative microscopy, biophysics, and comparative genomics. NCEMS support will enable coordinated data curation and development of reproducible pipelines and training for trainees at the interface of mesoscale structure and emergent cellular morphogenesis.

title: Mesoscale Emergence of Exosome Biogenesis Microdomains: Integrating Endosomal Proteomics, Lipidomics, and Imaging
title_norm: mesoscale emergence of exosome biogenesis microdomains integrating endosomal proteomics lipidomics and imaging
abstract_text: The research domain is exosome biogenesis, specifically the formation of intraluminal vesicles within multivesicular bodies via mesoscale endosomal microdomains, which is critical for explaining redundant biogenesis pathways and context dependent cargo variations. The scientific gap is how these microdomains determine selective cargo sorting and vesicle size distributions, which currently remains unpredictable from individual sorting motifs and single molecule targeted assays alone. This project will integrate public data to identify latent microdomain states, utilizing data harmonization, Similarity Network Fusion, and Multi Omics Factor Analysis to build coarse grained mechanistic models linking membrane composition to cargo selection. Datasets from ExoCarta, Vesiclepedia, PRIDE Archive, and BioImage Archive will be integrated by mapping identifiers to standard ontologies and applying batch correction methods to generate joint embeddings for comprehensive analysis. This research will produce a framework of cooperative mesoscale assemblies to explain extracellular vesicle heterogeneity and reconcile conflicting mechanistic studies regarding single linear biogenesis pathways.
full_text: This project studies exosome biogenesis to determine how mesoscale endosomal microdomains control cargo sorting and sizes of intraluminal vesicles. Current assays identify lipid drivers and protein motifs but mechanisms of single molecules cannot explain redundant pathways of biogenesis. This study asks how states of microdomains link compositions of membranes to sizes of vesicles to explain heterogeneity of exosomes. The overall design involves secondary analyses of public datasets to infer states of latent microdomains and build mechanistic models. Key methods utilize factor analysis and spatial statistics alongside hierarchical Bayesian models to evaluate physical remodeling of membranes. The team will validate results through replications across held out studies and analyses of sensitivity for protocols of isolation. The project utilizes public databases including Vesiclepedia and ExoCarta alongside resources from the Image Data Resource (IDR) and Metabolomics Workbench. The team will integrate distinct datasets by mapping identifiers to standard ontologies and utilizing frameworks to generate joint embeddings. The team will mitigate limitations of missing data and confounding protocols by deploying tolerant algorithms and excluding uncalibrated images. The proposed timeline of 30 months features milestones for releasing an initial atlas of data and establishing models of mechanisms. A cross disciplinary collaboration is necessary because harmonizing repositories and building physical models requires expertise beyond a single laboratory. The team will support open science by depositing curated tables and providing containerized workflows through platforms like GitHub Pages. The collaborative team comprises investigators and students across diverse disciplines to provide training opportunities like rotations and annual workshops.

abstract_original:
Exosomes originate from intraluminal vesicles (ILVs) within multivesicular bodies, formed in mesoscale endosomal microdomains (50–500 nm) enriched in ESCRT components, tetraspanins, and specific lipids. The emergent phenomenon is that collective microdomain organization yields selective cargo sorting and vesicle size distributions not predictable from individual sorting motifs.

We will synthesize: (i) exosome and endosome proteomics datasets (ExoCarta/Vesiclepedia-linked studies; PRIDE), (ii) lipidomics of extracellular vesicles and endosomal fractions (LIPID MAPS; Metabolomics Workbench), (iii) imaging datasets of ILV formation and endosomal microdomains (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR for EM of MVBs), (iv) RNA cargo profiles (exosomal RNA-seq in GEO), and (v) perturbation screens affecting EV secretion (DepMap; published CRISPR screens).

We will quantify ILV size distributions and microdomain organization from EM and fluorescence images using segmentation and spatial clustering metrics. Multi-omic integration will identify latent microdomain states defined by protein–lipid–RNA composition. Mechanistic modeling will connect ESCRT polymerization and membrane composition to observed ILV size distributions using coarse-grained membrane remodeling models. Predictive models will link microdomain states to cargo enrichment patterns.

Hypotheses: (1) exosome biogenesis proceeds through discrete mesoscale microdomain states that determine cargo classes; (2) lipid composition (ceramides, cholesterol) acts as a mesoscale controller of domain stability and ILV size; and (3) cell-type differences in EV cargo reflect microdomain state occupancy more than expression of individual cargos.

Expected insights include a unified mesoscale model of ILV microdomains, identification of compositional signatures predicting cargo selection, and open resources for EV biogenesis imaging/omics integration.

This requires team science across membrane biology, proteomics/lipidomics, quantitative imaging, and biophysical modeling. NCEMS support is needed to harmonize diverse public datasets and establish open, reproducible pipelines and training for trainees in integrative mesoscale analysis of extracellular vesicle biogenesis.

title: Deciphering the Sequence Grammar of Mesoscale Viscoelasticity in Biomolecular Condensates
title_norm: deciphering the sequence grammar of mesoscale viscoelasticity in biomolecular condensates
abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates formed by liquid liquid phase separation create membraneless cellular compartments, and determining their viscoelastic properties and physical transitions to disease linked solid states holds critical importance for the field. To determine how primary protein sequences and local structural disorder dictate condensate maturation, this research will train graph neural networks, computer vision, and fine tuned BioBERT natural language processing models on a knowledge graph. Datasets including PhaSePro, DrLLPS, AlphaFold, and Europe PMC will be structured into a knowledge graph linking conditions and properties, with protein sequences represented as node and edge graphs incorporating structural contact probabilities. Establishing sequence to property relationships will yield a predictive model for normal condensate function and pathological aggregation, directly facilitating the identification of disease causing mutations and therapeutic targets.
full_text: Liquid liquid phase separation creates membraneless compartments linked to disease but quantitative physical measurements remain unstandardized and scattered. This study asks how protein sequences dictate viscoelastic properties in order to predict pathological aggregation and identify therapeutic targets. The analytical strategy integrates protein sequences and physical measurements into a knowledge graph to train machine learning models. The team applies natural language processing (NLP) using BioBERT alongside graph neural networks and computer vision with attention mechanisms. Validation involves testing models on independent datasets to predict state shifts and comparing predictions against structural cryo-ET data. The team integrates data from PhaSePro and CD-CODE alongside the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database and the Electron Microscopy Data Bank. These diverse sources populate a knowledge graph linking proteins and physical properties while representing sequences as node and edge graphs. The researchers will standardize fragmented measurements into uniform units using NLP and impute missing data through network proximity. The project spans a 24 month timeline yielding a standardized database alongside a predictive web tool and synthesis manuscript. This methodology requires cross disciplinary collaboration spanning soft matter physics and computational biology and machine learning engineering for neural networks. The team will release an open access database and archive data on Zenodo while publishing findings via open access. The team unites computational biologists with physicists and machine learning engineers to train two postdoctoral fellows and one graduate assistant.

While the ability of proteins to phase separate is well-documented, the mesoscale material properties—such as viscosity, surface tension, and hardening over time—emerge from complex, non-linear interactions that remain poorly understood. We propose to synthesize data from the PhaSePro and DrLLPS databases, combined with structural disorder predictions from AlphaFold (pLDDT scores) and experimental rheology data scattered across literature repositories. The central hypothesis is that specific 'grammars' within intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs)—defined by charge patterning, residue spacing, and aromatic content—deterministically encode the emergent viscoelastic evolution of condensates, distinct from simple phase separation propensity. Our approach involves training deep learning models (specifically Graph Neural Networks) on integrated sequence-rheology datasets to map molecular features to mesoscale material states. We will validate these models by cross-referencing with cryo-electron tomography data from the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) that visualizes condensate morphology in situ. Expected insights include a predictive framework for how pathogenic aggregates (e.g., in neurodegeneration) transition from liquid to solid states, an emergent property not predictable from single-molecule dynamics. This project necessitates NCEMS support to bring together soft matter physicists, computational biologists, and machine learning experts to standardize heterogeneous rheological data and develop novel biophysical classifiers.

title: Emergent Chromatin Rheology: Synthesizing 1D Sequence and 3D Topology to Predict Nuclear Stiffness
title_norm: emergent chromatin rheology synthesizing 1d sequence and 3d topology to predict nuclear stiffness
abstract_text: Nuclear mechanobiology explores how mesoscale chromatin folding patterns and topological domains determine the physical stiffness and rheological properties of the cell nucleus, connecting previously independent observations of macroscopic mechanics and genomic topology. Current biophysical models treat the nucleus as a homogeneous material, leaving a critical gap in understanding how three dimensional genomic architectures translate into specific nuclear mechanical properties. To determine how topologically associating domains and epigenetic marks dictate bulk nuclear stiffness, this computational synthesis project will utilize coarse grained Langevin dynamics simulations and Graph Convolutional Networks to analyze chromatin interaction graphs. Datasets from the 4D Nucleome Data Portal, ENCODE, and biomedical repositories will be aligned to the GRCh38 reference genome and merged to link three dimensional contact frequencies with physical mechanics metrics. Establishing this predictive link between chromatin topology and mechanical properties will explain how cells alter physical stiffness during migration, differentiation, and disease progression without altering their DNA sequence.
full_text: This project in nuclear mechanobiology explores how chromatin architecture translates into physical stiffness to address critical knowledge gaps. Cellular mechanics and genomic topology are documented independently but current biophysical models omit the spatial topology of chromatin. This study determines how chromatin topology dictates nuclear viscoelasticity to explain stiffness alterations during disease and cellular differentiation. The computational synthesis project integrates existing genomic and mechanical datasets to conduct polymer simulations and train regression models. The approach combines Langevin dynamics in OpenMM and LAMMPS with graph convolutional networks in PyTorch Geometric for predictions. The team validates model predictions through leave one out cross validation and benchmarks against published experimental microrheology data. The project extracts data from the 4D Nucleome Data Portal and ENCODE Project Portal alongside Dryad and PubMed Central. The team aligns datasets to the GRCh38 reference genome to build a unified structure linking physical metrics and epigenetics. The team mitigates discrepancies from divergent experimental techniques by thoroughly normalizing the extracted values for stiffness and viscosity. The two year project advances from database construction to simulation development before finishing with model training and publication preparation. This synthesis of genomic topology and biophysical mechanics demands cross disciplinary expertise in soft matter physics and data science. The team will distribute toolkits and harmonized databases on Zenodo and Hugging Face while publishing in open access journals. The group includes principal investigators and postdoctoral fellows alongside a graduate student to facilitate cross disciplinary genomics training.

abstract_original: This proposal investigates the emergent rheological properties of chromatin at the mesoscale, specifically how local genomic folding patterns dictate the physical stiffness and plasticity of the cell nucleus. The spatial organization of the genome is not merely a packing mechanism but an emergent mechanical scaffold that influences gene expression and nuclear stability. We will synthesize high-resolution Hi-C and Micro-C data from the 4D Nucleome Project, mechanics data from atomic force microscopy (AFM) studies of isolated nuclei, and transcriptomic data from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). The novel hypothesis is that specific topologically associating domains (TADs) and chromatin loops act as 'mechanical springs' whose collective stiffness emerges from the interplay of epigenetic marks and loop extrusion factors, independent of the underlying DNA sequence length. By employing polymer physics simulations informed by real-world Hi-C contact maps and machine learning regression models, we aim to correlate 3D chromatin architecture with nuclear stiffness measurements. We expect to reveal how changes in mesoscale chromatin folding—driven by differentiation or disease—result in emergent mechanical softening or stiffening, impacting nuclear migration and integrity. This transdisciplinary synthesis requires a team of genomicists, mechanical engineers, and polymer physicists to bridge the gap between sequence-based genomics and physical mechanics.

title: The Emergence of Metabolic Channeling: Mapping Transient Metabolons via Integrated Interactomics
title_norm: the emergence of metabolic channeling mapping transient metabolons via integrated interactomics
abstract_text: The research examines metabolic channeling and the temporary grouping of successive enzymes into metabolons, which form based on metabolic requirements to concentrate intermediates, shield unstable substrates, and accelerate reactions. The mechanics of these weak enzyme connections remain incompletely modeled because standard structural biology approaches generally omit the temporary associations that facilitate substrate movement. The primary objective is to identify specific conditions where temporary enzyme groupings control substrate movement, and this project will analyze protein interaction networks to simulate restricted metabolic flux models using calculated enzyme grouping probabilities. The study will utilize STRING, BioGRID, BRENDA, and the Human Protein Atlas, combining fixed protein interaction networks and spatial records with active kinetic variables to generate probability distributions for mathematical models. This work will provide an alternative to uniform solution assumptions by demonstrating how the spatial arrangement of enzymes within these temporary groupings facilitates higher reaction speeds.
full_text: This research investigates metabolic channeling into metabolons because standard methods of structural biology omit weak connections facilitating movement of substrates. Dynamic structures of enzymes form to concentrate intermediates and accelerate reactions while mechanics of weak connections remain incompletely modeled. The study identifies conditions where temporary groups of enzymes control movement of substrates to challenge assumptions of uniform solutions. The core analytical strategy centers on building and simulating models of metabolic flux that incorporate specific spatial restrictions. The team will apply spatial restrictions based on the statistical likelihood of the temporary grouping of enzymes during metabolic processes. Key methods involve the analysis of networks of protein interaction and the simulation of restricted models for metabolic flux. The project relies on specific databases including STRING and BioGRID along with BRENDA and the Human Protein Atlas. The integration of these distinct variables will generate probability distributions for the mathematical models of the proposed study. This work will provide an alternative to uniform solution assumptions by demonstrating how the spatial arrangement of enzymes within these temporary groupings facilitates higher reaction speeds.

Unlike stable protein complexes, metabolons are dynamic structures that emerge in response to metabolic demand, creating localized pools of intermediates that increase flux and protect unstable substrates. We will synthesize protein-protein interaction (PPI) data from STRING and BioGRID, enzymatic kinetic parameters from BRENDA, and spatial proteomics data from the Human Protein Atlas. Our hypothesis is that low-affinity, transient interactions between metabolic enzymes, often ignored in standard structural biology, create emergent 'super-highways' for substrates that defy diffusion-limited kinetics. The analytical strategy involves constructing spatially-constrained metabolic flux models that incorporate probability distributions of enzyme clustering derived from PPI networks. We will simulate these models to identify conditions under which channeling emerges as a dominant regulatory mechanism. Insights will likely redefine our understanding of metabolic efficiency, showing how mesoscale organization enables reaction rates impossible in a well-mixed solution. This project requires NCEMS resources to unite enzymologists, systems biologists, and network scientists to integrate static interaction maps with dynamic kinetic data.

title: Lipid Raft Dynamics and the Emergence of Signal Fidelity in T-Cell Activation
title_norm: lipid raft dynamics and the emergence of signal fidelity in tcell activation
abstract_text: Immunology and biophysics define atomic scale interactions between T cell receptors and peptide MHC complexes, but the critical function of plasma membrane lipid rafts in antigen discrimination remains poorly integrated. The field currently lacks a mesoscale model integrating fragmented membrane lipid composition data with protein dynamics to explain how T cells distinguish self from non self antigens. This project will determine how lipid and protein clustering filters biochemical noise and amplifies antigenic signals by synthesizing secondary data into multi scale computational frameworks using coarse grained molecular dynamics and agent based modeling. The project will integrate datasets from LIPID MAPS, BioImage Archive, and Protein Data Bank by creating a unified ontology schema, converting lipid abundances into surface densities, and standardizing microscopy trajectories into HDF5 format. This research will establish a novel mechanism for mesoscale signal to noise management based on dynamic molecular clustering, advancing signal amplification paradigms beyond individual lock and key binding events.
full_text: This study addresses the absence of models linking the composition of lipid rafts to protein dynamics during antigen discrimination. Atomic interactions between receptors and Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) molecules are defined but data regarding the plasma membrane remains fragmented. The proposed study asks how molecular clustering manages noise to amplify signals instead of relying on singular binding events. This project of data synthesis integrates tracking of single molecules and microscopy information into multi scale models without new experiments. The analytical approach utilizes coarse grained molecular dynamics in GROMACS and agent based modeling alongside advanced spatial statistics. Validation utilizes hold out testing where models of the resting state predict activated organizations for evaluation via the Bhattacharyya distance. The team will harvest information from the BioImage Archive and EMPIAR alongside databases like SABIO-RK and the Protein Data Bank. Data integration combines a unified schema of ontology with the conversion of lipid abundances into parameters of surface density. The mismatch of structure between records of list based composition and coordinate based information is mitigated by unifying all trajectories. The three year timeline advances from initial curation of data and development of ontology to the final release of platforms. This cross disciplinary collaboration is essential to link lipid chemistry with outcomes of signaling using knowledge from biophysics and immunology. Outputs including an open source simulator and related databases will be deposited into public repositories like GitHub and Zenodo. The team unites a computational biophysicist and a systems immunologist with postdoctoral fellows and a graduate student receiving training.

T-cell receptor (TCR) triggering exhibits remarkable sensitivity and specificity, an emergent property that cannot be explained by simple ligand-receptor binding affinity. We will synthesize lipidomics datasets, single-molecule tracking data of TCR dynamics from the biological literature, and super-resolution microscopy data (STORM/PALM) available in the BioImage Archive. title: Emergent Mechanics of the Cytoskeleton: From Molecular Motors to Cellular Tensegrity
title_norm: emergent mechanics of the cytoskeleton from molecular motors to cellular tensegrity
abstract_text: The field of cellular mechanics investigates how interactions among cytoskeletal components and molecular motors produce cell stiffness and shape stability, bridging established individual protein structures with macroscopic whole cell rheological properties. Because existing models isolate single filament types and oversimplify the cytoplasm, how the mesoscale topological arrangement of multi filament structures translates into macroscopic global stress propagation remains incompletely understood. This project will determine how mesoscale network topology dictates cellular rigidity and phase transitions by extracting mathematical graphs from structural images using geometric deep learning and executing finite element active gel mechanical simulations. Structural images from the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive and the BioImage Archive will be converted into computational graphs, mapped with transcriptomic motor density parameters, and imported into physical simulation software. The resulting computational framework will mathematically reconcile discrete network behavior with continuous whole cell mechanics, shifting predictive mechanotransduction models from biochemical composition variables toward topological structure variables.
full_text: The domain of cellular mechanics investigates how mesoscale topological arrangements of cytoskeletal components translate into macroscopic global stress. Atomic structures of proteins are established but existing models oversimplify the cytoplasm leaving effects of structural heterogeneity unclear. This study investigates how network topology dictates rigidity to shift predictive models from biochemical composition to structural variables. The overall design extracts mathematical graphs from structural imaging data to run mechanical simulations and compare stress fields. The methodology combines geometric deep learning for graph extraction and finite element analysis for simulations of mechanical forces. Simulated stress maps are validated against datasets of traction force microscopy and matched to data from pharmacological interventions. Data sources include the Cytoskeleton Registry and the BioImage Archive alongside specific records from the Protein Data Bank. The team will integrate datasets by mapping parameters of motor density onto computational graphs derived from structural images. Limitations of modeling individual motors are mitigated by applying continuous distributions of active dipole force during simulations. The first year standardizes data pipelines while subsequent years focus on mechanical simulations and refinement of scaling laws. This cross disciplinary collaboration is required to unite expertise in biological imaging with models of mathematical physics. Derived graphs and software code will be deposited in Zenodo while findings are shared via open access publications. The team includes a structural biologist and postdoctoral researchers while offering external training opportunities through organized computational workshops.

We will synthesize data from the Cytoskeleton Registry, cryo-electron tomography of cytoskeletal networks, and traction force microscopy datasets. title: Viral Capsid Polymorphism: Emergent Geometry from Identical Subunits
title_norm: viral capsid polymorphism emergent geometry from identical subunits
abstract_text: In structural virology and computational biophysics, viral capsid polymorphism allows identical coat proteins to self assemble into multiple closed shell geometries, yielding final architectural structures described by existing physical theories. To identify structural determinants of capsid plasticity and predict geometry from monomer topology, this computational project will map assembly energy landscapes and train equivariant graph neural networks utilizing topological data analysis and symmetry aware molecular docking. The project will integrate structural and thermodynamic data from VIPERdb, UniProt, and the Protein Data Bank into a central database, standardizing coordinates to a common icosahedral frame and processing subunit interfaces. This predictive framework will link viral genetic sequences to physical assembly geometry, yielding structural principles applicable to the physical design of protein nanocages and virus like particles.
full_text: This project in structural virology and computational biophysics studies how atomic interfaces dictate geometries of polymorphic viral capsids. The study predicts capsid geometry from monomer topologies to provide structural principles for the design of protein nanocages. This computational synthesis study integrates structural and thermodynamic data to map energy landscapes and train machine learning models. The team applies topological data analysis and molecular docking via HADDOCK2.4 with graph neural networks and literature mining. Validation utilizes negative controls and structural data from after 2023 to correlate calculated energy states with experimental stability. The team extracts information from the Protein Data Bank and VIPERdb and collects thermodynamic records from open access publications. The team integrates these datasets into a central database by aligning structural coordinates to a common icosahedral frame. The team addresses structural inaccuracies by restricting data to resolutions under four Ångströms and applying topological data analysis. The three year project begins with database construction before advancing to model training and the dissemination of results. This cross disciplinary collaboration integrates expertise in structural biology and artificial intelligence to process massive volumes of data. Project outputs feature open access publications and an open source library as well as a public database hosted on Zenodo. The team includes principal investigators and postdoctoral fellows and one graduate student to provide opportunities for cross disciplinary training.

We will synthesize structural data from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) covering a wide range of viral families, along with thermodynamic stability data from literature. The novel question is: What are the hidden 'assembly codes' within the protein interface sequences that allow for emergent geometric flexibility versus rigidity? We will apply geometric deep learning and symmetry-aware molecular docking simulations to map the energy landscapes of capsid assembly. We expect to discover conserved interfacial motifs that act as 'hinges,' allowing emergent curvature variations that facilitate viral evolution and immune evasion. title: The Emergence of Synaptic Memory: Nanocolumns and PSD Stability
title_norm: the emergence of synaptic memory nanocolumns and psd stability
abstract_text: Within neurobiology, the Post Synaptic Density organizes into trans synaptic nanocolumns that align receptor and scaffold protein clusters, serving a vital role because memories persist long term despite rapid synaptic protein turnover. Currently, structural, functional, and proteomic datasets exist in isolation, leaving no unified model to explain how nanocolumn alignment and synaptic stability are maintained during continuous protein turnover. The primary objective will determine how trans synaptic alignment generates stable transmission despite stochastic turnover by integrating existing datasets using computational synthesis, spatial statistics, point cloud to geometric mesh pipelines, reaction diffusion simulations, and Bayesian parameter estimation. Databases including EMPIAR, Allen Brain Institute, CRCNS, and SynaptomeDB will be integrated by converting point cloud coordinates into three dimensional meshes, populating these with kinetic parameters, and executing reaction diffusion models. This project will elucidate the mechanisms of memory stability during molecular turnover, providing a vital mesoscale structural framework to understand synaptic dysfunction across various neurological disorders.
full_text: This neurobiology project investigates the post synaptic density (PSD) because no unified model explains the stability of trans synaptic nanocolumns during protein turnover. Synaptic proteins turn over rapidly while memories persist but current structural and functional and proteomic datasets remain completely isolated. The proposed study investigates how nanocolumn alignment maintains transmission during protein turnover to explain the stability of memory and synaptic dysfunction. The team integrates existing datasets through computational synthesis and mathematical modeling instead of generating new wet lab data. Methods include spatial statistics and Bayesian estimation alongside simulations of reaction diffusion (MCell and BlenderNEURON) across converted geometric meshes. The team validates results by comparing synthetic miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) against empirical data to assess structural parameters. Data sources include structural imaging (BioImage Archive and EMPIAR) and functional records (Allen Brain Institute) and proteomic databases (SynaptomeDB). The team converts spatial coordinates of point clouds into geometric meshes populated with molecular densities to generate synthetic electrophysiological outputs. The difficulty of integrating static coordinates with dynamic traces is mitigated by developing a specialized mesoscale mapping pipeline. The three year project involves data aggregation initially and simulations at a large scale followed by model refinement and final publication. This scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to link static nanostructures with dynamic neural functions across neurobiology and data science. The team shares models and results through open access publications alongside code on GitHub and standardized data on Zenodo. The diverse team of biophysicists and data scientists provides training for early career researchers through annual hackathons and workshops.

Memory is not stored in single molecules but in the emergent stability of these supramolecular assemblies. We will synthesize super-resolution microscopy data of synaptic proteins, electrophysiological datasets (e.g., from the Allen Brain Institute), and proteomic turnover rates. Our hypothesis is that the alignment of presynaptic release sites with postsynaptic receptor nanodomains creates an emergent 'quantal efficiency' that is robust against molecular turnover. We will use reaction-diffusion simulations and stochastic modeling to integrate spatial maps with functional transmission data. Insights will reveal how the brain maintains stable information storage (memory) despite the rapid turnover of individual synaptic proteins, a fundamental paradox of neuroscience. This synthesis requires neurobiologists, biophysicists, and stochastic modelers to bridge the gap between static nanostructure and dynamic neural function.

title: Emergent Selectivity in the Nuclear Pore Complex: A Data-Driven Transport Model
title_norm: emergent selectivity in the nuclear pore complex a datadriven transport model
abstract_text: The Nuclear Pore Complex governs selective transport mechanisms through its intrinsically disordered FG nucleoporin network, constituting an important biological phenomenon established via structural snapshots and single molecule kinetic tracking data. An understanding of how these components interact collectively in a crowded environment remains absent, revealing the lack of a unified physical model explaining this functional permeability barrier. As the primary objective, this project will determine how the mesoscale organization of tethered FG nucleoporins creates a selective transport barrier, synthesizing biophysical data to build a computational model using coarse grained molecular dynamics and machine learning. Researchers will utilize the Protein Data Bank, BioImage Archive, and UniProt, integrating these resources by harmonizing disparate structural coordinates into a unified scaffold and mapping sequences to reference proteomes. The resulting computational framework will elucidate complex transport mechanisms, providing necessary foundational knowledge for downstream investigations into viral entry processes, nuclear targeted drug delivery, and transport related neurodegenerative diseases.
full_text: This project studies selective transport in the Nuclear Pore Complex to explain how disordered proteins form permeability barriers. Current structural snapshots and single molecule tracking data cannot explain collective protein interactions within a crowded cellular environment. The study investigates how mesoscale protein organization creates barriers to inform research on viral entry and neurodegenerative diseases. The team will build a computational model of the pore by synthesizing existing biophysical data without new experiments. The approach utilizes coarse grained molecular dynamics and polymer density functional theory alongside machine learning for interaction parameterization. The team will validate models against a withheld subset of single molecule data and unused cryo-ET density maps. Primary data sources include the Protein Data Bank and the BioImage Archive alongside established repositories like MassIVE and UniProt. The researchers will integrate these sources by harmonizing structural coordinates and translating raw trajectories into unified density maps. The team will mitigate dataset heterogeneity and organism discrepancies through automated coordinate harmonization pipelines and reference proteome standardization. The three year timeline progresses from static scaffold assembly to mathematical modeling and concludes with large scale simulation. This complex scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to unite structural biology with polymer physics and computational data science. The project will deliver open access publications alongside containerized simulation software and integrated models hosted on GitHub repositories. The interdisciplinary team unites senior scientists with postdoctoral fellows and one graduate student while providing training workshops and hackathons.

The NPC acts as a selective gate, an emergent property that functions without energy consumption at the pore itself. We will synthesize structural models of the NPC (PDB-Dev), single-molecule transport kinetics data, and biophysical characterizations of FG-nup phase behavior. The scientific question is how the collective behavior of tethered, disordered proteins creates a 'selective filter' that allows rapid passage of transport factors while excluding inert molecules. We will employ coarse-grained molecular dynamics and polymer density functional theory to model the pore environment based on synthesized structural data. Expected insights include a unified physical model of nucleocytoplasmic transport that explains how mesoscale crowding and weak transient interactions generate emergent gating selectivity. This requires a collaboration between structural biologists, polymer physicists, and computational chemists.

title: Mitochondrial Cristae Morphodynamics and the Emergence of Bioenergetic Efficiency
title_norm: mitochondrial cristae morphodynamics and the emergence of bioenergetic efficiency
abstract_text: The research domain of mitochondrial bioenergetics investigates how the mesoscale geometry of inner membrane cristae affects proton diffusion and ATP synthesis, addressing the inability of bulk gradient theories to explain respiratory efficiency. A critical gap exists because unintegrated static structural data and tomographic data prevent the development of quantitative models explaining how mesoscale membrane geometry influences local proton diffusion kinetics. This project will determine how membrane curvature dictates respiratory chain organization and whether cristae junctions trap protons by applying computational tools like RELION and COMSOL Multiphysics to construct three dimensional geometric models and simulate functions. The study will segment tomographic data from the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive into three dimensional meshes and map atomic structures from the Protein Data Bank onto these meshes using subtomogram averaging coordinates. This research will establish a quantitative biophysical link between mesoscale membrane architecture and metabolic output, providing a structural basis to understand pathological metabolic changes in aging and disease.
full_text: The field of mitochondrial bioenergetics lacks quantitative models for explaining how geometry of membranes influences kinetics for diffusion of protons. Researchers possess static structural models of cristae but lack integration of these datasets for analyzing dynamic bioenergetic functions. The primary question explores how curvature of membranes organizes respiratory chains to provide models for understanding metabolic diseases. The overall design utilizes a computational approach to construct geometric models of mitochondria and simulate dynamic bioenergetic functions. The team will apply software tools including IMOD and FEniCS to solve equations of Nernst-Planck for bioenergetic simulations. The team will validate these computational results by comparing production of ATP against published rates for consumption of oxygen. The project will utilize datasets from the Protein Data Bank and the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR). Researchers will segment images from EMPIAR into meshes and map structural coordinates from the databases onto these geometric structures. The study relies exclusively on existing datasets and mitigates this limitation by validating simulations against published records of phenotypes. The timeline spans three years to develop pipelines for segmentation before executing simulations and publishing the finalized databases. This broad scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to unite expertise in structural biology with modeling of reaction diffusion. The project will release an open access database and provide all simulation code through repositories on GitHub and Zenodo. The team unites postdoctoral fellows with a graduate student to provide educational training through an interactive modeling workshop.

title: Ribosome Collisions and the Emergence of Translational Quality Control
title_norm: ribosome collisions and the emergence of translational quality control
abstract_text: The molecular biology and biophysics domains focus on the mesoscale phenomenon of ribosome collisions and translational bursting on mRNA because specific collision geometries initiate essential quality control pathways. Current research lacks a unified physical model connecting mRNA sequence information to mesoscale ribosome traffic dynamics to quantitatively understand how structural collision states determine specific signaling outcomes. This computational project will determine how local sequence landscapes dictate ribosome jamming probabilities and signaling outcomes by applying footprint to structure mapping, unsupervised machine learning, and totally asymmetric simple exclusion process simulations. The research will integrate Protein Data Bank structural data to categorize NCBI SRA ribosome profiling reads by length and combine these mapped footprints with transfer RNA abundance data to parameterize the simulations. This work will establish a dynamic model of translational flow to elucidate congestion principles for optimizing transgene design and identifying transcript features implicated in neurodegenerative diseases.
full_text: Biophysics lacks unified physical models connecting availability of tRNA and sequence information to translational bursting and ribosome collisions. Current models use mean field approximations of codon optimality but lack quantitative knowledge regarding density of ribosomes and structural states. The study determines how sequence landscapes dictate probabilities of jamming to optimize design of transgenes and understand neurodegenerative diseases. This computational synthesis project integrates existing transcriptomic and structural data to build predictive models of traffic without wet lab experiments. Researchers will apply Nextflow genomic workflows and unsupervised machine learning models alongside the Totally Asymmetric Simple Exclusion Process (TASEP). The team will validate results via cross validation by training models on control states and testing on different cell types. The project utilizes structural data from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and transcriptomic information from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). Researchers will combine mapped structural footprints with usage of codons and abundance of tRNA to parameterize simulations of TASEP. The team will mitigate disparities in pipelines of public data by implementing a uniform Nextflow workflow to normalize raw reads. The three year timeline encompasses construction of data pipelines before development of models and creation of a web portal. The project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to integrate expertise across genomics and structural biology for analysis of heterogeneous datasets. The team will release an open access database mirrored on Zenodo alongside an open source package and public workshops. The multidisciplinary team contains principal investigators and early career researchers who will receive direct mentorship during the proposed project.

While translation is often modeled as a linear process, ribosomes frequently form 'traffic jams' at the mesoscale, which serve as emergent signals for mRNA degradation or protein folding stress. We will synthesize ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) data, cryo-EM structures of colliding ribosomes, and transcriptomic decay rates. The novel hypothesis is that the spatial patterning of ribosome queues acts as a mesoscale sensor for cellular stress, integrating codon usage bias and tRNA availability into a collective decision-making process. We will develop analytical models of traffic flow on mRNA tracks to predict collision probabilities and link them to cellular outcomes found in public datasets. We expect to reveal how the cell utilizes the emergent statistics of ribosome traffic to regulate proteostasis. This requires the synthesis of genomics, structural biology, and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.

title: Emergent Synchronization in Ciliary Arrays: Hydrodynamics and Coupling
title_norm: emergent synchronization in ciliary arrays hydrodynamics and coupling
abstract_text: Cellular biophysics research investigates metachronal waves and coordinated beating patterns in dense arrays of cilia, phenomena where molecular structures and hydrodynamic coupling drive crucial macroscopic fluid transport. The underlying mechanisms driving independent cilia to spontaneously synchronize remain undetermined because current fluid dynamics models do not incorporate biological variables like ciliary stiffness, waveform asymmetry, and mucus rheology. This project will determine how structural stiffness, fluid rheology, and hydrodynamic coupling control emergent synchronization by parameterizing multi scale physics models that integrate computer vision architectures, finite element analysis, and computational fluid dynamics. Structural records from the Protein Data Bank and ClinVar will establish mechanical stiffness, while computer vision pipelines will extract time series kinematic data from BioImage Archive videos to parameterize combined hydrodynamic simulations. This research will produce biologically parameterized models to identify causes of synchronization failure in ciliopathies, enabling the prediction of disease phenotypes directly from structural defect data.
full_text: This project in cellular biophysics explores metachronal waves of cilia to integrate structural data and uncover mechanisms of synchronization. The structure of axonemes and hydrodynamic coupling are known but current models of fluids omit stiffness and rheology. The study investigates how structural stiffness and the rheology of fluids control synchronization to predict the phenotypes of hydrocephalus. The strategy extracts kinematic and rheological data to parameterize a multi scale model for simulating the synchronization of waves. Key tools include OMERO for standardization and U-Net architectures for segmentation alongside elastic rod models to represent mechanical properties. The team validates results through leave one out cross validation and benchmarks predicted rates of flow against clinical records. The utilized datasets include the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and ClinVar alongside supplementary videos of microscopy from previous publications. Computations of mechanical stiffness integrate with time series data from video pipelines to parameterize forces in the simulation of fluids. The raw videos exhibit heterogeneous resolutions so researchers will build a standardization pipeline using OMERO to convert the formats. The three year timeline advances from data harvesting to the development and final validation of the coupled model of hydrodynamics. Linking information about molecular structures to macroscopic waveforms within physics based simulations requires cross disciplinary collaboration across multiple fields. The team will release an open source framework and public databases alongside open access publications to disseminate all findings. Principal investigators and postdoctoral fellows will collaborate with a graduate assistant to provide cross disciplinary training in computational physics.

We will synthesize high-speed video microscopy data of ciliary beating, structural data of the axoneme (PDB), and fluid dynamics parameters. Our hypothesis is that emergent synchronization is robust to noise and individual defects due to long-range hydrodynamic interactions at the mesoscale. We will use computational fluid dynamics (CFD) coupled with elastic rod models to simulate ciliary fields. Insights will explain how biological systems achieve robust fluid transport and how defects in this emergent synchronization lead to ciliopathies. This necessitates a transdisciplinary team of fluid dynamicists, cell biologists, and computational physicists.

title: The Extracellular Matrix as a Mechanical Memory: Emergent Reciprocity in Tissue Homeostasis
title_norm: the extracellular matrix as a mechanical memory emergent reciprocity in tissue homeostasis
abstract_text: Mechanobiology investigates the dynamic reciprocity between cells and the extracellular matrix, highlighting the critical importance of mechanical memory accumulation within mesoscale architecture for understanding macroscopic tissue properties. The mechanisms of structural memory remain undefined, as it is not understood how molecular gene expression of remodeling enzymes translates into mesoscale fiber architecture to drive emergent tissue mechanics. This project will determine the conditions required to convert transient enzyme expression into permanent mechanical topology by harmonizing public datasets to parameterize multiscale computational models utilizing agent based modeling and finite element analysis. Data from the Gene Expression Omnibus, BioImage Archive, and atomic force microscopy repositories will be integrated through spatial registration and deconvolution algorithms to construct digital volumes with voxels containing multidimensional parameter vectors. This research will produce a mechanistic framework connecting molecular inputs to mesoscale properties, providing structural explanations for self sustaining fibrotic disease and collective cell migration dynamics.
full_text: The study focuses on mechanobiology and how expression of remodeling enzymes translates into architecture of the extracellular matrix (ECM). While molecular components and macroscopic properties are known the lack of data integration leaves mechanisms of structural memory undefined. The proposed study asks how transient expression becomes permanent topology to provide a mechanistic model of self sustaining fibrosis. The study synthesizes heterogeneous public datasets to parameterize and validate a multiscale computational model of the extracellular matrix. The analytical approach utilizes a Common Coordinate Framework alongside modeling via FEniCS and PhysiCell to simulate behaviors of cells. The team will validate results through leave one out cross validation by testing architectural predictions against late stage datasets. The proposed project incorporates public databases including the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and the Human Cell Atlas (HCA). The team will integrate datasets by registering spatial transcriptomics and histological imaging to construct a digital volume of tissue. The study resolves gaps in spatial resolution by deploying algorithms to map profiles of expression onto spatial tissue atlases. The three year timeline encompasses initial acquisition of data followed by model calibration and the release of public tools. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to accurately translate molecular transcriptomic data into physical parameters for the computational simulations. The team will share open source software via GitHub and Docker alongside open access publications and community training workshops. The team comprises computational postdoctoral fellows and a graduate student who will train through cross disciplinary data sprints.

The ECM is not a static scaffold but a dynamic mesoscale material that accumulates 'mechanical memory' through remodeling, influencing future cell behavior. We will synthesize atomic force microscopy (AFM) maps of tissue stiffness, RNA-seq data of matrix-remodeling enzymes, and histological imaging. The central question is how local remodeling events integrate over time to create emergent stiffness gradients that guide cell migration and differentiation. We will employ agent-based models where cells modify a finite-element mesh (the ECM) based on local strain, creating a feedback loop. Expected insights include understanding how fibrosis emerges as a runaway feedback loop of this mechanical memory. This project requires NCEMS support to unite tissue engineers, data scientists, and mechanobiologists.

title: The Glycocalyx Code: Emergent Immune Evasion via Bulky Glycan Shields
title_norm: the glycocalyx code emergent immune evasion via bulky glycan shields
abstract_text: The cell surface glycocalyx exhibits emergent biophysical properties that regulate immune cell access to tumor cells, yet research across glycobiology and immunology remains disconnected despite known upregulation of bulky glycoproteins. Consequently, the macroscopic physical barrier function of the glycocalyx remains uncharacterized, leaving a critical gap in understanding how collective physical properties mechanically exclude immune receptors independently of chemical recognition. To determine how glycosyltransferase transcription drives glycocalyx density and immune exclusion, this project will apply neural network machine learning and coarse grained molecular dynamics simulations within a custom Python package to calculate biophysical barrier scores. The study will integrate paired transcriptomic and mass spectrometry glycomic data from sources including The Cancer Genome Atlas and GlyGen to train predictive structural models providing input parameters for polymer physics simulations. This research will produce a biophysical barrier score establishing an immune evasion mechanism challenging standard protein centric models that could explain immunotherapy failure despite high tumor mutational burdens.
full_text: This study explores how the cell surface glycocalyx creates a mechanical barrier to immune receptors without chemical recognition. Current knowledge details enzymatic glycosylation pathways and receptor interactions but leaves the macroscopic physical barrier function completely uncharacterized. Predicting immunotherapy failure through a biophysical barrier score reveals novel immune evasion mechanisms challenging standard models of immunology. This study synthesizes public data by applying machine learning to transcriptomics and modeling physical repulsion of immune receptors. Key analytical methods utilize neural networks and molecular dynamics alongside polymer simulations within a custom package named GlycoPhysics. Validation involves correlating biophysical barrier scores with spatial exclusion in pathology images and stratifying patients using clinical data. The project utilizes datasets including The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and Protein Data Bank (PDB) alongside other repositories. The team will integrate datasets by training machine learning models on paired transcriptomic and mass spectrometry information from cell lines. These integrated predictions of the glycocalyx structure will subsequently serve as input parameters for the polymer physics simulations. The three year timeline encompasses model development followed by physics simulations and concludes with clinical validation and deployment. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to integrate methodologies from computational glycobiology and soft matter physics alongside immunology. Open science initiatives include releasing an open access database alongside an open source software tool and summer school. The team combines principal investigators and a programmer with trainees in physics and immunology while providing training opportunities.

We hypothesize that the physical height and density of the glycocalyx act as a 'kinetic trap' for immune receptors, an emergent biophysical barrier distinct from chemical recognition. We will synthesize glycomics data, atomic force microscopy measurements of cell surface height, and immune cell adhesion assays. By modeling the steric repulsion and thermodynamic entropy of the polymer brush layer using the synthesized data, we aim to predict immune evasion thresholds. Insights will reveal how cancer cells exploit this emergent physical barrier to evade T-cell attack, offering new perspectives for immunotherapy. This requires a synthesis of glycobiology, polymer physics, and immunology.

title: Symmetry Breaking in the Centrosome: Emergent Spindle Bipolarity
title_norm: symmetry breaking in the centrosome emergent spindle bipolarity
abstract_text: Cell biology and biophysics research investigates centrosome separation and symmetry breaking during bipolar mitotic spindle assembly, which constitutes a critical bistable system driven by molecular components including Eg5, Nek2, and pericentrin. This project will determine quantitative thresholds and network topologies governing monopolar to bipolar spindle transitions through a data synthesis approach utilizing a graph database, Graph Neural Networks, and differential equations for dynamical systems modeling and bifurcation analysis. The research will integrate MitoCheck, BioGRID, PhosphoSitePlus, and DepMap datasets into a graph database linking physical interactions weighted by phosphorylation and spatially constrained by imaging data to supply dynamical model parameters. This research will provide a quantitative multi scale model of centrosome symmetry breaking to predict spindle failures and explain mechanisms of centrosome amplification and chromosomal instability in cancer.
full_text: Although components (Eg5 and pericentrin) are known the exact force thresholds and influence of pericentriolar material phase separation remain unclear. This project evaluates thresholds of spindle states to model mechanisms of centrosome amplification and chromosomal instability in cancer. The overall design features a three phase approach of data curation and mathematical modeling using only public datasets. The analytical strategy applies Graph Neural Networks and differential equations alongside MATCONT software for the analysis of bifurcations. The project validates results by comparing simulated protein knockdowns against RNAi and CRISPR screening data targeting F1 scores above 0.8. The proposed study utilizes multiple public databases including MitoCheck and BioGRID alongside resources from The Cancer Genome Atlas. The team integrates these resources into a graph database linking protein interactions to supply parameters for mathematical modeling. The project mitigates the limitation of missing edge weights by deploying Graph Neural Networks to impute required values. The thirty month timeline encompasses initial data curation before proceeding to mathematical modeling and a final validation phase. The ambitious scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration merging expertise from cell biology with theoretical physics and computational biology. The project shares mathematical models on BioModels and harmonized datasets on Zenodo while publishing open access research findings. The research team unites three distinct laboratories and includes two full time postdoctoral fellows alongside one graduate student.

The centrosome, a mesoscale organelle, must duplicate and separate to define the axis of division. We will synthesize high-content screening image data of mitosis, phosphoproteomic time-course data, and protein interaction networks. The hypothesis is that the transition from a monopolar to a bipolar state is an emergent bifurcation driven by a threshold in motor protein forces and kinase activity gradients. We will use dynamical systems theory to model the stability landscape of spindle poles based on integrated molecular data. We expect to identify the critical control parameters that ensure robust symmetry breaking, a process that fails in cancer. This requires cell biologists, mathematicians, and image analysis experts.

title: Autophagosome Biogenesis: Emergent Membrane Remodeling from Protein Scaffolds
title_norm: autophagosome biogenesis emergent membrane remodeling from protein scaffolds
abstract_text: Autophagosome formation entails the physical transformation of a flat cellular membrane into a closed vesicle originating from omegasomes, representing a critical biophysical phenomenon where individual component structures are established. To determine how protein density induces curvature and lipid mechanics prevent membrane collapse, this project will synthesize diverse structural and fluorescence datasets into biophysical models using spatial registration, graph neural networks, and phase field simulations. Atomic structures from the Protein Data Bank and AlphaFold Database will be mapped to electron density volumes, and fluorescence density fields will be integrated onto a canonical triangulated mesh representing the membrane surface. This project will yield quantitative models of membrane mechanics detailing vesicle closure energetics, thereby transitioning the field beyond qualitative observations to provide physical variables for neurodegenerative disease research.
full_text: This project investigates the biophysics of autophagosome formation to explain how transient interactions generate curvature and drive vesicle sealing. The study asks how proteins and lipids govern curvature and closure energetics to provide quantitative models for research on neurodegenerative diseases. The overall study design synthesizes diverse structural and fluorescence datasets to build a biophysical model of changes in membrane shape. The team will apply spatial registration algorithms and graph neural networks to generate triangulated meshes and phase field simulations. Results will be validated by comparing predicted curvature against cryo-ET data and by testing yeast models against mammalian datasets. This project will utilize databases including the Protein Data Bank and AlphaFold Database alongside BioGRID and the Image Data Resource. Spatial registration will map atomic structures to volumes of electron density while integrating fluorescence fields onto a canonical triangulated mesh. Graph neural networks will predict protein clustering from interaction networks to mitigate the static nature of existing structural data. The three year timeline encompasses the construction of static models followed by dynamic model development and cross validation through workshops. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to integrate biological data into physical models using expertise from cell biologists and biophysicists. The team will publish in open access journals and share code via the BioModels Database and a public web portal. The team comprises cell biologists and biophysicists to train postdoctoral researchers and graduate students through an external summer school.

We will synthesize data on Atg protein interactions, membrane curvature sensing, and lipid composition during starvation responses. We will employ Helfrich bending energy models coupled with protein density fields derived from fluorescence microscopy data. Insights will elucidate the energetic requirements for this mesoscale remodeling and how it is regulated by cellular energy states. This synthesis needs membrane biophysicists, autophagy researchers, and computational geometers.

title: Stress Granules vs. P-Bodies: Emergent Sorting in RNA Phase Separation
title_norm: stress granules vs pbodies emergent sorting in rna phase separation
abstract_text: Cellular biology and soft matter physics highlight the critical importance of selective RNA sorting between distinct liquid liquid phase separated ribonucleoprotein condensates, specifically Stress Granules and Processing Bodies with known transcriptomes. Current research lacks a unified physical framework explaining the mesoscale thermodynamic rules that prevent interacting liquid phases from mixing because existing data is fragmented across differing experimental conditions. This project will determine the sequence based structural rules and thermodynamic principles governing RNA partitioning by utilizing Nextflow bioinformatics pipelines, graph neural network classifiers, and multicomponent Flory Huggins solution theory to model phase behavior computationally. Raw sequencing data from repositories including Gene Expression Omnibus, ENCODE, and PRIDE will be processed through a uniform pipeline and mapped into a unified graph database linking molecular sequences and phase behavior metrics. Defining these mesoscale RNA sorting rules will establish a crucial foundation for understanding membraneless cellular organization, stress induced gene regulation, and pathological aggregation mechanisms in neurodegenerative diseases.
full_text: This project bridges cellular biology and soft matter physics to determine physical frameworks for sorting RNA into condensates. Fragmented experimental data obscures the mechanisms of RNA sorting between well characterized structures like Stress Granules and Processing Bodies. The study defines how thermodynamic rules govern RNA partitioning to elucidate cellular organization and pathological aggregation during disease. The study synthesizes public datasets through bioinformatics and machine learning to model RNA localization and thermodynamic phase behavior. The analytical approach applies pipelines for sequence processing and a graph database alongside neural networks to predict localization patterns. The team will validate results through cross validation and direct benchmarking against independent datasets such as APEX-seq records. The proposed study will analyze public records from established repositories including the Gene Expression Omnibus and ArrayExpress databases. The project integrates these datasets by processing raw data and mapping all molecular entities into a single database. The team will mitigate batch effects from disparate mapping protocols by reprocessing information through a standardized computational pipeline. The three year timeline dedicates early phases to data ingestion and later years to model training and refinement. The project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to successfully merge transcriptomics and machine learning models with soft matter physics. The team will publish findings in open access journals and host predictive models within an open source package. The core team includes postdoctoral fellows and a graduate student while organizing workshops for the technical training of experimentalists.

Current research lacks a unified physical framework explaining the mesoscale thermodynamic rules that prevent interacting liquid phases from mixing because existing data is fragmented across differing experimental conditions. This project will determine the sequence based structural rules and thermodynamic principles governing RNA partitioning by utilizing Nextflow bioinformatics pipelines, graph neural network classifiers, and multicomponent Flory Huggins solution theory to model phase behavior computationally. Raw sequencing data from repositories including Gene Expression Omnibus, ENCODE, and PRIDE will be processed through a uniform pipeline and mapped into a unified graph database linking molecular sequences and phase behavior metrics. We will use multicomponent Flory-Huggins solution theory adapted for sequence-specific interactions to model the sorting behavior. title: Collapse of the Chaperone Network: Emergent Proteostasis Failure in Aging
title_norm: collapse of the chaperone network emergent proteostasis failure in aging
abstract_text: The research domain encompasses the chaperone protein network and the systemic failure of protein folding during aging, which is critical for explaining the nonlinear dynamics of network wide proteostasis collapse. Although studies catalog individual protein folding thermodynamics, the field lacks quantitative models explaining how cellular chaperone networks operate collectively at the mesoscale to drive sudden systemic failure. To determine if chaperone networks undergo percolation phase transitions and identify critical nodes, this project will construct capacity constrained flow network models utilizing weighted graph generation, Monte Carlo simulations, and the Newman Ziff algorithm. The analysis will integrate proteomics and interaction data from PRIDE, BioGRID, and AlphaFold DB into a relational database using Uniprot identifiers, synthesizing weighted interaction graphs from abundance estimates and physical binding affinities. This mechanistic phase transition framework will provide a quantitative metric for aging related cellular failure, identifying structural network targets for therapeutic intervention to prevent systemic collapse.
