title: Emergent Antibiotic Resistance in Biofilms: The Role of Matrix Architecture
title_norm: emergent antibiotic resistance in biofilms the role of matrix architecture
abstract_text: In physical microbiology, the mesoscale architecture of the extracellular polymeric substance matrix governs antibiotic tolerance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus, presenting a critical phenomenon determining bacterial survival during antimicrobial exposure. The causal relationship between biofilm spatial assembly and bacterial resistance phenotypes remains unestablished because prior studies isolate structural imaging data from transcriptomic data. To determine how mesoscale topology generates physical and chemical gradients dictating antibiotic tolerance, this computational data synthesis project will integrate multimodal measurements using convolutional neural networks, metabolic modeling, and reaction diffusion simulations. Structural geometries from the BioImage Archive and literature derived diffusion coefficients will drive multiphysics simulations, which will map physical gradients against local chemical environments inferred from Sequence Read Archive transcriptomic data. This systems level framework will identify protective matrix features and will transition antimicrobial research to a physical model informing the design of therapeutic adjuvants that disrupt spatial architecture.
full_text: A critical gap in physical microbiology is how mesoscale assembly of the extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix determines antibiotic tolerance. Current hypotheses emphasize diffusion barriers and metabolic heterogeneity but understanding of links between spatial architecture and physiology remains incomplete. The proposed study investigates how topology of the EPS matrix generates gradients to dictate tolerance and inform design of therapeutics. This project integrates structural imaging and profiles of transcriptomics into a unified framework for modeling without acquiring new data. The team will utilize convolutional neural networks for segmentation of images and Flux Balance Analysis for modeling metabolism. The team will validate predictions of transport using data from fluorescence recovery and evaluate models of survival with separate data. Researchers will source data from the BioImage Archive and the Gene Expression Omnibus alongside literature databases like PubMed. The team will simulate physical gradients using geometries of images to map environments inferred from data of transcriptomics. The project will mitigate background noise and sparse annotations of images by training convolutional neural networks for segmentation. Over a timeline of three years the team will curate data before constructing models and validating the theoretical framework. Cross disciplinary collaboration is necessary to merge physical and biological perspectives for interpretation of emergence at the mesoscale. The researchers will publish findings in open access journals while sharing code through GitHub and data on Zenodo. The team includes principal investigators and postdoctoral fellows alongside graduate students receiving training in techniques of physical microbiology.

title: GPCR Oligomerization Landscapes: Emergent Signaling Bias via Allostery
title_norm: gpcr oligomerization landscapes emergent signaling bias via allostery
abstract_text: The research domain of G protein coupled receptor oligomerization explores how receptor organization into dimers and nanoclusters modulates trafficking, ligand binding cooperativity, and emergent signaling bias to control pharmacological outcomes. A unified framework integrating fragmented structural and dynamic data remains lacking, preventing the determination of how specific interface geometries dictate allosteric cross talk and drive mesoscale signaling bias. This project will determine how oligomer geometry alters allosteric pathways to create emergent signaling profiles by synthesizing existing data through knowledge graphs, Markov state models, graph neural networks, and thermodynamic mass action models. The study will integrate Protein Data Bank, GPCRdb, ChEMBL, and Human Cell Atlas datasets into a knowledge graph by normalizing pharmacological data into uniform bias factors and harmonizing sequences using generic numbering. This framework will identify conserved interface codes to explain different pharmacological profiles between recombinant monomeric systems and native tissues, and will enable the design of drugs targeting specific oligomeric states.
full_text: This project investigates G protein coupled receptor (GPCR) oligomerization and emergent signaling bias to integrate fragmented mesoscale data. The primary research question asks how oligomer geometry alters allosteric pathways to enable the design of state specific drugs. The study design synthesizes existing structural and pharmacological data through computational modeling to link oligomer populations to signaling outputs. Key methods include knowledge graphs and Markov State Models (MSMs) alongside Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and thermodynamic models. Results will be validated by correlating simulated stability metrics with literature bias factors and tissue specific drug response data. The project will utilize datasets from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and ChEMBL alongside Human Cell Atlas transcriptomics data. Distinct datasets will be integrated by constructing a knowledge graph and harmonizing sequence data through generic numbering schemes. The team will mitigate the limitation of data fragmentation by normalizing diverse pharmacological values into uniform bias factors. The three year timeline includes knowledge graph construction before training neural networks and concluding with external validation efforts. This broad scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to merge expertise in structural biology with computational chemistry and pharmacology. The researchers will release an open access database and an open source software package alongside public scientific publications. The team includes specialists and early career researchers who will receive training through synthesis hackathons and virtual sessions.

title: Nuclear Speckles as Splicing Hubs: Emergent Amplification of Gene Expression
title_norm: nuclear speckles as splicing hubs emergent amplification of gene expression
abstract_text: Within the domain of nuclear biology, nuclear speckles are phase separated condensates containing splicing factors that play a crucial role in altering RNA splicing efficiency through spatial organization. The open scientific gap is the quantitative relationship between physical distance to nuclear speckles and RNA splicing rates, because existing data remain unsynthesized regarding how proximity impacts processing kinetics. The primary objective will determine if spatial distance dictates splicing efficiency for multi intron genes across cell types by integrating secondary data utilizing generalized additive models, graph neural networks, and biophysical two phase kinetic modeling. Genomic, transcriptomic, and super resolution microscopy datasets from ENCODE and 4D Nucleome Data Portal will merge into a unified vector structure associating speckle distance scores with splicing and transcription rates. This research will output a novel framework demonstrating whether three dimensional spatial positioning relative to nuclear bodies serves as an independent variable predicting RNA processing beyond linear DNA sequences.
full_text: This project in nuclear biology investigates the quantitative relationship between the spatial distance to nuclear speckles and RNA splicing efficiency. Current data show nuclear speckles are phase separated condensates but lack synthesis explaining how physical proximity impacts processing kinetics. The proposed study examines if spatial distance regulates splicing to establish three dimensional position as an independent regulatory variable. The overall design involves secondary data synthesis of two cell lines to correlate spatial distances with splicing kinetics. Key methods feature generalized additive models for spatial statistics and graph neural networks for the prediction of splicing. The team validates predictive models using leave one chromosome out cross validation and testing against a third cell line. Datasets include sequencing records from the ENCODE Project and the 4D Nucleome Data Portal alongside super resolution microscopy archives. Researchers merge these datasets into a unified vector structure associating the distance score of each gene with splicing efficiency. The team mitigates technical noise and batch effects from multi modal integration through the application of combat-seq tools. The two year timeline progresses from data curation to the development of biophysical models and final manuscript preparation. This project demands cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in spatial statistics and RNA biology for data interpretation. The team will release an open access database and computational toolkits alongside peer reviewed publications via public repositories. The research group includes principal investigators and postdoctoral fellows providing direct training and a virtual data integration workshop.

title: Thylakoid Stacking and the Emergence of Photosynthetic Robustness
title_norm: thylakoid stacking and the emergence of photosynthetic robustness
abstract_text: Plant thylakoid membrane mesoscale stacking represents a crucial physical mechanism regulating energy distribution between photosystems to maintain light harvesting, and molecular structures of individual photosynthetic components are known at near atomic resolution. However, structural studies lack corresponding functional data, and existing functional models rely on simplified geometric assumptions rather than physical structures to explain how three dimensional restructuring produces light harvesting robustness. The project will determine how grana geometry modulates excitonic networks by extracting physical geometries via image segmentation tools, populating them using protein packing algorithms, and simulating quantum energy transfer across these integrated composite structures. Structural image data from public microscopy archives will be segmented into three dimensional meshes and populated with atomic structures guided by proteomics databases to create digital models correlated with time resolved data. This research will yield a physical model linking mesoscale membrane geometry to quantum efficiency, offering vital structural data to inform artificial photosynthetic systems and stress tolerant agricultural crops.
full_text: This study investigates membranes of plant thylakoids to understand how physical restructuring regulates the distribution of energy during fluctuating light. High resolution structures for components of photosynthesis are known but existing models rely on simplified assumptions of geometry. The research investigates how geometry of the membrane modulates excitonic networks to inform development of crops that tolerate stress. The team will extract physical geometries from image data to simulate the transfer of excitonic energy across these composite models. Key methods include algorithms for image segmentation and tools for protein packing alongside machine learning and modeling of excitonic networks. Computational predictions of energy transfer will be benchmarked against a curated database of historical measurements from experimental spectroscopy. The project integrates databases like the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and the Gene Expression Omnibus with custom data from spectroscopy. Image data of structures will be segmented into surface meshes and populated with atomic structures of proteins using data from proteomics. Researchers will overcome the lack of a centralized repository for spectroscopy data by manually curating information from published literature. The three year schedule includes building a repository of data before executing simulations of energy transfer and performing cross validation. This project requires expertise across disciplines in structural biology and quantum biophysics to connect biological contexts with physical models. The team will publish findings in journals with open access and deposit outputs from simulations in repositories like Zenodo. The team includes principal investigators and postdoctoral researchers who will lead a virtual workshop for scientists at early career stages.

title: Exosome Loading and Sorting: Emergent Communication Packets
title_norm: exosome loading and sorting emergent communication packets
abstract_text: The research domain of extracellular vesicles investigates selective cargo loading into exosomes 30 to 150 nanometers in size, where sorting mechanisms involving physical membrane properties require validation across diverse biological cell types. A specific scientific gap exists regarding the rules governing molecule inclusion during exosome cargo sorting due to a disconnect between biological content catalogs and unvalidated biophysical phase separation models. This computational data synthesis project will construct a unified biophysical model of exosome sorting by harmonizing multi omics datasets into a Neo4j graph database to perform biophysical feature extraction, Helfrich Hamiltonian thermodynamic modeling, and machine learning classification. The project will integrate datasets including ExoCarta, Vesiclepedia, and AlphaFold DB within the graph database using UniProt primary keys and algorithms that normalize mass spectrometry spectral counts against housekeeping proteins. This work will yield a mechanistic biophysical framework determining universal sorting codes, establishing knowledge necessary for understanding metastasis, interpreting liquid biopsies, and engineering targeted therapeutic delivery vectors.
full_text: This project examines extracellular vesicles to connect biological catalogs with physical models for selective loading into small exosomes. Current models connect exosome biogenesis to physical membrane properties but hypotheses about lipid phase separation require broader biological validation. The study seeks a universal biophysical sorting code to provide a mechanistic framework for engineering targeted therapeutic delivery. This computational synthesis project harmonizes multiple omics and structural datasets into a graph database for classification by machine learning. The proposed approach relies upon a Neo4j database alongside Python libraries and Helfrich Hamiltonian models for feature extraction. The team will validate results by achieving high classification accuracy and comparing simulated in silico knockouts against published experiments. The study extracts structural and biological information from public repositories including ExoCarta and the Protein Data Bank (PDB). The researchers will map these distinct datasets into a graph database using primary identifiers and spectral normalization algorithms. The researchers will resolve varying data quality and missing structural information through strict filtering and the generation of computational models. The three year timeline advances from initial database construction through thermodynamic modeling before concluding with validation via machine learning. This complex scope requires diverse collaboration to integrate specialized scientific expertise across vesicle biology and artificial intelligence disciplines. title: Synthetic Cell Assembly: Predicting Emergent Life-like Behaviors from Component Integration
title_norm: synthetic cell assembly predicting emergent lifelike behaviors from component integration
abstract_text: The bottom up synthetic biology domain investigates the minimal requirements for emergent behaviors such as motility and division in synthetic cells, requiring an integrated mesoscale understanding of kinetic, structural, and omics data. Currently, the field lacks the ability to predict emergent system failures, such as membrane lysis and transcription stalling, that occur when integrating isolated genetic and membrane components. This project will synthesize existing data to train machine learning models predicting system stability through a computational meta synthesis that will integrate metabolic flux and biophysical membrane models utilizing graph neural networks, physics informed neural networks, and Bayesian inference. Datasets from the BioModels Database, BRENDA, LipidMaps, and SynBioHub will be integrated by standardizing metadata to construct a knowledge graph mapping molecular components and interactions weighted by kinetic parameters derived from literature. The resulting predictive framework will transition synthetic cell construction from trial and error processes to rational design and identify fundamental biophysical constraints relevant to self replication and life origins.
full_text: The proposed study examines minimal requirements for emergent cellular behaviors to resolve unpredictable system failures in bottom up synthetic biology. Existing knowledge includes structural data on liposomes and omics data but lacks an integrated understanding of interactions at the mesoscale. This project trains machine learning models to predict system stability and identify fundamental biophysical constraints for the origins of life. The overall design is a computational synthesis of public data integrating models of metabolic flux and biophysical membranes. Key methods include Bayesian inference and neural networks alongside the standardization of metadata using the Synthetic Biology Open Language. The team validates results computationally through cross validation by evaluating predictions against unpublished negative data from failed experimental constructs. This project uses multiple public datasets from the BioModels Database and SynBioHub alongside community repositories like the PRIDE archives. The team integrates these datasets by standardizing metadata to construct a knowledge graph of molecular components weighted by kinetic parameters. The project mitigates data sparsity and heterogeneity in formats through Bayesian inference and the manual extraction of negative results. This project spans two years and six months to complete data harvesting before finalizing model training and computational validation. rephrased_abstract: The bottom up synthetic biology domain investigates the minimal requirements for emergent behaviors such as motility and division in synthetic cells, requiring an integrated mesoscale understanding of kinetic, structural, and omics data. Currently, the field lacks the ability to predict emergent system failures, such as membrane lysis and transcription stalling, that occur when integrating isolated genetic and membrane components. This project will synthesize existing data to train machine learning models predicting system stability through a computational meta synthesis that will integrate metabolic flux and biophysical membrane models utilizing graph neural networks, physics informed neural networks, and Bayesian inference. Datasets from the BioModels Database, BRENDA, LipidMaps, and SynBioHub will be integrated by standardizing metadata to construct a knowledge graph mapping molecular components and interactions weighted by kinetic parameters derived from literature. The resulting predictive framework will transition synthetic cell construction from trial and error processes to rational design and identify fundamental biophysical constraints relevant to self replication and life origins.
abstract_original: This final project proposes a meta-synthesis of data from 'bottom-up' synthetic biology to understand the minimal requirements for emergent life-like behaviors (motility, division, homeostasis). We will synthesize data from disparate synthetic cell projects (e.g., liposome encapsulation, minimal genome reconstitution). The goal is to train machine learning models to predict which combinations of modules (energy, information, containment) yield emergent system-level stability vs. collapse. This is the ultimate test of understanding emergence: can we predict the transition from non-living matter to a living system? This requires a broad coalition of synthetic biologists, systems theorists, and AI researchers to define the design rules of life at the mesoscale.
